examples.name: path-expression
examples.title: Function plot with pathExpression
examples.summary: The curve y = sin(x)·e^(−x/4) over two periods, sampled into one smooth path by pathExpression and stroked over faint axes.
examples.prompt: Plot the function y = sin(x)·e^(−x/4) as a smooth curve over faint axes.
examples.hand_built: Plotting a function with pathExpression is the lesson; for a graph with axes, ticks and marked roots and extremes use MathPlot, or LineChart with fn.
teaches: Plot a function as one path with pathExpression: expressionX and expressionY in the parameter a[0]
Sweep the parameter with start, end and count (here 0 to 4π in 120 samples)
Map function space to pixels inside the expressions: x = 20 + a[0]·25.465, y = 100 − 75·f
Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre
pitfalls: The sweep parameter is a[0] (u is an alias); start/end are in function units, not pixels, so scale x yourself: 320 px / 4π = 25.465
Screen y grows downwards: write 100 - 75 * f, not 100 + 75 * f, or the plot is upside down
A pathExpression is a polyline through `count` samples: too few and curves look faceted (120 is plenty for two periods)
Stroke the path (style stroke): with the default fill paint the open curve is filled to its chord

examples.name: 3d-scene-recipe
examples.title: A lit 3D shape you can drag to turn, by hand
examples.summary: The 3D recipe written out: a window-filling canvas, clearDepth3D, a perspective camera3D whose distance follows the aspect, two directional lights, one meshPrimitive3D torus, a matrix3D chain of tilt and spin driven by two touchExpressions, a theme paint colour and drawMesh3D; in mono a hidden-line wireframe instead.
examples.prompt: Show one 3D shape, lit, that I can drag to turn; write the camera, the lights and the transforms out so I can see how 3D works.
examples.hand_built: The ops themselves are the lesson. For a scene of several parts, a product turntable or an assembly, call Scene3D: it frames the camera at every angle and aspect, places parts by size and position, and adds autorotate, assembly and the mono look.
teaches: The order: clearDepth3D, camera3D, lights3D, meshPrimitive3D (an id), then per draw: matrix3D identity and its chain, a paint colour, drawMesh3D of that id
The 3D viewport is the whole window, drawn at the canvas's top left: make the 3D canvas fill the window, and give camera3D aspect componentWidth() / componentHeight()
Frame for the narrow side: eye distance = d * max(1, componentHeight() / componentWidth()), so a portrait window moves the camera back as much as it narrows the view

Orbit: two touchExpressions on touchX() and touchY() (stopMode gently, so a release coasts) become angles in radians for matrix3D rotate about X (tilt) and Y (spin); clamp tilt with the touch's min and max
matrix3D ops post-multiply: identity, rotate X, rotate Y, then the mesh; angles are radians
Lights are directions the light travels (down and into the screen is [x, -y, -z]); the colour is the paint colour, lit by 0.2 ambient plus each light's |N.L| times its intensity
Mono: {"$if": "theme.mono"} in the commands picks a hidden-line wireframe (drawMesh3D wireframe, edges [0, 1] draws the quads without diagonals) in onSurface instead of the lit fill
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only, and the Java JSON parser drops the 3D operations. Don't use it for a screen that must play on Android today

A 3D canvas that does not start at the window's top left, or does not fill it, draws its scene off-centre and outside its box: the players draw into a window-sized buffer placed at the canvas's origin
matrixSave / matrixRestore do not save the 3D matrix: start each object's chain again with matrix3D identity
matrix3D needs an op; {"translate": [x, y, z]} is an error, write {"op": "translate", "x": .., "y": .., "z": ..}
Lighting is two-sided Lambert with a fixed 0.2 ambient and colours multiply: a dark theme colour stays dark, and lights brighter in sum than about 1.2 wash a light colour out to white

snippets.note: camera3D: perspective, fovY 0.6 rad, aspect from the canvas, eye distance from a variable
lights3D: a warm key light from the upper left, a cool fill from the right
meshPrimitive3D torus: major and minor radius, 32 segments, built by the player
touchExpression on touchX(): the drag accumulates and coasts; it becomes the spin angle

examples.name: operators
examples.title: Operators and precedence
examples.summary: Seven formulas over two exported variables (a = 7, b = 3) with their live results: precedence, parentheses, left-to-right evaluation, float division, % and unary minus.
examples.prompt: Show a small cheat sheet of arithmetic formulas over a = 7 and b = 3 (a + b * 2, (a + b) * 2, a - b - 1, a / b, a % b, -a % b, -b * -2) with each computed result next to it.
teaches: Write a value as an infix formula string over @variables: "@a + @b * 2" compiles to one float expression that re-evaluates when a or b changes
Rely on the usual precedence (* / % before + -, unary minus binds tightest) and group with parentheses; equal operators run left to right
Expect % to truncate like Java's float %: the result takes the sign of the left operand, so -7 % 3 is -1, not 2
pitfalls: The infix parser knows only + - * / % and unary minus: no ^, no comparison (<, >, ==) and no && or ||; write pow(x, n), and step() or ifElse() for comparisons (EXP-06)
Write a variable as @name; a bare name also resolves when it is declared, but bare width and height mean componentWidth() and componentHeight(), so don't name your own variables that and drop the @
-3 directly after an operator, a comma or a parenthesis is folded into a negative literal; -@b is a CHANGE_SIGN operation on the variable
A device reader refuses an expression longer than 32 RPN tokens (numbers, variables, operators and functions each count); split a long formula into named resources.variables

When a row of formula, result and note no longer fits, a plain row squeezes the last child to 0 wide: make it a collapsibleRow and give the note a collapsiblePriority (1) so it is the one dropped; unprioritized children are kept first

snippets.note: a exported (export: true) so the host can change it; every formula below follows
@a + @b * 2 → 13: * binds before +
-@a % @b → -1: % keeps the sign of the left side
textFromFloat with decimal 2 and flags 7 shows 2.33

examples.name: math-library
examples.title: Math function reference
examples.summary: Sixteen expression functions evaluated on sample arguments (sqrt, pow, exp, ln, log, hypot, square, atan2, floor, ceil, round, fract, abs, sign, max), each shown with its result.

teaches: Call the math functions inside any expression string: sqrt, pow(x, n), exp, ln (natural), log (base 10), hypot(x, y), square, floor, ceil, round, fract, abs, sign, min, max
Check rounding on negative numbers: floor(-2.5) is -3, ceil(-2.5) is -2, fract(-2.25) is -0.25 (x minus its truncation)
Print a computed value with textFromFloat; flags 519 (7 + 512 OPTIONS_ROUNDING) rounds the last decimal instead of cutting it

round is Java's Math.round, half rounds UP: round(-2.5) = -2 (the C++ player gives -3, see the family's findings)
mad(a, b, c) is a * b + c in the reference (and the TS player); the C++ player computes a + b * c, so mad(2, 3, 4) shows 14 instead of 10. Write a * b + c until it is fixed

atan2(y, x) returns radians: atan2(1, 1) = 0.785

ln(10): natural log
fract(-2.25) → -0.25: fract truncates

examples.name: easing-curves
examples.title: Easing curves compared
examples.summary: Linear, ease-in (square), ease-out, smooth_step and smootherstep drawn over each other on one unit-square chart, each a pathExpression in t = a[0], with a legend.
examples.prompt: Plot five easing curves from 0 to 1 on the same chart (linear, ease in, ease out, smoothstep, smootherstep) with a colour legend and the formula under each name.
teaches: Shape a 0..1 parameter with plain expressions: square(t) eases in, 1 - square(1 - t) eases out, smooth_step(t, 1, 0) and t*t*t*(t*(6*t - 15) + 10) ease both ends
Plot y = f(t) as a pathExpression with start 0, end 1 and a[0] as t, mapping it into the box with x = left + w * t and y = bottom - h * f(t)
Reuse one id per curve ("easeIn", "smooth"…) and draw it with drawPath after setting the stroke
pitfalls: smooth_step takes (value, max, min): smooth_step(t, 1, 0) is the usual smoothstep(0, 1, t). Not clamp's order
pathExpression without flags 4 (LINEAR) joins the samples with splines; 64 linear samples are enough for these curves, a straight line needs only count 2
The JSON parser has no smoothstep, mix or ease names: write the polynomial, and keep it under 32 RPN tokens

A canvas drawn at its header size (literal coordinates) runs off a narrower host and leaves a strip in a wider one: when the drawing is one composition (chart and legend, dial and readout), scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: ease in: square(a[0])
ease out: 1 - square(1 - a[0])
smooth_step(a[0], 1, 0): value first, then max, then min
smootherstep t³(t(6t − 15) + 10) as a 64-sample linear pathExpression

check.describe: Five curves from bottom-left to top-right: a grey diagonal, blue below it, green above it, yellow and red S-curves crossing at the centre, the red steeper. Resized, the chart and its legend are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 240)) and centred: smaller at 234 wide with the legend still beside the chart, centred at 1:1 in a 540 wide box.

examples.name: remap-ranges
examples.title: Mapping values between ranges
examples.summary: Three readings in their own units (temperature −10…40 °C, gain −60…0 dB, speed 0…120 km/h) normalised with clamp((v − lo) / (hi − lo)) and placed on tracks with lerp; the out-of-range speed pins to the end.
examples.prompt: Show temperature, audio gain and speed on horizontal tracks, each mapped from its own range onto the track, with values past the end clamped.
teaches: Normalise a value to 0..1 once, as a named expression: tTemp = clamp(0, 1, (@temp + 10) / 50)
Map the normalised t onto pixels with lerp(start, end, t): cx = lerp(20, 340, @tTemp)
Clamp before mapping so an out-of-range input (speed 140 on a 0..120 scale) pins to the end instead of drawing off the track
pitfalls: clamp takes (min, max, value): the value is LAST, clamp(x, 0, 1) is always 0 (it is min(max(a, c), b), so only the max has to be in the middle)
lerp(a, b, t) does not clamp: lerp(30, 340, 1.17) is 392, past the track, which is why t is clamped first
A gradient set on the paint stays set when you change the colour: the marker after the gradient track would be painted with the gradient. Clear it with {"shader": 0} in the next paint's ops

Tracks drawn to x = 340 only fit the 360 header width: read componentWidth() into a variable (@r) and use it for the right ends, the gradient and the lerp targets; text that only fits when wide can go in a conditionalOperations on that width

snippets.note: clamp(0, 1, @speed / 120): 140 km/h pins to 1
lerp(20, @r, @tTemp): 0..1 onto the track, whose right end @r = componentWidth() - 20 follows the live width
{"shader": 0} clears the gradient before the solid marker

check.describe: The temperature marker sits two thirds along the gradient track (23 °C), the gain bar fills 70 % (−18 dB), the speed bar is full with its thumb at the end and a red "over range" note. Resized, the tracks run from 20 px to the live width minus 20 (@r = componentWidth() - 20) and the values, the formula and the markers stay right-aligned at the same fractions, at 234 and at 540 wide; below 320 wide the formula and the over-range note are left out (a conditionalOperations on @r) so they do not run into the title and the Speed label.

examples.hand_built: The tracks are drawn by hand because their positions are the remap expression being taught; use the ProgressBar or Slider component for an ordinary bar.

examples.name: polar-trig
examples.title: Compass bearing with atan2
examples.summary: A compass dial of 60 ticks placed with sin/cos in a loop, a needle that points at an exported target with atan2, and the bearing (degrees) and distance (hypot) printed beside it.
examples.prompt: Draw a compass dial with tick marks and N/E/S/W, and a needle pointing from the centre at a target point; show the bearing in degrees and the distance to the target.
teaches: Place items around a circle from a loop index: x = cx + r * sin(i * 0.10472), y = cy − r * cos(i * 0.10472) (6° steps, 0° at the top, clockwise)
Point at a target with atan2(dx, −dy) for a compass bearing (0 at north, clockwise); keep the angle in one named variable and reuse it for both needle ends
Convert radians to 0..360 degrees with (angle * 57.29578 + 360) % 360, and measure the distance with hypot(dx, dy)
Vary a tick's length without a branch: 74 + 6 * step(i % 5, 0) is 74 every fifth tick and 80 otherwise
pitfalls: Every trig function works in radians and there is no deg() or rad() in JSON: multiply by 57.29578 or 0.0174533
atan2 takes (y, x). In screen coordinates y grows downward, so a compass bearing is atan2(dx, -dy), not atan2(dy, dx)
% of a negative angle stays negative (-90 % 360 = -90): add 360 before taking % 360

A canvas drawn at its header size (literal coordinates) runs off a narrower host and leaves a strip in a wider one: when the drawing is one composition (chart and legend, dial and readout), scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: b = atan2(@tx - 110, 115 - @ty): bearing in radians
60 ticks around the dial; the long ones every fifth via step(i % 5, 0)
needle tip: 110 + 62 * sin(@b), 115 - 62 * cos(@b)
hypot(@tx - 110, @ty - 115): distance
textMerge(number, "°") keeps the unit against the digits

check.describe: The red needle points up and to the right at the yellow target; the readout says 53° and 75 px. Resized, the compass and its readout are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 230)) and centred: smaller at 234 wide, 1.5× at 540×345, the bearing and distance unchanged.

examples.name: branchless-select
examples.title: Branchless selection with step and ifElse
examples.summary: Three batteries (18, 42, 86 %) in a loop: red, amber or green fill chosen by step() masks used as paint alpha, a status word picked the same way, and a time estimate chosen by ifElse(left, to-full, charging).
examples.prompt: Show three battery levels from an array; colour each red below 20 %, amber up to 50 % and green above, label it Low/Medium/Good, and show minutes left, or minutes to full when that battery is charging.
teaches: Turn a comparison into a 0/1 mask with step(x, edge), which is x > edge: low = 1 − step(v, 20), mid = step(v, 20) * (1 − step(v, 50)), high = step(v, 50)
Pick a colour by drawing each candidate with its mask as paint alpha: only the one whose mask is 1 shows, with no conditional block
Choose between two numbers with ifElse(otherwise, then, condition): ifElse(v * 6, (100 − v) * 1.2, charging) is the time to full while charging, else the time left
Use max() as a lower bound instead of a branch: the fill is never thinner than 8 px
pitfalls: ifElse takes (else, then, condition), condition LAST: it returns the second argument when the third is > 0, else the first
step(x, edge) is 1 when x > edge, strictly: step(20, 20) = 0, so 20 % counts as Low here
Paint alpha set from a mask stays on the paint: reset {"alpha": 1} before the next solid drawing
Text can't change inside a loop (each label is one text id), so the per-row numbers are drawn outside the loop with arrayGet(@levels, 0…2)

Labels drawn at x = 246 fall off a host narrower than about 330 dp: when the canvas is one composition, scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / 360, componentHeight() / 200) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: low mask: 1 - step(level, 20)
band mask: step(level, 20) * (1 - step(level, 50))
max(37, 29 + 1.16 * level): a minimum width without a branch
ifElse(level * 6, (100 - level) * 1.2, charging)
one loop draws the three batteries from the levels array

check.describe: Top battery 18 % red, Low, 108 min left; middle 42 % amber, Medium, 69 min to full (charging); bottom 86 % green, Good, 516 min left. Resized, the batteries, percentages and labels are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 200)) and centred: at 234 wide the Low / Medium / Good labels and time estimates stay visible beside smaller batteries; at 540 they are centred at 1:1.

examples.hand_built: The batteries are drawn by hand because their colours and labels are the step/ifElse selection being taught; use the BatteryIndicator component for an ordinary battery.

examples.name: conditional-blocks
examples.title: Threshold categories with conditionalOperations
examples.summary: An air-quality reading whose badge and advice come from conditionalOperations blocks: eq for no data, nested gt/le pairs for each band (AND), and the scale marker from a clamped expression.
examples.prompt: Show an air quality index with a coloured category badge (Good, Moderate, Unhealthy for some, Unhealthy) and one line of advice for the band the value falls in, plus a scale with a marker.
teaches: Draw a block only when a comparison holds with conditionalOperations {condition: gt|ge|lt|le|eq, v1, v2, commands}: v1 is compared to v2
Test a band (50 < v ≤ 100) by nesting two blocks: a gt block containing a le block
Write the else branch as its own block with the complementary condition; there is no else
Keep continuous things (the marker position) as expressions and use blocks only for content that differs per band
pitfalls: There is no else, and no and/or: nest for AND, repeat the block for OR, and write the complement for else
The condition names are gt, ge, lt, le and eq (case-insensitive); anything else becomes 0, which the reader does not treat as an error
eq compares floats exactly: use it on whole numbers or flags, not on computed fractions
Static text in the blocks is fine; a value that only changes size or position is cheaper as an expression than as four blocks

A canvas laid out with literal x coordinates (98, 179, 340) only fits its header width: compute the edges from componentWidth(), and when there is less room than the design needs, scale the drawing down as a whole (min(1, componentWidth() / 360)) rather than letting text run off the edge

snippets.note: eq: only when @aqi == 0, the "No reading" note
gt 50 containing le 100: the Moderate band
gt 150 alone: the open-ended top band
20 + 4 * @q * clamp(0, 1, @aqi / 200), @q being a quarter of the live scale width
@s = min(1, componentWidth() / 360): below the 360 design width the whole card is scaled down (and centred vertically); above it @r = componentWidth() / @s - 20 stretches the scale

check.describe: AQI 132: an orange "Unhealthy for some" badge, the sensitive-groups advice, and the marker between 100 and 150 on the scale. aqi 0, 30, 75 and 180 show No reading, Good, Moderate and Unhealthy. Resized, at 234 wide the card is scaled down as a whole (@s = 0.65) and centred vertically; at 540 the scale stretches to the live width (quarters of @r - 20) while the badge stops growing at 200 px.

examples.hand_built: The category badge is drawn by hand because its colour and text are chosen by the conditionalOperations being taught; use the Badge component for an ordinary badge.

examples.name: array-stats
examples.title: Array statistics
examples.summary: A week of step counts from a float array: bars scaled by arrayMax, the best day highlighted by a step mask, an average line, and total, average, best and standard deviation computed with arraySum, arrayLength, arrayMax and arraySumSqr.
examples.prompt: Show a week of step counts as a bar chart with the best day highlighted and an average line, and summary stats on top: total, average, best day and standard deviation.
teaches: Aggregate an array inside expressions: arraySum(@a), arrayLength(@a), arrayMax(@a), arrayMin(@a), arrayGet(@a, i)
Compute an average once as a named variable (avg = arraySum / arrayLength) and a standard deviation as sqrt(arraySumSqr(@a) / arrayLength(@a) − square(@avg))
Highlight the maximum without a branch: alpha 0.45 + 0.55 * step(arrayGet(@a, i), arrayMax(@a) − 1)
Print large numbers with thousands separators (flags 21: 16 GROUPING_BY3 + 5) and round in the expression with round()
pitfalls: There is no arrayAvg in JSON (the runtime has one): divide arraySum by arrayLength
arrayGet takes (array, index), array first
textFromFloat with decimal 0 cuts the fraction (8385.7 prints 8385) unless the rounding flag 512 is set; round() in the expression does the same and keeps the flags simple
floatArrays are exported by default: a host can replace the week's values and every statistic follows

Bars placed at 29 + i * 45.714 only span the header width: derive the slot from componentWidth() ((@r - 20) / 7) so they spread over any width, and scale the chart down as a whole where the four figures would no longer fit

The values are labelled on the canvas to keep the lesson on expressions in one place (rc-inspect flags it: text_in_canvas). In a real screen put labels and values in text components around the drawing.

snippets.note: avg = arraySum(@steps) / arrayLength(@steps)
std dev: round(sqrt(arraySumSqr / n − square(avg)))
bars scaled by arrayGet / arrayMax; the best day's mask from step()
arraySum with flags 21 → 58,700

check.describe: Seven bars, Saturday tallest and brighter; a yellow average line at about 70 % of the tallest; the stats read 58,700 total, 8,386 average, 12,100 best day and 2,139 standard deviation. Resized, below the 360 design width the chart is scaled down as a whole (@s = min(1, w / 360)) and centred vertically, so the four figures still fit on one line at 234 wide; wider, the figures spread over quarters and the bars over sevenths of the live width (@r = componentWidth() / @s - 20), at 540 wide too.

examples.hand_built: The chart is drawn by hand because its highlighted best day and average line are the array functions being taught; use the BarChart component for an ordinary bar chart.

examples.name: seeded-skyline
examples.title: Seeded random skyline
examples.summary: A night city generated from seeded randomness: 14 towers whose heights, window counts and lit windows all come from seed(n, rand()) keyed on the loop indices, under 50 seeded stars; identical on every render.
examples.prompt: Generate a night skyline: a row of towers of random heights with randomly lit windows, a moon and stars, the same picture every time.
teaches: Get a repeatable random number per item with seed(key, rand()): it reseeds the generator with key, then evaluates rand()
Recompute the same seeded value wherever it is needed (tower top, window rows, window y) instead of storing it: the same key always gives the same number
Combine nested loop indices into one key (i * 389 + j * 41 + k * 7 + 20000) for a value per window, and threshold it with step(…, 0.55) for on/off
Use seeded values in a loop's until: floor((40 + 110 * seed(…)) / 10) − 1 window rows per tower
pitfalls: Consecutive small seeds (i + 1) give first values that rise or fall in a ramp, because the seed is the float's bits: spread the keys with a multiplier (i * 97 + 3) and give x, y and size different multipliers or the stars fall on a line
rand() without seed() is different on every evaluation and every load; the C++ renderer needs --seed to pin it
A variable holding seed(…) is not a stored number but an expression; inside a loop write the seed inline with the loop index

A seeded scene drawn for a 360×200 box leaves a blank strip in a wider host: drive the loop count from componentWidth() and stand the towers on componentHeight(); since each tower is keyed by its index, the ones that were there keep their look

snippets.note: tower top: @h - 40 - 110 * seed(i * 97 + 3, rand()), standing on the live bottom edge
window rows from the same seeded height
lit or dark: 0.9 * step(seed(window key, rand()), 0.55)
50 stars with separate keys for x, y, size and brightness

check.describe: Fourteen dark towers of mixed heights with scattered amber windows, a pale moon top right and faint stars; the picture is the same on every render. Resized, the sky fills the box and the towers stand on its bottom edge: 9 towers at 234 wide, 21 at 540 (the loop runs to ceil(componentWidth() / 26)); the first towers keep their seeded heights and windows at any size, and the moon stays 60 px from the right.

examples.name: modifier-expressions
examples.title: Expressions in layout modifiers
examples.summary: A download card where layout modifiers take expressions: the bar is fillMaxWidth(@p), the percent bubble is offset by clamp(0, 280, @p * 328 − 24), equalizer bars get height from an array, and the caption fades with graphicsLayer alpha.
examples.prompt: A download progress card: a bar filled to the progress, a percentage bubble that rides above the end of the bar, a row of level bars, and a caption that fades in as progress grows.
teaches: Pass an expression to a size modifier: {"fillMaxWidth": "@p"} fills that fraction of the parent, {"height": "10 + 54 * arrayGet(@eq, k)"} sets pixels
Move a component with {"offset": {"x": expr, "y": 0}}, clamping the expression so it stays inside its box
Fade a component with {"graphicsLayer": {"alpha": "0.2 + 0.8 * @p"}}
pitfalls: spacedBy parses an expression but the layouts keep it as a constant: "spacedBy": "@gap" writes a variable id that is used as a number (NaN), and the children lose their positions. Use constant spacing
Padding takes an expression only in its single-number form ({"padding": "@pad"}); the list and object forms are read as constants
fillMaxWidth's fraction is of the parent's width after its padding; the bubble's offset is in pixels, so it multiplies by the track width (328) itself

Inside a modifier, componentWidth() is the width of the component being modified (the 48 dp bubble), not of its parent: for a position along the parent, derive it from windowWidth() minus the padding, or a weight/fraction
Ten 22 dp bars with 8 dp gaps overflow a narrower host: give each bar weight 1 with widthIn [0, 30] and an end padding for the gap, so they shrink but never grow past the design

snippets.note: fillMaxWidth: "@p" — the bar fills 65 %
offset x = clamp(0, windowWidth() - 80, @p * (windowWidth() - 32) - 24): the bubble follows the bar end at any width (the bar spans the window minus the 16 dp padding each side)
height from an array element
graphicsLayer alpha 0.2 + 0.8 * @p

check.describe: The blue bar is filled to 65 % with a 65 % bubble centred over its end, ten purple bars of different heights below, and a dimmed caption. Resized, the bubble stays centred over the bar end (65 % of the live width), and the ten bars share the row (weight 1, at most 30 dp each with an 8 dp end padding as the gap): thinner at 234 wide, as at 360 when wider.

examples.hand_built: The bar, bubble and level bars are built by hand because their modifier expressions are the lesson; use the ProgressBar component for an ordinary progress bar.

examples.name: text-formatting
examples.title: Number formatting flags
examples.summary: Eight numbers turned into text by textFromFloat flags and textMerge: thousands grouping, period-comma and underscore separators, negative parentheses, zero padding, mm:ss from seconds, a percent and whole-digit clipping.
examples.prompt: A reference card of number formats: $1,234.50, 1.234,50 €, 9_876_543, (42.50), 007, 07:05 from 425 seconds, 65 % and what happens when the whole digits are too few.
teaches: Add flags: AFTER 0 space/1 none/3 zero, PRE 0 space/4 none/12 zero, GROUPING 16 by 3, SEPARATOR 64 period-comma/128 space-comma/192 underscore, 256 negative in parentheses, 512 rounding
Build mm:ss from seconds: textMerge(textFromFloat(floor(@secs / 60), whole 2, flags 13), textMerge(":", textFromFloat(@secs % 60, whole 2, flags 13)))
Add a prefix or a unit with textMerge("$", number) or textMerge(number, " €"); nest textMerge for three parts
pitfalls: whole is the number of characters KEPT before the decimal point, separators included: 9,876,543 needs whole 9, and whole 3 prints 543
Without 512 (OPTIONS_ROUNDING) the decimals are cut, not rounded; with decimal 0 the C++ player ignores 512 too, so round() the value
A float holds about 7 significant digits: 1234567.89 is stored as 1234567.875; keep amounts below 2^24 or in cents
Inside a text value object decimal defaults to 3; set decimal 0 for whole numbers

A row of label and value with spaceBetween lets a long label push into the value when the host narrows: give the label column weight 1 and its texts maxLines 1 with ellipsis, so the value keeps its intrinsic width

snippets.note: textMerge("$", textFromFloat(@price, 7, 2, flags 23)) → $1,234.50
flags 87 = 64 PERIOD_COMMA + 16 BY3 + 7 → 1.234,50
flags 13 = 12 PAD_PRE_ZERO + 1 → 007
mm:ss from floor(s / 60) and s % 60, joined by textMerge

balance.meaning: account balance; negative shows in parentheses

big.meaning: a large count, grouped by thousands

code.meaning: a code shown zero-padded to 3 digits

secs.meaning: a duration in seconds, shown mm:ss

check.describe: Rows read $1,234.50, 1.234,50 €, 9_876_543, (42.50), 007, 07:05, 65% and 543. Resized, every formatted value stays whole at the end of its row: the label column takes what is left (weight 1) and ellipsizes on one line, so at 234 wide PERIOD_COMMA reads PERIOD_… beside 1.234,50 €; at 540 the rows spread out.

examples.name: text-ops
examples.title: String operations
examples.summary: A contact card built from three raw exported strings: textTransform capitalises the name, takes an upper-case initial and upper-cases the role, textMeasure sizes the role pill, textSubtext trims a preview and textLength counts its characters.
examples.prompt: A contact card from raw strings: "ada lovelace" shown as "Ada Lovelace" with an initial avatar, the role upper-cased in a pill that fits the text, and a 30-character preview of a message with its length.
teaches: Transform a string into a new text variable with textTransform {text, start, len, operation, varName}: 1 lower, 2 upper, 3 trim, 4 capitalise words, 5 capitalise first; len -1 runs to the end
Cut a substring with textSubtext {text, start, len, varName} and add an ellipsis with textMerge
Measure the rendered width with textMeasure (mode 0) after setting the paint's textSize, and size a pill with it: right = 122 + @roleW
Count characters with textLength {text, name} and print the count with textFromFloat
pitfalls: The JSON names for textTransform's operation are off by one in the reference parser: "uppercase" writes 1 (TEXT_TO_LOWERCASE), "lowercase" 2 (upper), "capitalize" 3 (trim). Write the number
textMeasure measures with the paint as it is at that point in the commands: set textSize first
textSubtext throws past the end of the string on Java (substring): keep start + len within the text, or use len -1
These operations are in the AndroidX profile: the header needs profiles 513 (the Java writer refuses opcode 199 without it)

A card drawn to x = 348 only fits the header width: draw it to componentWidth() - 12, and when the fixed-size text (a 21 px name, a 30-character preview) would no longer fit, scale the canvas down as a whole

snippets.note: textTransform operation 4: "ada lovelace" → "Ada Lovelace"
start 0, len 1, operation 2: the upper-case initial
textSubtext: the first 30 characters
textMeasure mode 0 → @roleW, the pill's width
textLength → @chars

msg.default: The engine might compose elaborate pieces of music

check.describe: A purple circle with A, "Ada Lovelace", a teal ANALYST pill fitted to its text, and the preview "The engine might compose elabo…" over "50 characters". Resized, the card fills the live width (right edge at componentWidth() - 12) with the divider following it; below the 360 design width the whole card is scaled down (@s = min(1, w / 360)) so the name and the preview stay inside it, at 234 wide too.

examples.hand_built: The avatar and role pill are drawn by hand because their text comes from the string operations being taught (and the pill is sized by textMeasure); use the Avatar and Badge components with fixed text.

host_variables.name: msg
host_variables.value: The engine might compose elaborate pieces of music

examples.name: system-values
examples.title: System values in expressions
examples.summary: A diagnostics card that prints the system values expressions can read: window size, the canvas's own size, density, font size, local time (timeInHr, timeInMin % 60) and day of year, plus a bar of the day elapsed.
examples.prompt: A diagnostics card listing the window size, this canvas's size, display density, font size, local time and day of year, each with the expression that reads it.
teaches: Read the environment inside any expression: windowWidth(), windowHeight(), componentWidth(), componentHeight(), density(), fontSize(), timeInHr(), timeInMin(), dayOfYear()
Lay out a canvas against its own size (right = componentWidth() − 12) so it fits any host size
Get the minute of the hour with timeInMin() % 60 (timeInMin is minutes since midnight) and zero-pad it with flags 13
pitfalls: timeInMin() is minutes since midnight and timeInSec() the second within the hour, not since midnight; timeInHr() is the hour
componentWidth() is the size of the component the expression belongs to, here the canvas; on a modifier it is that component's size
Pin the clock (render clock) when checking a time-dependent document; without it every time value reads the wall clock
fontSize() is the host's text size setting, 14 by default in the renderers

Right-aligned captions at componentWidth() - 24 collide with values at a fixed x = 112 once the host is narrow: below the design width, scale the drawing (and divide componentWidth() by the scale for its geometry) rather than overlapping

The values are labelled on the canvas to keep the lesson on expressions in one place (rc-inspect flags it: text_in_canvas). In a real screen put labels and values in text components around the drawing.

snippets.note: windowWidth() × windowHeight() via textMerge
the card fits the canvas: @w - 12, with @w = componentWidth() / @s
density() with 2 decimals
timeInHr() : timeInMin() % 60, zero padded
the day elapsed: 60 * timeInMin() / 1440

check.describe: At 10:08 on 28 October and density 1 the card reads 360 × 230, 360 × 230, 1.00, 14.0, 10:08 and 301. Resized, the window and canvas rows report the live size (234 × 230, 540 × 230) and the card, the day bar and the right-hand captions follow the width; below 360 wide the card is drawn scaled down as a whole (@s = min(1, componentWidth() / 360), geometry from @w = componentWidth() / @s) so the captions do not run into the values.

examples.name: sun-arc
examples.title: Sun position and daylight left
examples.summary: A sunrise-to-sunset arc: the time of day normalised between two exported times places the sun on a pathExpression arc, a second arc traces the daylight so far, a step mask dims the sun at night, and the daylight left is formatted as "3 h 32 min".
examples.prompt: A daylight widget: an arc from sunrise to sunset with the sun at its current position, the part of the day already gone highlighted, sunrise and sunset times, the current time and how much daylight is left.
teaches: Normalise the clock between two times with one named expression: t = clamp(0, 1, (timeInMin() − @rise) / (@set − @rise))
Place a point on an elliptical arc with x = cx − rx·cos(t·π), y = cy − ry·sin(t·π), and draw the elapsed part as a pathExpression whose angle is scaled by @t
Mask day and night with step(@now, @rise) * (1 − step(@now, @set)) and use it for the sun's alpha and halo
Format minutes as "h min" with floor(m / 60) and m % 60 joined by nested textMerge
pitfalls: Scale the angle inside expressionX/Y (cos(a[0] * @t)) and keep the pathExpression's start and end constant: the elapsed arc then always has its full sample count, however short it is
max(0, @set − @now) keeps the remaining time from going negative after sunset
clamp takes (min, max, value): the value is LAST, clamp(x, 0, 1) is always 0 (it is min(max(a, c), b), so only the max has to be in the middle)
A device reader refuses an expression longer than 32 RPN tokens (numbers, variables, operators and functions each count); split a long formula into named resources.variables

A canvas drawn at its header size (literal coordinates) runs off a narrower host and leaves a strip in a wider one: when the drawing is one composition (chart and legend, dial and readout), scale it as a whole with @fit = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H) and centre it with a translate

snippets.note: t = clamp(0, 1, (@now - @rise) / (@set - @rise))
day = step(@now, @rise) * (1 - step(@now, @set))
the elapsed arc: cos/sin of a[0] * @t
the sun at angle @t * π on the arc
"3 h 32 min of daylight left" from floor(m / 60) and m % 60
the full arc as a pathExpression, 0..π

check.describe: At 14:42: the yellow arc runs from the left end past the top, the sun sits on it two thirds of the way across, and the title reads "3 h 32 min of daylight left". At 21:00 the sun sits dimmed at the sunset end with 0 h 0 min. Resized, the arc, the sun and the labels are scaled as one (@fit = min(w / 360, h / 210)) and centred: smaller at 234 wide, centred at 1:1 in a 540 wide box, the sun at the same point of its path.

examples.name: integer-rating
examples.title: Integer star rating
examples.summary: A five-star rating driven by an exported integer: each star's filled/empty face is chosen by an integer-expression visibility (clamp(0, 1, @rating - k)), a Poor/Okay/Great label by integer division and abs, and a tap cycles 1→5 with valueIntegerExpressionChange (@rating % 5 + 1).
examples.prompt: A five-star rating bound to an integer the host can set; show filled stars up to the rating, a Poor/Okay/Great word, and let a tap on the stars cycle the rating from 1 to 5.
teaches: Write an integer expression wherever an int id is expected (visibility, valueIntegerExpressionChange): a string with an @variable and an operator, e.g. "clamp(0, 1, @rating - 2)", compiles to an IntegerExpression
Show the k-th filled star with visibility clamp(0, 1, @rating - k) (1 = VISIBLE, 0 = GONE) and its empty twin with 1 - clamp(0, 1, @rating - k), stacked in one box
Use integer division as a threshold: @rating / 4 is 1 only for 4 and 5; 1 - min(1, abs(@rating - 3)) is 1 only at exactly 3
Cycle a value on tap with {"type": "valueIntegerExpressionChange", "target": "@rating", "value": "@rating % 5 + 1"}
pitfalls: The integer infix knows only + - * / % (and unary minus) and abs, min, max, clamp; no bit operators, no float functions. / truncates toward zero
A string becomes an integer expression only when it contains an @reference AND one of + - * / %: "clamp(0, 1, @rating)" alone is not one; write "@rating - 0" or reference the variable directly
visibility values are 0 GONE, 1 VISIBLE, 2 INVISIBLE: an expression that can reach 2 hides without collapsing, so clamp it to 0..1
clamp takes (min, max, value) here too
Visibility changes animate (about 300 ms) in the players: capture a tap's result after the transition
The audit reports the tap's IntegerExpression as dead_code: the inspector doesn't count a ValueIntegerExpressionChange action as its reader (a false positive)

Five fixed 44 dp stars need 220 dp: in a narrower host a plain row squeezes the last ones to 0 wide. Give each star box weight 1 with widthIn [0, 44] and centre the row (horizontalArrangement center), since a weighted row fills its width

The stars are ★ text to keep the lesson on integer expressions (rc-inspect flags it: glyph_icon). In a real screen draw them (DRW-05 builds a star point by point) or make a Star component, and use @colors.* rather than literal colours.

snippets.note: rating, an exported integer (default 4)
third star filled when clamp(0, 1, @rating - 2) = 1
its empty twin: 1 - clamp(0, 1, @rating - 2)
Great when @rating / 4 = 1 (integer division)
Okay only at 3: 1 - min(1, abs(@rating - 3))
tap: valueIntegerExpressionChange @rating % 5 + 1 cycles 1..5

check.describe: Four yellow stars and one dark, "Great". rating 1 and 3 show one star "Poor" and three stars "Okay"; a tap on the stars goes 4 → 5, a second tap wraps to 1. Resized, the five stars stay centred: at 195 wide they shrink to share the row (weight 1, at most 44 dp each) and a tap on them still goes 4 → 5; at 450 they keep 44 dp.

examples.hand_built: The stars are integer-driven visibility built by hand because integer expressions are the lesson; use the Rating component for a real rating row.

examples.name: parameterised-card
examples.title: Host-parameterised profile card
examples.summary: A profile card whose name, subtitle, accent colour and progress are exported host variables with good defaults, so it renders well with no host and re-renders when the host sets them.
examples.prompt: Make a profile card template where the app can set the name, subtitle, accent colour and progress, and it still looks right with no data.
teaches: Export a float to the host with resources.variables {"progress": {"value": 0.65, "export": true}} and pass it to a ProgressBar as progress "clamp(0, 1, @progress)"
Export a colour with resources.colors (named colours are exported by default) and use it as "@colors.accent": in a background and as a component's color param
Export a string with a root variable {"vtype": "string", "export": true} and show it with text value "@name"
Give host-supplied strings maxLines 1 and an ellipsis: their length is unknown and the card can be narrower than the header

snippets.note: the exported accent colour and progress float
an exported string variable
ProgressBar progress clamp(0, 1, @progress) in the host's accent colour, safe for any host value
the host name, one line with an ellipsis

check.describe: Defaults show Ada Lovelace with a purple avatar and a 65% bar; variables {name: Grace Hopper, subtitle: COBOL committee, accent: #FF26A69A, progress: 0.3} change all four. Resized, the card fills the width and the text column takes the remaining width (weight 1): the progress bar stretches, and a name or subtitle too long for a narrow card ends in an ellipsis.

pitfalls: clamp takes the value last: clamp(0, 1, @progress). clamp(@progress, 0, 1) always gives 0 (the middle argument is the maximum)
resources.variables entries are exported only with "export": true, while resources.colors entries are exported unless "export": false
A weighted child ignores the row's spacedBy (the row overflows by the gap): space the avatar from the text column with a fixed 16 dp spacer box instead
textFromFloat pads the number to `whole` digits with leading spaces; flags 4 (no leading pad) keeps "30% complete" flush with the bar
A host string in a narrow card wraps word by word and pushes the rest of the column out of the card unless it is limited to one line

examples.name: host-data-chart
examples.title: Sparkline from host data
examples.summary: A sparkline drawn from an exported float array the host can replace; the line scales to the array's length, minimum and maximum.
examples.prompt: Draw a sparkline of weekly revenue where the app supplies the numbers as an array of any length.
teaches: Export a float array to the host with resources.floatArrays {"data": {"value": [...], "export": true}}
Pass it by name to a Sparkline ("values": "@data"): the chart reads it with arrayGet in a loop, so a host array of another length or range still fills it
Let the chart fill the space left under the title: a box with weight 1 then fillMaxWidth, and the Sparkline with fill: true

snippets.note: the exported series and its default
Sparkline over @data, filling the weighted box

data.meaning: the series to plot, any length >= 2

check.describe: The default series draws a rising line ending in a dot at the top right; render_rc with variables {data: [a falling series]} draws a falling line. Resized, the title stays at the top and the sparkline fills the rest of the box, with the end dot following.

pitfalls: rc-inspect interact doesn't accept float_array variables yet (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS I8); use render_rc variables
values is the NAME of a float array ("@data" from resources.floatArrays), not a JSON list
In a column, write weight before fillMaxWidth on the chart's box: with fillMaxWidth first the box came out 0 wide and the line collapsed to the left edge
Weights ignore spacedBy: space the title from the weighted chart box with a fixed 12 dp spacer box

examples.name: battery-gauge
examples.title: Battery gauge
examples.summary: A battery icon filled to a host-supplied battery level (0-100) that turns red below 20%, with the percentage under it.
examples.prompt: Make a battery widget that fills to the phone's battery percentage and turns red when it drops below 20%.
teaches: Take the level from an exported host float (resources.variables battery, default 76) and pass it to BatteryIndicator as level "@battery"
Turn the fill red below 20% with the component's lowAt (warnAt 20 too, so there is no amber step)
Show "76%" as one centred text under the icon with textMerge of a textFromFloat(clamp(0, 100, @battery), flags 4) and "%"

snippets.note: battery, set by the host
BatteryIndicator: level @battery, red below lowAt 20
textMerge(textFromFloat(clamp(0, 100, @battery), flags 4), "%"), centred
clamp(0, 100, @battery): the value goes last

check.describe: Default: a green fill at 76% and "76%". variables {battery: 15}: a short red fill with a ! and "15%". Resized, the background fills the box and the battery shrinks to the narrow width, centred over its percentage.

pitfalls: batteryLevel() (system variable 38) is an rcj/json2rc extension: the Java parser rejects it ("Unknown token in expression") and Android's RemoteContext defines no battery id, so a portable document takes the level from a host variable
clamp takes the value last: clamp(0, 100, @battery). clamp(@battery, 0, 100) returns 0 for any level
textFromFloat pads to `whole` digits with a leading space (" 15"), which shifts centred text; flags 4 drops the padding
BatteryIndicator's own percentage sits beside the icon and is cut in a narrow box: pass showPercent false and put the number under it

examples.name: bubble-level
examples.title: Bubble level
examples.summary: A spirit level: a green bubble offset from the centre by the accelerometer's X and Y readings, clamped to a circle inside the dial.
examples.prompt: Build a bubble level that uses the phone's accelerometer to move a bubble around a round dial.
teaches: Read the device tilt with accelerationX() and accelerationY() (m/s², about ±9.8 at 90°) inside an expression
Clamp a 2-D offset to a circle: scale it by 72 / max(hypot(dx, dy), 72), which is 1 inside the radius
Compute the bubble position once in canvas variables and reuse it for the bubble and its highlight

Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre; the background drawRect runs before it, to componentWidth() × componentHeight()

snippets.note: dx = -8 * accelerationX(): the bubble rises against the tilt
dy = 8 * accelerationY()
k = 72 / max(hypot(@dx, @dy), 72): radial clamp
the bubble at (@bx, @by)

check.describe: With no sensor input the bubble sits in the centre ring; system_variables {17: 4, 18: -3} move it up and to the left; {17: 9, 18: -9} pins it to the dial's edge on the diagonal, still inside the dial. Resized, the background fills the box and the level (dial, cross-hair and bubble travel) scales to the shorter side, centred.

pitfalls: Clamping x and y separately (min/max per axis) keeps the bubble in a square, so on a diagonal it leaves a round dial; clamp the length of the offset instead
accelerationX/Y are 0 with no sensor (and in a static render), so the default state is the bubble centred; pin system variables 17 and 18 to preview a tilt
The sign is a design choice: a real bubble moves toward the raised side, i.e. opposite to the acceleration on that axis

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: a background drawRect to the literal header size leaves the rest of a bigger box unpainted, and literal positions get cut off in a smaller one

examples.name: ambient-dim
examples.title: Ambient light dimming
examples.summary: A transit card that is a bright card in normal light and switches to black with white and yellow text when the ambient light sensor reads under 10 lux.
examples.prompt: Make a transit card that switches to a black, high-contrast look when the room is dark.
teaches: Read the ambient light sensor (lux) with lightLevel in an expression or a condition
Override a paint only in low light: conditionalOperations lt lightLevel 10 right after the normal paint
Keep the normal-light colours as the default path, so the card looks right when no sensor is present

Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre; the background drawRect runs before it, to componentWidth() × componentHeight()

snippets.note: card colour: black when lightLevel < 10
the label turns yellow in low light

check.describe: system_variables {26: 300} gives the light blue card; {26: 2} gives a black card with white and yellow text. Resized, the background fills the box and the card scales to fit, centred (bright at 540×180, light level 300).

pitfalls: Write lightLevel (or light()), not lightLevel(): both the Java parser and json2rc reject lightLevel() with "Unknown token in expression", although accelerationX() takes parentheses
With no sensor value the player reads 0 lux, which is "dark": a document checked without system_variables shows the low-light variant

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: a background drawRect to the literal header size leaves the rest of a bigger box unpainted, and literal positions get cut off in a smaller one

examples.name: dynamic-colors
examples.title: Material dynamic colour card
examples.summary: A now-playing card whose every colour is a Material dynamic colour role (color.system_neutral1_900, accent1_200, ...), so it re-themes with the device palette and keeps sensible fallbacks.
examples.prompt: Make a now-playing music card that picks up the device's Material You wallpaper colours.
teaches: Name resources.colors entries after Material roles ("color.system_accent1_200") so the host can substitute its palette
Give each role a fallback value that works on its own (a dark-theme tone here)
Reference the roles everywhere with "@colors.color.system_...": backgrounds, text colours and a component's color param (the Card's surface)
Give single-line labels maxLines 1 and an ellipsis so a narrower card truncates them instead of wrapping word by word

snippets.note: five roles with dark-theme fallbacks
the Card's surface in accent2_800
the artwork tile in accent1_200
title text in neutral1_50

check.describe: inspect_theme lists the five roles; render_rc variables {color.system_accent1_200: #FFFFB4A9} recolours that tile; a host's own palette wins over the document's fallbacks. Resized, the card fills the width, centred in the box, the text column takes the rest of the row and each line ends in an ellipsis rather than wrapping when narrow.

pitfalls: On Android the _900 shades are the dark ones and _50/_100 the light ones, so a dark card uses neutral1_900 for its background and neutral1_50 for its text
Reference a role as "@colors." + the full role name, prefix included: "@colors.color.system_accent1_200"
A weighted text column ignores the row's spacedBy (the row overflows by the gap); separate the artwork from the text with a fixed 16 dp spacer box
The role colours are not theme names, so the mono looks keep them: a document that must also work on a 1-bit display gives each role a mono-dark / mono-light value

examples.name: font-scale
examples.title: Font-scale aware card
examples.summary: A reminder card whose title, body and button height are computed from the system font size, so the card grows when the user enlarges text.
examples.prompt: Make a reminder card whose text and button get bigger when the user turns up the system font size.
teaches: Derive a scale from the system text size: scale = fontSize() / (14 * density()) (1.0 at the default 14 sp)
Size text with it: fontSize "@titleSize" where titleSize = 20 * @scale, inside a Card whose content slot is your own nodes
Size a container with it too (button height 40 * @scale) and let the wrap-content Card grow around it

snippets.note: the font scale, from the fontSize() system variable
a text size derived from it
the hand-built button's height follows the scale

check.describe: At the default (fontSize 14) the card is about 120 px tall; system_variables {33: 21} (1.5x) makes the text and the button larger and the card taller. Resized, the card fills the width; in a narrow box the title and body wrap and the card grows taller.

pitfalls: fontSize() is in pixels (the C++ renderer sets 14 * density), so divide by density() as well as by 14 to get a pure scale factor
A fixed height (the button's) does not follow the font scale by itself; derive it from the same @scale, or large text is clipped inside it
examples.hand_built: The button is a box built by hand because Button has a fixed 40 dp height and text size that do not follow the font scale; use Button when the size need not scale.

examples.name: tap-counter
examples.title: Tap counter
examples.summary: A number with a +1 button that increments it on each tap and a Reset button that sets it back to 0.
examples.prompt: Make a counter widget with a +1 button that increments the number on each tap and a Reset button.
teaches: Increment a variable on tap: a Button whose onClick is valueFloatExpressionChange (value "@count + 1")
Set a variable to a fixed value on tap: a second Button (style outlined) with onClick valueFloatChange
Declare the state once in resources.variables ({"count": 0}) and show it with textFromFloat

snippets.note: the counter state: a float variable starting at 0
the +1 Button's onClick: count = count + 1
the Reset Button's onClick: count = 0
textFromFloat(@count, 3 digits, no decimals)

check.describe: Three taps on +1 show 3; a tap on Reset shows 0 again. Resized, the two buttons stay centred: at 234 wide they shrink to share the row (each Button fill: true in a box of weight 1, capped at 120 by widthIn) instead of pushing Reset off the edge, and at 540 they keep 120.

pitfalls: valueFloatChange only sets a constant; incrementing needs valueFloatExpressionChange with an expression that reads the target ("@count + 1")
textFromFloat `whole` is the number of integer digits kept (3 here, enough up to 999), and inside a text value `decimal` defaults to 3, so set "decimal": 0 for a whole number

Declare the state in resources.variables, not as a root tree variable: the Buttons' onClick actions target it by name ("@count"), and a root variable passed into a component call is flagged (root_number_variable)

A Button wraps its label, and two side by side overflow a host narrower than the header: put each in a box with weight 1 and widthIn [0, 120] and give the Button fill: true, so they shrink but never grow past 120; separate them with a fixed spacer box, since weights ignore spacedBy

examples.name: toggle-switch
examples.title: Toggle switch
examples.summary: A Wi-Fi row with an iOS-style switch: each tap flips a 0/1 variable that moves the thumb and recolours the track.
examples.prompt: Add an iOS-style on/off switch to a Wi-Fi settings row; tapping it toggles it and the thumb slides and the track turns green.
teaches: Toggle a 0/1 variable on tap with onClick valueFloatExpressionChange (value "1 - @on")
Move the thumb with an expression of the state: cx = 20 + @on * 32
Swap the track colour with conditionalOperations (gt @on 0.5) around a paint change

snippets.note: onClick: on = 1 - on
when on > 0.5, switch the paint to the accent colour before drawing the track
the thumb's x follows the state

check.describe: Starts off (grey track, thumb left); one tap turns it on (teal track, thumb right). Resized, the label takes the free width (weight 1) and the 72×48 switch stays against the right edge: a tap 60 px from the right turns it on at 234 and at 540 wide.

expect.changed_variables: on goes from 0 to 1; the thumb x from 20 to 52

pitfalls: Toggle with valueFloatExpressionChange "1 - @on"; valueFloatChange can only set a constant
conditionalOperations only swaps the paint for the draws that follow it inside the same canvas; set the default paint first, then override it in the branch
drawRoundRect needs both rx and ry (there is no default and no radiusX/radiusY spelling)
examples.hand_built: Built by hand to teach the toggle itself (a tap writing 1 - @on, a thumb at an expression of the state, a paint swapped by conditionalOperations); use the Switch component in a real screen.

examples.name: multi-click
examples.title: Tap, double tap and long press
examples.summary: One tile with three click modifiers, counting single taps, double taps and long presses separately.
examples.prompt: Make a tile that does something different on a tap, a double tap and a long press.
teaches: Handle a double tap with multiClick clickType 2 and a long press with clickType 1
Stack onClick and multiClick modifiers on one component, each with its own actions
Count each gesture in its own variable with valueFloatExpressionChange

snippets.note: multiClick clickType 2 (double tap): doubles + 1
multiClick clickType 1 (long press): longs + 1
a plain onClick for the single tap

check.describe: A single tap raises the Tap count to 1. Double taps and long presses are not dispatched by the C++ or TypeScript players, so only the structure (three click modifiers) can be checked offline. Resized, the tile fills the box at 234 and 540 wide and a tap anywhere on it still counts.

pitfalls: clickType 0 is a single tap, 1 a long press, 2 a double tap; only Android dispatches 1 and 2, the C++ and TypeScript players ignore them
A multiClick takes its actions under "actions" (an array), while onClick takes the action or array directly
onClick and multiClick go on the same component as separate modifiers; inspectors that count click targets show the tile once

examples.name: drag-slider
examples.title: Drag slider
examples.summary: A 0–100 slider: touchMode 6 maps the finger's x straight to a clamped value, so the thumb, the filled track and the label follow the finger.
examples.prompt: Build a horizontal 0–100 slider I can drag, with the thumb following my finger and the value shown above it.
teaches: Map the finger position to a clamped 0–100 value with touchExpression (min, max, an expression of touchX(), touchMode 6 for absolute position)
Position the thumb and the filled track from the touch-driven variable
Show the live value with textFromFloat in drawTextAnchored

snippets.note: touchExpression: value = (touchX() - 20) / (width - 40) * 100, clamped 0..100, touchMode 6 (absolute position)
the thumb at 20 + (width - 40) * @value / 100
textFromFloat(@value, 3 digits, no decimals)

check.describe: Starts at 30; a drag from x=100 to x=240 leaves the thumb under the finger at 84 (a tap at x=150 gives 50). Resized, the track spans the box minus 20 px each side and the value follows the live componentWidth(): at 195 wide a drag to x=152 gives 85, at 450 wide a drag to x=372 gives 85, the thumb under the finger both times.

pitfalls: touchMode 6 (STOP_ABSOLUTE_POS) is the only absolute mode: the value is the expression of the finger position. Modes 0–5 are relative: the value moves by how far the expression changes from the touch-down, so the thumb would not jump to where you tap

touchExpression takes `expression` as an array (one infix string element is fine) and an integer `touchMode`; a bare infix string or a named stopMode only works in json2rc and rcj, not in the Java parser
min and max clamp the value; leaving out min switches to wrap mode (see INT-05)
Paint is stateful: the second drawLine reuses the stroke width and cap set before the first, and the thumb paint must switch back to style fill

A canvas background drawn as drawRect(0, 0, 300, 100) leaves the rest of a wider host unpainted: use a background modifier (or componentWidth()/componentHeight()) so it fills whatever box the host gives
examples.hand_built: Built by hand to teach touchExpression (a finger position mapped to a clamped value that the thumb and fill follow); use the Slider component in a real screen.

examples.name: fling-wheel
examples.title: Fling prize wheel
examples.summary: A six-colour prize wheel: a horizontal drag turns it, and a fast release keeps it spinning until it decelerates to a stop.
examples.prompt: Make a prize wheel I can spin with a swipe; it should keep spinning after I let go and slow down to a stop.
teaches: Make a value fling: touchExpression with expression ["touchX()"] and touchMode 0 (gently) carries the release velocity on and eases to a stop
Wrap an angle by leaving out min: max 360 makes the value wrap instead of clamp
Rotate a group of draws by the touch value with save { rotate(angle, pivot) ... }

snippets.note: angle follows the horizontal drag (1 px = 1 degree), wraps at 360, and keeps going on a fast release

@s = (min(componentWidth(), componentHeight()) - 60) / 240, then translate to the live centre (componentWidth() / 2, componentHeight() / 2 + 10) and scale by @s, so the wheel drawn at a fixed 120 radius fits any box
save + rotate(@angle) around the six drawSector calls, about the origin the outer save moved to the wheel centre
one 60 degree sector
the fixed pointer: a small triangle built with pathCreate / pathAppendLineTo / pathAppendClose

check.describe: A 100 px drag released at 1000 px/s keeps the wheel turning for about two seconds after the release; at 3 s and at 4 s the frames are identical (settled). Resized, the wheel stays centred and scales with the smaller side (radius (min(w, h) - 60) / 2): smaller at 195×300, centred in the wide 450×200 box, with the pointer still on top; the same fling spins it the same angle, since a pixel is a degree at any size.

pitfalls: The fling velocity is found by perturbing touchX() inside the expression array itself: ["touchX()"] flings, but a single infix element such as ["touchX() * 2"] compiles to a separate expression and releases with zero velocity
Leaving out min turns on wrap mode (around max); min 0 clamps instead
drawPath with an inline SVG string is padded to 1024 floats (about 4 KB) by the Java parser; build small shapes with pathCreate / pathAppendLineTo so the document stays small and byte-identical
Draw the pointer after the save block: everything inside save { rotate } turns with the wheel, everything after it stays put

Draw a canvas around a translated centre and scale it from componentWidth()/componentHeight() rather than placing it at the header size literal coordinates (150, 160): the rotate pivot then is just the origin, and the drawing fits any box

examples.name: pager
examples.title: Swipe pager with dots
examples.summary: Three full-width cards swiped horizontally; the strip snaps, animated, to the nearest page and a dot indicator follows.
examples.prompt: Make a horizontal pager of three cards I can swipe between; it should snap to the nearest card and show page dots.
teaches: Track a horizontal swipe in pixels with touchExpression ["touchX()"] (default and max 2 * @w with @w = componentWidth(), min 0, touchMode 1 so it stops where released)
Snap to a page by rounding: page = round((2 * @w - @px) / @w)
Slide to the snapped page with an animated expression {"value": "@w * -@page", "anim": 0.35} and translate the strip of pages by it
Move the active dot with the same animated value (cx = 160 - @shift / 18), so the dot and the strip stay in step

snippets.note: the swipe, in px: dragging left lowers px; it starts at, and is capped by, 2 * @w (page 0), so the range follows the live width
page index: the nearest whole page, in page widths of the live componentWidth()
strip offset, animated over 0.35 s whenever page changes
page 2’s card: the strip is translated by the animated shift, then by one page width (@w) per card
the active dot, derived from the same animated shift: -20 - @shift / @w * 20 around the centred dots

check.describe: Starts on Today with the first dot lit; a 200 px swipe left lands on This week, with the second dot lit. Resized, a page is the live componentWidth() wide and the cards, labels and dots follow the box: at 234×200 a 140 px swipe (over half a page) lands on This week, at 540×260 a 300 px swipe does, with taller cards and the dots still at the bottom.

pitfalls: The Java JSON parser does not read touchSpec, so the notch stop modes (notchesEven and friends) cannot be configured from JSON, and on Android they index an empty spec; snap the displayed value with round() instead
Delta touch modes (0–5) move the value by the drag distance, so a leftward swipe lowers px; start at max (2 * @w = page 0) so swiping left can reach the later pages
Only the display snaps: the touch value keeps the fractional position, so the next swipe starts from where the last one ended rather than from the page boundary
A touchExpression expression element that is an infix formula is compiled separately; keep ["touchX()"] and scale afterwards if you want a release velocity

A pager that hard-codes the page width (360, 720) breaks as soon as the host is narrower or wider: read componentWidth() into a variable and use it for the page width, the touch range (defaultValue and max accept expressions) and the page index
examples.hand_built: Built by hand to teach the swipe mechanism (touchExpression in pixels, snapping by rounding, an animated translate shared with the dots); use the Pager component in a real screen.

examples.name: tabs
examples.title: Tabs with panels
examples.summary: Three tabs (Songs, Albums, Artists): tapping one shows its panel through visibility modifiers and slides the underline under it.
examples.prompt: Make a tab bar with three tabs (Songs, Albums, Artists); tapping a tab shows its panel and slides an underline under it.
teaches: Bind the Tabs component's selected index to a document variable ("selected": "@tab"): a tap sets it and the underline slides by itself
Show one panel at a time with a visibility modifier bound to a variable that is exactly 0 or 1, computed from the index in resources.variables: show1 = 1 - min(1, abs(@tab - 1))
Stack the panels in one box so the gone ones take no space

snippets.note: tab, and show0..show2: 1 for the selected panel, 0 for the others, derived from @tab
Tabs bound to @tab: a tap sets the index
visibility: @show2
1 - min(1, abs(@tab - 2)): 1 only on the third tab

check.describe: Starts on Songs (the Songs card); a tap on Artists shows the Artists card and slides the underline under the third tab. Resized, the three tabs share the width: tapping the third tab moves the underline under Artists at 234 and at 540 wide.

expect.layout_changes: the Artists panel becomes visible and Songs goes

pitfalls: visibility takes a DECLARED variable that is exactly 0 or 1: a resources.variables expression of the tab index works (1 - min(1, abs(@tab - i))); a number literal is a variable id, and an inline function call in the modifier is not
Tabs only sets the index: the panels are yours to switch, by visibility (they take no space when gone) or by graphicsLayer alpha (CMP-06)
Stack the panels in one box: gone panels take no space, so the visible one fills it
Accessibility inspectors may still list the hidden panels (the inspector does not yet drop GONE components)

examples.name: host-actions
examples.title: Media controls that reach the app
examples.summary: Previous / play-pause / next IconButtons and a seek Button: every tap sends the app a named action (hostNamedAction), the seek one with a payload, and the play-pause tap also flips an exported playing variable that swaps the icon.
examples.prompt: Make media controls: previous, play/pause and next buttons; each tap must reach the app, and play/pause must toggle its icon.
teaches: Send the app a tap by name with {"onClick": {"type": "hostNamedAction", "name": "next"}}; the app receives "next" and nothing in the document changes
Attach a payload with "value": a fixed string ({"type": "hostNamedAction", "name": "seek", "value": "90"}); a "@variable" there is sent as the literal text, not its value

Do both from one tap with a list: [{"type": "valueFloatExpressionChange", "target": "@playing", "value": "1 - @playing"}, {"type": "hostNamedAction", "name": "playPause"}], so the app is told and can also read the exported playing

Library IconButton and Button take the same action or list in their onClick param and label the target from label; swap the play and pause icons with two canvases whose visibility is "@playing" and "1 - @playing"

snippets.note: a tap the app receives by name: hostNamedAction "next"
a named action with a payload: "seek" with the fixed string value "90"
one tap, two actions: flip the exported playing (1 - @playing) and tell the app "playPause"
playing: an exported float the app can read, 0 or 1
the icon slot: a box stacking the play canvas (visibility "1 - @playing") and the pause canvas (visibility "@playing")
the status line: two texts in a box, Paused shown by visibility "1 - @playing", Playing by "@playing"

playing.meaning: 1 while playing, 0 while paused; the app can set it to reflect its own state

check.describe: Starts paused (play triangle on the filled button, status "Paused"); a tap on the middle button shows the pause bars and "Playing", and sends the app playPause. Previous, next and the seek button change nothing on screen: their actions go to the app. Resized, the centred row keeps its three 40 dp buttons and the seek button under it.

expect.changed_variables: playing goes from 0 to 1; the play canvas goes (visibility 0) and the pause canvas shows (visibility 1)
expect.host_actions: playPause is sent on the middle button; previous, next and seek (value "90") on the others

pitfalls: An exported variable alone only changes what the app can read; the app is told about a tap only by a hostNamedAction, so a tap that must reach the app carries one (alone or in the onClick list)
hostNamedAction value is a fixed string: "@playing" would arrive as the text "@playing"; to send live state, export the variable and have the app read it when the action arrives
hostNamedAction has no visible effect in a renderer: the inspector's interactions task lists it under the target (HostNamedAction with its name and value text ids); do not expect a variable to change
visibility reads an integer: a float that is exactly 0 or 1 ("@playing") and the integer expression "1 - @playing" both work; a fraction (0.999) would hide the component
Keep the play and pause canvases the same size in one box so the button does not change size when the icon swaps

examples.name: column-stack
examples.title: Column stack
examples.summary: Three 60 dp squares stacked in a column 8 dp apart, centred in the document.
examples.prompt: Stack three coloured squares vertically with an 8 dp gap, centred in the screen.
examples.hand_built: The coloured squares are plain boxes on purpose: the column, its alignment and its spacedBy gap are the lesson; in a screen the children would be components such as Card or ListItem, stacked the same way.
teaches: Stack children vertically with a column
Centre them across the column with horizontalAlignment center, and as a group along it with verticalArrangement center
Put an even 8 dp gap between children with the spacedBy modifier

snippets.note: a column with fillMaxSize, spacedBy 8 and centred alignment
cross-axis centring; verticalArrangement centres the group on the main axis
spacedBy is a modifier, not a column property

check.describe: Three squares at x=120, y=52/120/188 (Java reference layout), 8 px apart. Resized (200×300, 450×220) the column of three squares stays centred in the document.

pitfalls: spacedBy is a modifier ({"spacedBy": 8} in modifiers), not a column property
In a column, horizontalAlignment is the cross axis and verticalArrangement the main axis; the parser reads either spelling for the same field, so verticalAlignment center also centres the group

examples.name: row-arrangements
examples.title: Row arrangements
examples.summary: Six labelled rows of three squares, one for each horizontalArrangement: start, center, end, spaceBetween, spaceEvenly and spaceAround.
examples.prompt: Show how start, center, end, spaceBetween, spaceEvenly and spaceAround distribute three squares in a row, one labelled row each.
examples.hand_built: Plain squares, so the only thing that changes from row to row is horizontalArrangement; a real row arranges components (Button, Chip, IconButton) the same way.
teaches: Distribute a row's children along its width with horizontalArrangement (start, center, end, spaceBetween, spaceEvenly, spaceAround)
Centre children across the row with verticalAlignment center
Give each demo track the remaining width with weight 1 after a fixed-width label (a text with a width modifier)

snippets.note: horizontalArrangement spaceBetween: first and last squares touch the ends
spaceEvenly: four equal gaps, ends included
spaceAround: half-size gaps at the ends

check.describe: In each 236 px track the squares sit left, centred, right, at both ends, with four equal gaps, and with half gaps at the ends. Resized (240, 540 wide) the label column keeps its width and each track takes the rest, so the arrangements spread over the wider tracks and pack tighter in the narrow ones.

pitfalls: Arrangement only shows when the row is wider than its children: give the row a width (here weight 1) or every value looks like start
In a row the main axis is horizontalArrangement and the cross axis verticalAlignment; the parser reads either spelling of each for the same field, so the name does not switch axes

examples.name: box-alignment
examples.title: Box alignment
examples.summary: Nine labelled tiles in one 300×300 box, each placed at one of the nine alignments from top-start to bottom-end.
examples.prompt: Place nine labelled tiles in one box, one at each corner, edge midpoint and the centre.
examples.hand_built: Plain labelled tiles, so the nine box alignments are all that is on screen; a real overlay, such as a Badge on an Avatar's corner, aligns a library component the same way.
teaches: Overlap children by putting them in a box; each child is laid out on top of the previous one
Place a child at a corner, edge or centre with the box's horizontalAlignment (start/center/end) and verticalAlignment (top/center/bottom)
Give each child its own position by wrapping it in a fillMaxSize box with its own alignment
Make a fixed-width label tile from a single text: width, clip, background, vertical padding and textAlign center

snippets.note: top-start: a fillMaxSize box with horizontalAlignment start, verticalAlignment top
bottom-end: horizontalAlignment end, verticalAlignment bottom
the outer box stacks nine full-size layers
a tile as one text: fillMaxWidth 0.3 (never overlaps when narrow), clip, background, padding [0, 11], textAlign center

check.describe: Tiles at the four corners, the four edge midpoints and the centre of the padded box. Resized (200×300, 450×220) the tiles stay at the nine anchors: each tile is 30 % of the width, so they never overlap, and labels that no longer fit end in an ellipsis.

pitfalls: Alignment belongs to the container, not the child: there is no per-child align modifier, and contentAlignment is not a JSON key. Wrap each child in its own fillMaxSize box to align children differently
A box with no children defaults to center/center but one with children defaults to start/top in the Java parser
textAlign centres text only inside the text's own width: give the text a width (or fillMaxWidth), otherwise it wraps its content and there is nothing to centre in
Fixed-width tiles in a box overlap once the box is narrower than three of them: size them as a fraction of the width ({"fillMaxWidth": 0.3}) and give the labels maxLines 1 with an ellipsis

examples.name: weights
examples.title: Proportional weights
examples.summary: A row split 1:2:1 and a column split 1:1, both filling whatever size they get.
examples.prompt: Split a row into three boxes in a 1:2:1 ratio and the space below into two equal halves.
examples.hand_built: Plain weighted boxes, because the 1:2:1 and 1:1 split is the lesson; in a screen put components (Card, StatTile) inside the weighted boxes, or use AdaptiveSplit or TwoColumns for a split that adapts.
teaches: Split a row's width between children with weight (1:2:1)
Let the last section take the remaining height with verticalWeight in a column (weight alone is horizontal)
Separate weighted children with fixed-size spacer boxes, which weights do account for

snippets.note: three boxes, weights 1, 2 and 1
a column taking the rest of the height (verticalWeight 1), split 1:1 with verticalWeight
an 8 px spacer box between weighted children

check.describe: At 360 wide the middle box is twice the side ones; at 600 wide still 1:2:1. Resized (240×360, 540×300) the weights keep their 1:2:1 and 1:1 shares of whatever space there is.

pitfalls: Weights ignore spacedBy: a 1:2:1 row with spacedBy 8 overflows by the gaps (the Java reference does this too); use spacer boxes between weighted children
weight is horizontal; in a column use verticalWeight

examples.name: size-constraints
examples.title: Size constraints
examples.summary: Five labelled boxes showing fixed width/height, size, and how widthIn and heightIn clamp a fill or an explicit size.
examples.prompt: Show how width, size, widthIn(min, max) and heightIn constrain boxes, with each rule written above its box.
examples.hand_built: Plain boxes, so each size rule (width, size, widthIn, heightIn) is visible on its own; library components size themselves, so constrain a box around a Button or Card the way these boxes are constrained.
teaches: Fix a box's size with width/height, or both at once with size
Cap a fillMaxWidth box with widthIn(min, max) so it stops growing on wide screens
Raise or cap an explicit width or height with widthIn / heightIn (width 40 + widthIn(100, 260) is 100 wide)

snippets.note: width 120 + height 28
size 40: one value for both axes
fillMaxWidth then widthIn [100, 260]: fills, but never wider than 260
width 40 + widthIn [100, 260]: the minimum wins, 100
height 80 + heightIn [16, 40]: clamped to 40

check.describe: Java reference: at width 200 the boxes are 120×28, 40×40, 176×28, 100×28, 120×40; at width 500 the third is 260×28 and the rest are unchanged. Resized (220, 540 wide) only the fillMaxWidth bar changes: it fills the width up to its 260 cap; the fixed and widthIn-bounded boxes keep their sizes, which is the point.

pitfalls: widthIn/heightIn take a two-element array [min, max]
widthIn's minimum does not lift a fractional fillMaxWidth(0.3): at width 200 it stays 52.8 wide in the Java reference whatever the modifier order
