An explicit size is still clamped by widthIn/heightIn: height 80 + heightIn(16, 40) is 40 tall, and width 40 + widthIn(100, 260) is 100 wide

examples.name: padding-offset-border
examples.title: Padding, offset and border
examples.summary: An outer card with a 2 dp rounded border and 16 dp padding, holding an inner card nudged by offset (8, 8) with rounded, clipped corners.
examples.prompt: A card with a 2 dp rounded outline and 16 dp padding containing a smaller rounded card nudged 8 dp right and down.
examples.hand_built: The card is written out because its border, padding and offset modifiers are the lesson; for a real card use Card, which draws its mono outline as a background ring since border can't take a theme colour.
teaches: Draw a rounded outline with the border modifier {width, cornerRadius, color}, then inset the content with padding
Shift a child without changing the layout of its siblings with offset {x, y}
Round a card's corners with clip roundedRect before its background, so the background is clipped too

snippets.note: border 2 dp, corner 16, then padding 16
offset {x: 8, y: 8}
clip roundedRect 12 then background: the order matters

check.describe: The purple inner card starts 8 px right and below the outer card's padded corner (at 44, 44 instead of 36, 36), with rounded corners. Resized (200, 450 wide) the bordered frame fills the document inside its padding; the offset card keeps its size and its (8, 8) shift.

pitfalls: border cannot take an @colors reference: give it a literal colour
Modifier order is the paint order: clip must come before background or the background corners stay square; padding after background insets the content, not the background
offset moves only the drawing: the inner card keeps its layout slot, so it can overflow the outer padding (here it ends 8 dp further right and down)
border's cornerRadius only rounds with "shape": 2 (ROUNDED_RECTANGLE); the default shape 0 is a plain rectangle in Java, whatever the radius

examples.name: spacers
examples.title: Toolbar spacers
examples.summary: A toolbar row whose weighted spacer pushes two icon buttons (search, more) to the right end at any width.
examples.prompt: A toolbar with a title on the left and two action icons pushed to the right edge.
examples.hand_built: The row, its weighted spacer and the 12 dp gap are written out because they are the lesson; for a real app bar use TopBar, which pushes its actions slot to the end the same way.
teaches: Push the following children to the end of a row with a spacer carrying weight 1
Put a fixed gap between two icons with a spacer of width 12
Centre the title and the IconButtons vertically in the toolbar with verticalAlignment center

snippets.note: spacer with weight 1 takes all the free width
a fixed 12 dp spacer between the icons

check.describe: The More options button's 48 dp touch target is flush with the 16 dp padded right edge, Search 12 dp before it, at every width. Resized (240, 540 wide) the weighted spacer absorbs the change: Inbox stays at the start and the two icon buttons at the end.

pitfalls: A spacer with no modifiers gets weight 1 in the Java parser; a spacer with any modifier (such as width 12) gets no weight, so state the weight explicitly when you add one
Padding takes a list: [all], [horizontal, vertical] (here [16, 0]) or [start, top, end, bottom]; a three-value list writes no padding at all

examples.name: flow-chips
examples.title: Wrapping tag chips
examples.summary: Twelve library Chips of different lengths (three preselected) in a flow that wraps them onto new lines and scrolls when they outgrow the box.
examples.prompt: A wrapping row of rounded tag chips of different lengths that flows onto new lines.
teaches: Wrap children onto new lines when the row is full with a flow
Fill the flow with library Chip calls: each is a tappable pill (a 0/1 selected state, preset with "selected": 1) in a 48 dp tall touch target
Space flow items with padding on a wrapper box (8 dp at the end only: the chip's 48 dp target already spaces the lines), since a flow ignores spacedBy

snippets.note: a fillMaxWidth flow of twelve chips
one item: a wrapper box with end padding around a Chip

check.describe: Three lines of chips at width 360, Kotlin, Compose and Canvas filled (selected); the twelfth chip, Accessibility, wraps to a fourth line below the fold and scrolls into view. Resized: at 540 wide the chips fill two lines; at 240 wide they need more lines than than 140 dp holds, so the root scrolls vertically (verticalScroll) instead of overflowing.

pitfalls: A flow ignores the spacedBy modifier (the Java reference and the C++ player both lay the chips edge to edge); give each item its own gap with padding on a wrapper
A Chip is 48 dp tall (its 32 dp pill plus 8 dp above and below), so lines of chips need no bottom gap; add one and the lines drift apart

Do not fold the gap into the chip as a leading padding ([padding, clip, background, padding]): the Java player treats that first padding as a margin, but the C++ player paints the background over it, so keep the separate wrapper box
The Java layout reference measures text with a stub (100×10), so check line counts with the C++ or TypeScript layout, not java-layout.sh
A flow grows taller as its box narrows: in a fixed-height widget give the container a verticalScroll (or fewer items) or the last lines overflow the document

examples.name: fitbox-responsive
examples.title: Responsive fitBox
examples.summary: One weather card in a large, a medium and a small layout inside a fitBox, which shows the first one that fits the space it gets.
examples.prompt: A weather widget that shows a large, medium or small layout depending on how much space it gets.
examples.hand_built: The three variants are plain fixed-size columns, each in its own colour, so the one fitBox picks is obvious at a glance; a real weather widget would fill each variant with a WeatherIcon and Card-style surface.
teaches: Offer alternative layouts of the same content as fitBox children, ordered largest first: the first that fits without shrinking is shown and the others are gone
Give each alternative a fixed size (360×180, 230×130, 130×80) so the fit test has something to compare
Centre the chosen layout by letting the fitBox wrap it inside a centring box

snippets.note: fitBox with three children: large, medium, small
the smallest fallback, 130×80, with only the temperature

check.describe: Large card at 400×200, medium at 250×150, small at 150×100 (render_rc with width/height). The medium and small renders are the resize checks; wider than 400 the large card stays 360×180, centred.

pitfalls: Children are tried in order and the first that fits wins, so put the largest first; a fallback that is listed first hides the others
Give each alternative a fixed size: a fillMaxSize child takes whatever space it is given, so it always fits and the fallbacks after it never show

examples.name: vertical-scroll-list
examples.title: Vertical scrolling list
examples.summary: A 360×400 contact list of 12 ListItem rows (Avatar, name, preview line) in a column that scrolls when dragged.
examples.prompt: A scrollable contact list with a round avatar, a name and a message preview on each row.
teaches: Make a column taller than the document scroll with the verticalScroll modifier
Bind the scroll position to a variable (resources.variables scroll: 0, verticalScroll "@scroll") so the player can drive and read it
Fill the scrolling column with library ListItem rows, an Avatar in each one's leading slot: the column only scrolls, the rows bring their own 64 dp height, padding and text styles

snippets.note: the scroll position variable, starting at 0
verticalScroll bound to @scroll
one row: a ListItem with title, subtitle and an Avatar in its leading slot

check.describe: Before the drag rows 1–6 are visible; after dragging (180,350)→(180,50) the list is scrolled to its end, showing rows 7–12. Resized (300×560, 540×300) the rows stretch to the width and the list scrolls in whatever height it gets; the same swipe moves it by the same 300 dp.

pitfalls: A list only scrolls if its content is taller than the viewport: here 12 × 64 dp rows in a 400 dp document

examples.name: horizontal-carousel
examples.title: Horizontal carousel
examples.summary: Five 200 dp destination cards in a row that scrolls sideways when dragged.
examples.prompt: A horizontally swipeable carousel of destination cards.
examples.hand_built: The cards are plain full-height columns because the lesson is horizontalScroll with each card's text anchored to its bottom; the library Card wraps its content's height, so it cannot fill the carousel's height and anchor text there. Use Card when its content can start at the top.
teaches: Let a row wider than its container scroll sideways with horizontalScroll bound to a variable
Space fixed-width cards with a spacedBy 12 modifier (fine here: no child has a weight)
Anchor a card's text to its bottom with verticalArrangement bottom

snippets.note: horizontalScroll bound to @scroll, after the padding
one card: width 200, fillMaxHeight, rounded, bottom-aligned text
the scroll position variable

check.describe: At rest cards 1 and 2 show; after dragging from x=330 to x=30 cards 3 and 4 are in view. Resized: at 540 wide more of the cards show after the same swipe; at 160 high the cards fill the shorter height, their captions staying at the bottom.

pitfalls: Bind the scroll position to a variable: the C++ player does not scroll a constant position such as {"horizontalScroll": 0}
For snapping pages instead of free scrolling see INT-06 (pager)

examples.name: visibility
examples.title: Gone versus invisible
examples.summary: Two A-B-C lists side by side: on the left B is gone and its space collapses, on the right B is invisible and leaves a gap.
examples.prompt: Three items where the middle one has visibility gone, then invisible (two variants side by side).
examples.hand_built: The A, B and C bars are plain texts so the visibility modifier is the only thing that differs between the columns; it works the same on a wrapper box around any component (Card, ListItem).
teaches: Hide a component with the visibility modifier, which reads an integer variable: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible
Collapse a hidden item's space with gone (0), or keep its space with invisible (2)
Declare each visibility as an exported integer in resources ("@leftB") so the host can show or hide the item

snippets.note: exported integers leftB = 0 (gone) and rightB = 2 (invisible)
B with visibility @leftB (0, gone): C moves up
B with visibility @rightB (2, invisible): a gap stays

leftB.meaning: visibility of the left B: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible

rightB.meaning: visibility of the right B: 0 gone, 1 visible, 2 invisible

check.describe: Left: A then C directly below it. Right: A, an empty slot the size of B, then C (Java reference: right C 44 px lower than left C). Setting rightB to 1 shows B again. Resized (240, 540 wide) the two panels share the width; at 240 the "B invisible (2)" caption wraps, and the gap B leaves is still there.

pitfalls: visibility takes an integer variable id, not a boolean or a string: a literal such as {"visibility": 2} is read as variable id 2, not the value invisible
Unexported integers used only by visibility are reported as dead_code by the audit; exporting them (the host's switch) avoids it
Invisible keeps B's space and its spacedBy gap; gone removes both

examples.name: collapsible-row
examples.title: Collapsible app bar (priorities)
examples.summary: An Inbox app bar shown at five widths: a collapsibleRow drops its children by collapsiblePriority as space runs out (the unread Badge first, then share, then search), keeps the unprioritized title and overflow menu longest, and a weighted spacer keeps the IconButtons pushed to the end at every width.
examples.prompt: An app bar (title "Inbox", a "12 new" chip, search, share and an overflow menu) that drops its least important items as it narrows: the chip first, then share, then search; the title and the overflow menu stay. Show it at 328, 240, 200, 152 and 112 dp.
examples.hand_built: The bar is a collapsibleRow written out, not a TopBar, because dropping actions by collapsiblePriority is the lesson and TopBar has no priorities; its actions are library IconButtons and the unread count a Badge.
teaches: Let a collapsibleRow decide what fits: children are kept in priority order (highest first) and dropped from the lowest priority up once the next one no longer fits
Rank children with collapsiblePriority {orientation: horizontal, priority: N}; leave the must-stay ones (title, overflow menu) without a priority, which counts as the highest
Push the actions to the end with an unprioritized weighted spacer: it takes only the space left over and never causes a drop
Size the container, not the collapsibleRow, when its children include a weight: give the row fillMaxWidth inside a box of the width you want
Give a component call a priority by wrapping it in a box that carries the collapsiblePriority modifier: a call such as IconButton or Badge takes no modifiers of its own
pitfalls: Unprioritized children all tie at the top and keep document order among themselves: at 112 dp the title (first) stays and the overflow menu (last) goes

The fit test adds up the children's widths only, not spacedBy: with spacedBy 10 a 225 dp row keeps 220 dp of children and overflows by 20 dp. Build gaps into the children's own widths (as the 76 dp title box does) instead
Priorities compare by the integer part of their difference, so values less than 1 apart tie and 2, 2.5, 3 is not a consistent order (at 250 dp Java keeps 3 and 2 and drops 2.5): use whole numbers
Dropping stops at the first child that does not fit: a lower-priority child that is narrow enough to fit is dropped too, so give similar-sized items adjacent priorities

Don't give the weighted spacer a priority: it is then ranked and dropped like any other child as soon as space is short (at 200 dp a priority-0 spacer went while 40 dp were still free), and the remaining items re-centre instead of staying at the ends
A child with a weight makes a row or collapsibleRow ignore its own width modifier and fill its parent (Java, matched by both players): wrap it in a box of the width you want

A nested collapsibleRow is measured against the width left after its earlier siblings in document order, not after the higher-priority ones, so its own drops can interleave oddly with the parent's (an inner label kept while a higher-priority sibling goes, then the reverse a few dp narrower)
A demo of fixed widths overflows a narrower host if one of them is as wide as the header's content area: make the widest one fillMaxWidth so it becomes the live, resizing case

snippets.note: the whole bar: collapsibleRow with title, Badge, spacer and three IconButtons
the Badge's wrapper box, collapsiblePriority 1: the first to go
the search IconButton's wrapper box, priority 3: the last action to go
unprioritized weighted spacer: takes the leftover width only

check.describe: Five bars: the first is full width (328 dp at 360) and shows everything; 240 dp drops the "12 new" Badge; 200 dp also drops share; 152 dp also drops search (title and overflow menu left); 112 dp keeps only the title. The IconButtons (48 dp targets) stay right-aligned in every bar. In mono the bars are outlined so their widths stay visible. Resized: the full-width bar is the live one — at 300 wide (268 dp) it has already dropped the Badge, at 540 it shows everything with the icons at the far end; the four fixed-width bars below are unchanged.

examples.name: collapsible-column
examples.title: Collapsible weather column
examples.summary: A narrow weather widget at four heights: a collapsibleColumn keeps city and temperature (no priority), then the icon, high/low and condition by vertical collapsiblePriority, and three tied forecast rows that drop from the bottom up.
examples.prompt: A tall, narrow weather widget (city, sun icon, temperature, condition, high/low, three hourly forecast rows) that sheds content as it gets shorter: the forecast rows go first from the bottom, then the condition, then high/low, then the icon; city and temperature always stay. Show it at 256, 208, 164 and 100 dp.
teaches: Stack a widget's content in a collapsibleColumn so rows that don't fit the height are dropped instead of clipped
Rank the rows with collapsiblePriority {orientation: vertical, priority: N}; leave the rows that must stay (city, temperature) without one
Give repeated rows the same priority: tied children keep document order, so the forecast drops from the bottom row up
Put the padding and background on a wrapping box and give the collapsibleColumn fillMaxSize, so fillMaxWidth rows stay inside the padding
pitfalls: The priority's orientation must match the container: a horizontal collapsiblePriority on a collapsibleColumn child is ignored and the child counts as unprioritized (kept first)

A collapsibleColumn's own padding is not applied to its children's fill width: a fillMaxWidth row inside a padded collapsibleColumn comes out as wide as the column and offset by -padding (Java, matched by both players). Pad a wrapping box instead
Rows are kept in priority order, not document order: at 164 dp high/low (priority 3) stays while the condition above it (priority 2) goes, and the remaining rows close up

Dropping stops at the first row that does not fit: every row after it in priority order goes too, even one small enough for the space left (a 10 dp priority-1 row is dropped under a 40 dp priority-2 row that did not fit). Give similar-sized rows adjacent priorities
Give the rows fixed heights (here 20–48 dp boxes) when the result has to be predictable: a text's height depends on the font and the player

A row of fixed-width demo cards is wider than a narrow host: give the row a horizontalScroll (bound to a variable — a literal position leaves its touch expression unused, which the audit reports as dead code)

snippets.note: the collapsibleColumn with its eight rows, inside the padded card box
condition, vertical priority 2: goes before high/low (3) and the icon (4)
a forecast row, priority 1: the three tie and drop bottom-up

hour.meaning: hour of the first forecast row (0-23); the next rows are +3 h and +6 h

check.describe: Four cards: the first fills the height (256 dp at 300) and shows everything; 208 dp keeps one forecast row; 164 dp keeps city, icon, temperature and high/low (the condition and forecast are gone); 100 dp keeps city and temperature only. Verified against Java (java-layout.sh 360 300): the same rows are gone and the C++ and TS bounds match it. Resized: the full-height card is the live one — at 360×200 it (and the taller fixed cards, squeezed to the row) keep city, icon and temperature; at 360×400 it shows everything with room to spare; at 240 wide the row scrolls horizontally (horizontalScroll) rather than cutting the last card.

examples.name: state-layout
examples.title: Three-state status card (StateLayout)
examples.summary: A photo-backup card with three layouts (up to date, backing up, paused) held by a stateLayout and picked by an exported integer: each state's root taps to the next state, and components paired by animationSpec animationId (the card, its header row, the badge, the title) morph between them while the rest enter and exit.
examples.prompt: A photo backup status card with three states chosen by an integer the host can set: a compact "Up to date" row, an expanded "Backing up" card with a progress bar and Pause/Details buttons, and a red "Paused, no Wi-Fi" card with Retry. Tapping the card goes to the next state, and the card animates its size and the header between them.
teaches: Hold one layout per state as the children of a stateLayout and pick one with indexId, a variable (here an exported integer the host can set to 0, 1 or 2; use a float when an expression or a TextChoice reads it too, as both read an integer as 0)
Advance the state from each state's root: an onClick with valueIntegerChange to the next index (1, 2, then back to 0), with semantics describing what the tap does
Pair the parts that exist in every state with the same animationSpec animationId (card 200, header row 203, badge 201, title 202) so they morph in size and position; unpaired parts enter and exit
Size each state for its own content (72, 148 and 128 dp): only the current state is measured, so the stateLayout resizes with it
pitfalls: An onClick on the stateLayout itself is not dispatched by Java: put one on every state root
Pair components with animationSpec animationId: the `id` modifier (component id) does not pair them across states. The state roots need no component ids at all; give them distinct ones if you set any

Keep paired components at the same depth in every state (here each state's header is one row with animationId 203): during the transition the previous state's direct children that the new state lacks are painted as exiting, so a badge that is a direct child in one state and nested in another was painted twice (a stray green corner in the C++ player)
Keep a paired text the same size in every state: its bounds morph, and a text that grows is cut short mid-transition ("Photo" instead of "Photo backup")

The index is read at paint time and the new state is laid out on the next frame, so capture a change at least a frame later. An index with no matching child is ignored: with state 3 the card stays on the state it had (state 0 at start) in Java and C++, so keep the exported range 0..2

examples.summary: A run summary (8.42 km, 42:10 min, 5′01″ /km) twice: with the row's default centring the small units float at mid-height, with alignByBaseline on the number and the unit they share the number's text baseline.
examples.prompt: A run summary card with three stats (distance 8.42 km, time 42:10 min, pace 5′01″ /km), each a big number followed by a small unit that sits on the number's baseline, with a label below. Show the same card with default centring above it for comparison.
examples.hand_built: Each stat is a hand-built row of number and unit because baseline alignment is the lesson; the cards around them are library Cards, and a KPI without this lesson is a StatTile or BigNumber.
teaches: Put alignByBaseline on every text of a row to line their first baselines up, whatever their font sizes
Keep a unit next to its number in its own small row, and lay the stats out in a collapsibleRow with spaceBetween so a narrow card drops the last stat instead of cutting it

Player status (2026-10-29): the C++ player aligns baselines; the TS player ignores alignByBaseline and puts the units at the top of the row. The Java layout harness (MockRemoteContext) measures every text 100×10, so it can't check baselines

Weighted stat columns (weight 1 each) never shrink below their content: when the card narrows the numbers overlap and the last unit is cut. Size stats to their content in a collapsibleRow (spaceBetween) so the last one drops out; a weighted child is never dropped by a collapsibleRow

examples.name: watch-face
examples.title: A premium analog watch face with steps, battery and an always-on mode
examples.summary: A 227x227 round watch face drawn in 3.5 KB: faceted dauphine hands with drop shadows, a smooth sweeping second hand with a counterweight, exact 60-minute track and hour batons from two loops, a steps ring from host variables at nine, a battery ring from the system battery at three (amber below 40%, red with LOW below 20%), and the weekday and date at six. The always-on (mono) look drops the second hand, the gradient and the colour, and outlines the hands.
examples.prompt: Design a premium round watch face (227x227, it should scale to any round watch): analog hands with a smooth second hand, the date, a battery arc from the system battery that turns red when low, my steps as a ring from a host value, and an always-on mode.
examples.hand_built: A watch face is a drawing, not a layout: the hands, the dauphine facets, the shadows and the exact tick geometry are canvas commands in one 227-unit design space scaled to the screen; AnalogClock draws a plainer clock and has no complications.
teaches: One design space for every watch: k = min(componentWidth(), componentHeight()) / 227, a translate that centres it and a scale by k; the same document is crisp at 192, 227, 300 and 454 px
A smooth (sweeping) second hand: rotate by (continuousSec() % 60) * 6. continuousSec() has a fraction, timeInSec() does not (that is a ticking hand)

Faceted dauphine hands: two static triangles per hand (resources.paths), a light and a darker facet, drawn after a translate (1.2, 2.4) copy in black at alpha 0.45 for the shadow. The translate goes before the rotate so the shadow falls the same way whatever the hand's angle

Exact ticks with no table: a 60-step loop rotating i * 6 about the centre with paint alpha min(1, i % 5), so the hour positions are skipped; batons from a 1..11 loop whose length is ifElse(21, 17, step(i % 3, 0.5)) (longer at 3, 6, 9) and a double baton at 12

Battery from the system: batteryLevel() (system variable 38), its arc's sweep max(3.6, 3.6 * level) and its colour by two conditionalOperations (lt 40 amber, lt 20 red); the label swaps BATTERY for LOW the same way
Steps from the host: exported steps and stepGoal, a ring of 360 * clamp(0, 1, steps / goal) and the count grouped by thousands (textFromFloat flags 20: no padding, groups of three)
The date window: the weekday cut from "MONTUEWEDTHUFRISATSUN" with textSubtext at (weekDay() - 1) * 3, the day zero-padded (flags 12)

Always-on: every look-dependent command is a {"$if": "theme.mono"} fork; the mono-dark build is the ambient document (black dial, outlined hollow hands, grey batons, no second hand, so it repaints once a minute instead of every frame)

Light and dark: every colour of the face is a themed colour in resources.colors (dark: the charcoal dial; light: a porcelain dial with gunmetal hands), and the dial gradient takes them by name ("@colors.dialHi"), so the face follows the system theme; mono keeps to the theme tokens
pitfalls: batteryLevel() is a json2rc / C++ / TypeScript extension: the Java reference parser has no system battery (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U31) and refuses the expression. On Android today the host would export a float instead (as HST-03 does)
continuousSec() repaints every frame: right for the interactive face's sweeping hand, wrong for always-on. The mono look has no second hand, so it only wakes once a minute
The translate for a shadow must come before the rotate: after it, the shadow would turn with the hand and fall upwards at six o'clock
Text on a canvas does not take a font weight; the wordmark and figures are the default face at small sizes, so keep them few and short

snippets.note: the 227-unit design space scaled to the screen
the sweeping second hand: rotate (continuousSec() % 60) * 6, shadow first
steps and stepGoal exported for the app; batt reads batteryLevel()

Sizes 192, 300 and 454 are the same face scaled. light: a porcelain dial (white to pale grey), gunmetal faceted hands with soft grey shadows, black batons, deeper green, amber and red rings and a vermilion second hand; battery-low-light shows the red LOW ring on it.

examples.name: orbit-catcher
examples.title: Orbit catcher: a one-tap arcade game
examples.summary: A complete one-tap game in a single canvas: a glowing dot circles a planet, each tap reverses it, and you must catch each star before its countdown ring empties while dodging a red comet that shares the orbit. Score, best score, a start screen, a game-over screen and tap-to-restart are all real: the whole game state lives in a one-particle system whose equations advance every frame.
examples.prompt: Make an original tap game: a dot orbits a planet and each tap flips its direction, to catch stars that appear on the orbit. Keep a score, end the game when a star's timer runs out or a red comet hits you, and let me tap to play again.
examples.hand_built: A game loop is not a component: the state machine is a one-particle system whose equations are the game rules, and everything else is drawn by hand around it.
teaches: Persistent per-frame state: a createParticles system with count 1 is a set of variables the player integrates every frame (th, score, lf, alive, ...). Each particlesLoop equation is the next value of one variable, computed from the previous frame's values

The equations update simultaneously: every equation reads last frame's values, so a flag such as the catch c is seen by score, sa and lf on the frame after it is set. Guard one-frame events against firing twice: c = alive * step(cos(th - sa), 0.988) * (1 - c)

Game rules as branchless expressions: ifElse(else, then, cond) and step(a, b) (a > b ? 1 : 0) for the catch, the comet hit, the countdown, game over (alive), the cool-down after death (dT) and the restart (rs)

Tap input: onTouchDown on the canvas runs two valueFloatExpressionChange actions, @dir = 0 - @dir and @taps = @taps + 1. The game compares @taps with the count it last saw to detect a restart tap, so no action needs to know the game's state
Particle variables stay readable after the loop: the HUD's textFromFloat(score) and every drawCircle around the orbit use them directly
Deterministic levels: new star positions come from fract(sin(score * 91.7 + 3.1) * 437.5), not rand(), so a scripted tap sequence plays the same game in every player
Difficulty ramps with the score inside the equations: orbit speed 1.8 + 0.045 * min(score, 24) rad/s, the star's time max(1.6, 3.6 - 0.08 * score) s, the comet speed up with it
pitfalls: Never write ifElse(then, else, cond): the order is ifElse(else, then, cond). ifElse(0, dT + dt, alive) froze the death timer and made restart impossible

createParticles initialValues may use only literals and the particle index u: the C++ player evaluates them against an empty context, so a global (@taps) there reads 0. Do resets in the equations instead
A colour op in a paint bundle resets the alpha to the colour's own: set the alpha after the colour, in every bundle that needs it
Equations must stay at 32 RPN entries or fewer for Android (rc-inspect audit expression_too_long)
rc-render's `tap` event only fires onClick; the game listens to onTouchDown, so script down/up pairs

check.describe: Start: a dark starfield, a blue planet with a faint ring in the centre, a thin orbit, a cyan dot at the top, a yellow star and a red comet on the orbit, and 'Orbit catcher', two lines of rules and a pulsing 'Tap to start' over a dimmed scene, 'BEST 0' at the top. Playing (scripted taps): the score in the planet climbs (4 at 16 s), the star carries a countdown ring, the dot has a trail. Game over: 'Game over', 'Score 5', 'Tap to play again'. Restart: a new game at 0 with BEST 5 kept.

snippets.note: the game state: one particle, fifteen variables
the rules: one equation per state variable, run every frame
a tap reverses @dir and counts @taps
the score read straight from the particle variable
the star's countdown ring, 360 * lf
what the game is and how to play

examples.name: generative-art
examples.title: Generative art: a harmonograph that changes every minute
examples.summary: A slowly turning harmonograph drawn over an AGSL nebula, with fireflies carried by a vortex flow field. The figure is picked from the minute of the day, and over the last ten seconds of each minute it fades into the next. The nebula's hue drifts through the day.
examples.prompt: Make a piece of generative art for a phone or a frame: an evolving shader background, particles drifting in a flow field and a spirograph-like curve that slowly turns and becomes a different figure every minute. Gallery-worthy, and different every time you look.
examples.hand_built: A single canvas of maths: one AGSL shader, one particle system and two parametric paths. The component library has nothing for any of the three.
teaches: The figure is two rotating phasors, x = cx + R·e^(−0.02a)·(0.62·cos(a + p1) + 0.38·cos(a(n + d) + p2)), with y the same using sin. The integer n gives |n − 1| lobes. The small detune d makes the loops precess and fill the rose, and the damping spirals it inward. One pathExpression of 900 points over a = 0…24π draws it

Different every minute without jumping: nA comes from seed(m·3 + 1, rand()) with m = timeInMin(), and nB is the next minute's value. Both figures are drawn, crossfaded with fade = smooth_step(continuousSec() % 60, 60, 50), and the second figure is drawn only while fade > 0 (conditionalOperations)
A clock that moves smoothly all day: T = timeInHr()·3600 + continuousSec(). continuousSec() alone restarts every hour, which would make the phases jump

A flow field with no clumping: velocities from a stream function, vx = −k·sin(x·fx + k1)·sin(y·fy − k2), vy = −k·cos(x·fx + k1)·cos(y·fy − k2). This flow is divergence-free (Taylor-Green vortices). fx = 4π/W and fy = 4π/H make the field tile, so particles can wrap round the edges with %
Particles that never pop: each one has its own life and age = (age + 1) % life. It respawns at a random point (ifElse(rand()·W, …, age − 0.5)) exactly when its alpha, square(sin(π·age/life)), is 0

The glow is the same path stroked three times (7, 2.6 and 0.9 px at alpha 0.07, 0.22 and 0.9) with a sweep gradient. Eighteen beads ride the curve: the same formula evaluated in a loop at u = 75.4·fract(i/18 + T·0.003)

The AGSL background domain-warps uv three times with time-driven sines and mixes two cosine palettes. Its hue uniform is 0.62 + T·0.00004, so the colour drifts through the day. A vignette keeps the edges dark

Four looks. Dark is the nebula with pastel lines. Light lays a themed cream wash (@colors.wash: 84% cream in light, transparent in dark) over the same shader, so it reads as tinted paper, and the lines, sparks, beads and caption switch to deep inks through themed colours: the sweep gradient takes @colors refs. Mono ({"$if": "theme.mono"}) drops the shader, particles and glow: the figure is one hairline in onSurface with six dots, its phases from the minute (p1m = m·0.9), so an always-on screen repaints once a minute
pitfalls: Shader support: the AGSL nebula plays on Android 13+ (AGSL), in the C++/Skia player (SkRuntimeEffect) and in the TypeScript web player in a browser (transpiled to WebGL2). The headless TypeScript render (players/typescript/render.mjs) has no WebGL, so it stops at the shader with 'document is not defined'. Check the TypeScript side in a browser page instead (package_web)
A particle document needs frames: render with duration (and a seed) or the fireflies are still where they were seeded
Particle initialValues cannot read another particle variable ("rand() * @life" is refused: unknown token): give each its own expression
Keep each expression within Android's 32 entries: the figure formula is 26, so the frequencies and phases (nA, d, p1, p2) are separate named variables

rc-inspect's audit reports dead_code for k1, k2, fx, fy and the shader's hue uniform. They are read only by particle equations and a shader uniform, which the inspector does not count as reads (I18). The renders show them working
The ratio label switches figure at the middle of the crossfade (ifElse(nA, nB, fade − 0.5))

Resource variables are always written, even if only one look uses them (unlike canvas `variable`s, which are written at first use). The look-specific ones (T, fade, p1, k1, nB…) are declared at the top of the light/dark branch, so the mono documents carry no continuousSec() and do not repaint every frame
A paint `alpha` after a `color` replaces that colour's own alpha. Set a translucent themed colour without a following alpha op

snippets.note: AGSL nebula: three domain warps, two cosine palettes, vignette; uniforms iResolution, iTime = @T, uHue
180 fireflies: per-particle life and age, a divergence-free vortex field, wrap round and respawn at alpha 0
the harmonograph of the current minute, 900 points
crossfade over the last ten seconds of each minute
figure picked by seed(minute)
mono: the figure as one hairline in onSurface with six dots, its phases moving once a minute

check.describe: Dark nebula (violet, blue, teal or rose depending on the hour) with a glowing pastel harmonograph in the centre, beads on it, and warm firefly sparks drifting in swirls; a small centred caption 'Nº 0848 · 7-fold' at the bottom (edition = minute of the day + 1, and the figure's symmetry). 14:08 shows a different figure (3-fold); at :56 both figures are visible mid-crossfade; at 21:42 the figure and hue differ again. Resized, the figure stays centred at 0.4 × the short side and the particles fill the whole box. Light: cream paper with a faint tint of the nebula, deep-ink lines (indigo, teal, rose, ochre) and dark sparks. Mono-dark: a white hairline rose on black with a grey caption, no particles. Mono-light: the same in black on white.

examples.java_difference: json2rc writes 8 bytes fewer: after a paint with an AGSL runtime shader, {"shader": 0} becomes one PaintBundle SHADER 0 in json2rc and two in Java's parser (a minimal case: Java 249 B, json2rc 241 B). Both clear the shader, so the documents behave the same

examples.name: headphone-configurator
examples.title: A 3D product configurator: headphones to turn, recolour and explode
examples.summary: Wireless headphones built from 21 lit 3D draws of nine primitives (extruded arcs for the band, pad and yokes, a capped lathe for each cup, tori, dark cone drivers, cylinders) turn slowly on a turntable; a drag orbits the camera, four swatches cross-fade the shell and cushion colours, and Explode eases the parts apart while five labels, projected from 3D in the same canvas, follow their parts on the nearer cup. A fitBox swaps a phone layout (title above, swatch card below) for a tablet one (a side panel with specs), and the 3D framing follows.
examples.prompt: Make a product configurator for our Aura One headphones: a 3D model on a turntable people can drag round, colour swatches that repaint it, and an explode button that pulls the parts apart with labels. It should work on a phone (swatches under the model) and a tablet (a side panel).
examples.hand_built: Scene3D has no runtime colour or explode toggle and no projected labels: the camera orbit, the colour cross-fade (computed argb colours from float arrays) and the label projection are written by hand.
teaches: Orbit the camera instead of turning every part: eye = (-d cos(tilt) sin(spin), d sin(tilt), d cos(tilt) cos(spin)) and each part needs only identity + translate (+ its own rotation); turn the light directions by the same angles so the lighting stays on the viewer's side

Recolour a mesh at run time with a computed colour: resources.colors shell = {argb: [1, r, g, b]} where each channel is {value: arrayGet(@shR, @sel), anim: 0.5}, so a swatch tap cross-fades straight from the old colour to the new one
Explode an assembly with one eased variable: exA = {value: @ex, anim: 0.9}; every translate adds exA times the part's offset, and the camera distance grows with exA so the exploded model still fits

Label 3D parts from 2D: project each anchor with the same spin, tilt, distance and focal length (H / 2 / tan(fovY / 2)) in a loop over float arrays, and draw a dot, a leader line and textLookup's name after the meshes, faded in with exA
Put labels on the nearer side: the right cup is nearer while sin(spin) < 0, so the anchors' x is multiplied by the sign of -sin(spin)
Swap a phone and a tablet layout with a fitBox (a row with widthIn min 600 first, the column second), and let the 3D canvas behind them shift and reframe with step(componentWidth(), 599)
Draw a swatch row in one small canvas with a sliding selection ring (cx from an eased @selA) under a row of transparent tap boxes that carry the semantics and the onClick

Give a 3D product a mono look with one {"$if": "theme.mono"} around the meshes and draws: fewer segments, three saturating axis lights, every part filled in @colors.background and then drawn again as an onSurface wireframe with a small negative depthBias3D, so nearer parts hide the lines behind them; no turntable, no autorotation, no easing
Show a colour choice without hue in mono: outlined circles, the chosen one filled and ringed, and its name in text
Use the library Button for the toggle (label from a textLookup variable, fill, surface @colors.surface): it brings its light, dark and mono faces
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only
clamp(x, a, b) is min(max(x, b), a): the upper bound comes second. clamp(v, -1, 1) is always -1; write max(-1, min(v, 1))
A computed colour (argb/hsv) is written after all other resources and cannot read a root variable: keep the swatch index in resources.variables
The 3D buffer is window-sized and drawn at the canvas origin: keep the 3D canvas fillMaxSize behind the layout and move the model with a 2D translate rather than placing the canvas in the layout
rc-render with clock 0 (the epoch) freezes eased values in a touch simulation: pin a real date-time for interaction renders
Continuous repaint: the turntable reads continuousSec() every frame while shown

A short side panel must degrade: its content is a collapsibleColumn whose price, specs, sentence and hint are fixed-height slots with collapsiblePriority (sentence first, then the hint, then the specs from the bottom), so 640x360 keeps the title, colour, swatches, button and two specs without overlap
The TypeScript player carries paint state (stroke style) from one canvas into the next: end a canvas that strokes with a fill paint, or a library component's canvas drawn after it comes out outlined

check.describe: Phone: 'Aura One' and $349 at the top, dark (Midnight) headphones on a pale turntable disc, the band's ends straight over the aluminium yokes, the cups solid domes, a card below with 'Colour Midnight', four swatches (the first ringed) and an Explode view button. Exploded: the band lifts, cups move out, cushions in, yokes and sliders up in line under the band's ends, the dark 40 mm drivers between cups and cushions; five labelled leader lines (Headband, Foam cushion, 40 mm driver, Aluminium yoke, Ear cup) on the nearer cup, and the button says Assemble. examples.name: solar-system
examples.title: A 3D solar system that runs on the clock
examples.summary: The Sun and eight planets in 3D on a twinkling starfield: the Sun is a point light, so every planet shows a lit day side; the planets start where they really are today (mean longitudes from J2000 and the date) and run faster than real time at a chosen speed (a day, a week, a month or a year a second). A drag tilts and turns the camera from edge-on to straight down; tapping a planet's chip highlights its orbit and rings and names it in 3D; the panel fills a phone's width and sits in the corner of a wide window. Each orbit lies in its real plane (J2000 inclination and ascending node), with a Tilt ×5 checkbox to make the planes visibly different; a Zoom checkbox eases the camera in on the selected planet and follows it, gliding to a newly chosen one.
examples.prompt: Make a 3D solar system: the Sun and planets on their orbits moving with the clock but sped up, with a speed control, orbit rings, a starry background, drag to tilt the view, and tap a planet's name to see where it is.
examples.hand_built: Scene3D has no clock-driven orbits, point light or projected labels: the camera orbit, the sun-as-light, the date-anchored simulated time and the 2D highlight projected from 3D are written by hand.
teaches: Light a scene from inside: a single point light at the origin makes the Sun sphere fully lit (two-sided |N.L| is 1 everywhere) and gives each planet a day and a night side
Start the orbits at today's real positions: simT = year() - 2000 + dayOfYear() / 365.25 (years since J2000) and angle = simT * 2 pi / period + the planet's mean longitude at J2000

Change speed without the planets jumping: keep t0 and c0, and on a speed tap set t0 = @simT - @today and c0 = animationTime() before the new speed, so simT = today + t0 + (animationTime() - c0) * rate stays continuous

Draw every orbit ring with one unit torus scaled (r, 1, r) in a loop over a float array; draw the selected one first, thicker and in the accent colour, because the depth test keeps the first of two equal depths
Project the selected planet to 2D with the same spin, tilt, distance and focal length as the camera and draw a pulsing ring, a leader and its name after the meshes
Scatter 140 stars without random state on an R2 low-discrepancy sequence: x = fract(0.5 + i * 0.7549) * W, y = fract(0.5 + i * 0.5698) * H, each twinkling at its own rate

Give a dark art piece a designed light look: the same scene as a paper star chart (warm paper, grey dots for stars, darker orbit lines) from themed colours in resources.colors, the panel on @colors.surface

Fork the art for mono with {"$if": "theme.mono"}: no stars, glow or motion (the planets stand at today's positions), saturating axis lights so planets and rings come out flat onSurface, the Sun as a hidden-line wireframe, the chosen chip shown by a heavier ring

Use the library's ChoiceChips (segmented) for the speed, with extra onClick actions: t0 += (animationTime() - c0) * rateHeld, c0 = animationTime(), rateHeld = the new rate, so the simulated date never jumps
Use one overlay for every size: the panel is fillMaxWidth then widthIn max 340 inside a row arranged at the end, so it is full width on a phone and a corner card on a wide window

Put each circular orbit in its real plane: the planet at Ry(node) Rx(inclination) (r cos u, 0, -r sin u) with u = mean longitude - node; draw the ring as the unit torus rotated by the same two angles and scaled (r, 1, r), in the same loop over float arrays

Follow a chosen body with eased weights: w_k = {value: 1 - min(abs(@sel - k), 1), anim: 0.9} for each planet; the camera target is 0.7 * zoom * sum(w_k * position_k), so a new choice glides from the old planet's live position to the new one's

Zoom by easing the framed extent: ext = 6.15 + (sum(w_k * (0.65 r_k + 0.6)) - 6.15) * zA, and the camera distance is computed from ext and the window, so one formula frames both the whole system and a planet's neighbourhood
Project with the camera target: the label and the Sun's glow subtract (tx, ty, tz) before the spin and tilt, so they stay on their bodies when zoomed
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only
Mean longitudes on circular orbits: positions are right to a few degrees, not an ephemeris; sizes and distances are stylised (order kept)
A thin ring torus scaled by its orbit radius gets thicker with the radius; keep the minor radius small (0.005)
animationTime() is seconds since the document loaded: the simulated date restarts from today on every load
Continuous repaint in light and dark (stars, orbits, pulse); mono reads only the date and repaints on input
A custom themed colour (resources.colors) is not remapped by the mono palettes: everything drawn in mono uses theme tokens (onSurface, muted, primary, background, outline)
Real inclinations are small (Mercury 7°, the rest under 3.4°): from the default view the planes look alike; the Tilt ×5 checkbox scales every inclination (eased) to show them separate

snippets.note: the camera orbits a target that glides to the followed planet when zoomed
colour: the Sun as a point light; mono: saturating axis lights
every orbit from one unit torus, turned to its node and inclination
Mercury on its inclined orbit: node and inclination applied to the circle
simulated years since J2000 (mono: today)

the followed point: eased selection weights times the planets' positions
the starfield (colour looks only)

check.describe: Black space with faint twinkling stars; a glowing yellow Sun in the middle, eight thin blue-grey orbit ellipses, Earth's orbit in light blue, small lit planets (Saturn with its ring), 'Earth' labelled with a pulsing ring; 'Solar System' and 'Year 2026.8' at the top; a dark panel below with Earth's facts, eight planet chips (Earth selected) and four speed chips (Week/s selected). Later the planets have moved round their orbits; a drag changes the tilt; tapping Saturn moves the highlight and the label; Year/s makes the year count up fast. Light: the same chart on warm paper with grey star dots, darker orbit lines and a white panel. Mono: black (or white) page, the Sun as a wireframe globe, planets and Saturn's ring as solid onSurface discs, grey orbit lines, the chosen orbit and planet ring in onSurface, outlined chips (the chosen one heavier), no speed control; the year is today's. Zoomed on Earth: the Sun large at the lower left, Earth ringed and labelled, the inner orbits around them. Zoomed on Jupiter: Jupiter large at the left with its accent orbit, the Sun at the right edge. Edge-on with Tilt ×5: the orbit rings separate into differently tilted ellipses.

examples.name: terrain
examples.title: Little island: a 3D terrain with a sea-level slider
examples.summary: A procedural island on a block of earth, drawn in 3D from one height formula (two Gaussian hills plus sine ripples): flat-shaded low-poly bands of beach sand, grass, forest, rock and snow, sixteen cone trees, a turquoise shallows ring with white surf and a deep-blue sea block whose level a slider sets. The camera drifts round with the clock and a drag orbits it; day sky in light, starry night in dark, a hidden-line wireframe in mono.
examples.prompt: Make a little 3D world: a procedural island coloured by elevation (water, sand, grass, rock, snow) that slowly turns, which I can drag round, with a slider for the sea level.
examples.hand_built: One height expression is repeated per colour band (a min() at each band's top) and the shallows, surf, beach and tree visibility all follow the live sea level; Scene3D and Chart3D have no surface coloured by bands that move with a slider.
teaches: Elevation bands with one formula: each band is a meshExpression3D (surface general, x = u, z = v) whose y is min(h, top); drawn lowest band first, the strict depth test makes every point take the lowest band that reaches its height, so sand, grass, forest, rock and snow need no per-vertex colour

Bands that follow a live value: the beach's top is @sea + 0.035, the shallows are min(h + 0.1, @sea + 0.002) and the surf min(h + 0.03, @sea + 0.003), so raising the sea moves the coast, the beaches and the surf together; trees scale to 0 below @sea + 0.045

A diorama skirt: a general surface one grid ring wider than the land, x = clamp(-1, 1, u), whose outer ring drops to the base, gives vertical earth walls; the sea is a unit cube scaled to the live level and inset 0.003 so the earth wall stays in front of it
Trees are one cone drawn in a loop over a float array of [x, y, z, scale] (positions sampled on the grass by the generator), 16 draws instead of 16 meshes

The slider stays usable under a full-screen 3D view: the 3D canvas fills a column above a 76 dp spacer, and the slider (earlier in the document, so the 3D reads its live @sea) sits in that gap; the camera uses windowWidth() / windowHeight() because the 3D buffer is the window's
Sky: a theme colour gradient, and 40 seeded stars whose colour is transparent in light and white in dark; mono replaces the scene with one hidden-line wireframe of max(h, @sea) and stops the drift
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only. Don't use it for a screen that must play on Android today
A 3D canvas on top of a slider takes its touches (a drag on the slider orbits the island instead): keep the 3D canvas out of the slider's area
The slider is a touchExpression with the absolute-position stop mode: on release it coasts with the finger's speed, so a quick flick overshoots to the end; tests release with vx 0

meshExpression3D surfaces are rebuilt every frame in both players (no cache), so the drift costs eight 41 x 41 to 43 x 43 grids of a 75-token height expression a frame (about 14,000 evaluations), plus seven full-window composites and 16 tree draws: fine on a phone, heavy for a watch
The 40 stars use seed()/rand(): the C++ and TypeScript players scatter them differently (the rest of the picture matches to within a few pixels)
examples.java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players

camera framed for the window and the room the title and slider leave
orbit: drag accumulators that coast
the sea-level slider, before the 3D canvas so it reads the live value
the camera drift from continuousSec(), none in mono

check.describe: Title 'Little island' and a hint at the top, a 'Sea level  0 m' slider at the bottom; between them a square block of earth seen from above at an angle: a deep-blue sea with a turquoise shallows ring and white surf round a low-poly island — sand beaches, light and dark green slopes with small dark cone trees, grey rock and a snowy peak; brown earth walls below the sea's sides. Light: pale blue to cream sky; dark: navy night with stars. Later in time it has turned; dragging turns and tilts it; raising the slider floods the lowlands (only rock and snow above a ring of sand). Mono: a white (or black) hidden-line grid of the island with the sea flat.

examples.name: dna-helix
examples.title: The double helix: a 3D DNA model that unzips
examples.summary: Twenty base pairs of B-DNA in 3D: two sugar-phosphate backbones of beads on a string and base-pair rungs coloured by base (adenine coral, thymine amber, guanine blue, cytosine teal), with the real twist (10 pairs a turn) and minor groove. It turns slowly, a drag turns and tilts it, and an Unzip button eases the two strands apart from the top down, each half-rung staying with its strand; a caption gives the sequence and a legend. Ten meshes from expressions, no per-part geometry.
examples.prompt: Show a DNA double helix in 3D: two backbones of spheres and base-pair rungs coloured by base (A-T, G-C), turning slowly, draggable, with a caption; add an unzip animation. A crisp scientific-illustration look in light and dark.
examples.hand_built: The whole molecule is ten meshExpression3D surfaces (two beaded tubes along the helices and eight sets of half-rungs, one per strand and base, whose pairs are read from 20-bit masks inside the expression), which neither Scene3D nor Chart3D can express.
teaches: A beaded backbone as one surface: a tube round the helix (centre (cos a, y, -sin a), cross-section in the radial and binormal directions, which are exactly perpendicular to a helix's tangent) whose radius is a sphere's profile sqrt(r² - s²) around each base pair, with a thin linker between: one draw for 20 spheres and their string

Many separate parts in one grid: each half-rung takes five samples of u (its bead's centre, the cylinder from the bead to the pair's midpoint with a cap there, back to the bead), and a pair without this base collapses onto its bead, so every triangle joining one rung to the next lies inside a bead or the linker

Data inside an expression without arrays: floor(M / pow(2, floor(u))) % 2 reads bit i of a 20-bit constant M; one mask per strand and base (strand 1 has A at pairs 0, 6, 10, 13, 18 ...) decides which pairs that colour's mesh draws

The unzip is the clock, not an animated variable: the tap stores t0 = continuousSec(); zp = clamp((continuousSec() - t0) / 2.6) eased with smoothstep, and pair i opens by clamp((ez * 26 - 19 + i) / 5), so the fork runs from the top down and back when zipped; the offset is turned by -spin inside the mesh so the strands always part sideways on screen

Two buttons share the spot, shown by two int variables (isOpen / isClosed) the taps swap; the 3D canvas stops 124 dp above the bottom so they keep their taps, and a 2D translate of -33 dp centres the window-sized 3D buffer between the title and the caption
Mono: the same ten meshes on coarser grids, filled with the background under three saturating lights and then drawn as hidden-line wireframes; no turning
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only. Don't use it for a screen that must play on Android today
meshExpression3D surfaces are rebuilt every frame in both players (no cache): 10 meshes, about 6,500 vertices of 30 to 60-token expressions, on top of ten full-window composites; heavy for a watch

An animated variable ({"value": "@open", "anim": 2.4}) read by a meshExpression3D did not move the mesh in the C++ render, so the ease is built on continuousSec(); with the C++ renderer, simulate from a positive clock (a run ending at clock 0 starts at a negative epoch and continuousSec() then does not advance as expected)
valueFloatExpressionChange refuses a literal: set a number with valueFloatChange, an expression (here continuousSec()) with valueFloatExpressionChange
The inspector's audit calls zp, ez, ezk, oc and os dead code (dead_code, unused_variables): it does not see variables read inside meshExpression3D; they drive the unzip
The legend chips keep their base colours in mono
examples.java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players

examples.name: wave-interference
examples.title: Two-source wave interference on a 3D pond
examples.summary: A round pond in 3D whose surface is the sum of circular waves from two bobbing sources, animated from the clock and coloured by height through a 147-byte gradient texture; an XY pad sets the frequency (sideways) and the distance between the sources (up and down), and the readouts give f, d and the wavelength.
examples.prompt: Make a physics-class demo of wave interference that is also beautiful: a 3D water surface animated as the sum of circular waves from two sources, coloured by height, with a 2D control to change the frequency and the distance between the sources.
examples.hand_built: Chart3D draws z = f(x, y) over a square with flat colour bands; a round pond, colour by height through a texture, a live clock phase and the XY pad need the 3D ops by hand. The XY pad stays hand-built: no library component sets two values from one drag (two Sliders would lose the point of the demo); its colours are themed (resources.colors) and it has its own mono look.
teaches: Build a round surface with a general meshExpression3D: x = u*cos(v), z = u*sin(v) over u 0..4, v 0..2π, and y the sum of two waves sin(k*r - ω*t)/(1 + 0.35*r), each r written in polar form sqrt(u*u ∓ 2*u*s*cos(v) + s*s)

Colour a surface by its height: give meshExpression3D a uv pair ["0.5", "0.5 + 2 * height"] and bind a 2 x 32 gradient PNG with texture3D; the player multiplies the texel by the lighting, so the shading stays
Drive the waves from the clock: ph = ω * continuousSec() in a variable the height expression reads; the whole mesh is re-evaluated each frame (48 x 168 vertices)

Make an XY pad with two touchExpressions in touchMode 6 (absolute) on one canvas, each mapping touchX() or touchY() minus the canvas's root position (componentValue valueType 4 and 5) into a clamped range

Place the pad before the 3D canvas in document order (a touch variable is live only from its declaration on): a Box draws the overlay first and the transparent 3D canvas over it, and the 3D buffer only covers the pond

Frame the pond in the free part of the window: a 2D translate before the 3D draws moves the window-sized 3D buffer to the free region's centre, and the camera distance is the max of two fits (width and height of that region)

Make the mono look a ripple tank: a second texture whose crest rows are opaque white and the rest transparent (texels with alpha 0 are not drawn), multiplied by @colors.onSurface under three saturating lights, frozen in time

Theme a textured surface: the texel is multiplied by the paint colour, so a themed paint (white in light, a cool grey in dark) gives one gradient bitmap a bright daylight look and a moodier night look
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only
The waves repaint every frame (continuousSec()) and re-evaluate 8064 vertices a frame; keep the grid near this size
In the TypeScript web player a texture can be missing on the first frame (bitmaps decode asynchronously): the surface draws untextured white for a frame, then coloured
The surface expressions are long (two square roots per source, written twice: height and uv); Android's 32-entry expression limit does not apply as 3D does not play there yet, but it would
The phase is ω·t, so changing the frequency jumps the phase; harmless while dragging, but it is not a physical change of frequency in a running ripple tank

The water colour is a bitmap (a texture can't follow the theme), so the light and dark looks share one gradient and the dark look dims it with a themed paint colour (texel × paint): pond_water is white in light, #CCD6E4 in dark
examples.java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players

snippets.note: the round pond: polar x/z, the two-source height, uv by height
gradient texture on the surface (colour), crest texture (mono)
the phase from continuousSec()
the XY pad: frequency from touchX()

check.describe: Dark: a deep navy screen; 'Two sources, one pond' at the top; in the middle a round pond in perspective inside a grey stone rim, its surface rippling in rings from two small gold balls, deep navy in the troughs, cyan to white on the crests, with calm radial nodal lines between; at the bottom a rounded pad with a gold puck and readouts '1.0 Hz', '2.0 m', '1.1 m'. Later in time the ripples have moved and the view has swayed. Dragging the puck to the top right gives 1.8 Hz and 3.6 m: shorter waves, sources wider apart, many more nodal lines. Landscape: pond on the right, text and pad on the left. Small (2x2): the pond alone. Light: the same pond on a pale grey-blue page, brighter lagoon water, dark ink text, a white pad with an amber puck. Mono: the same layout in black and white, crests as solid onSurface bands (a ripple tank), still.

examples.name: earth-day-night
examples.title: The Earth right now: a textured globe with day, night and city lights
examples.summary: A turning 3D globe textured with a 768 x 384 map made from the catalog's own Natural Earth data, lit by a sun placed where it really is at the current clock (declination and equation of time from dayOfYear(), the subsolar longitude from UTC), so the day/night terminator is real; 16 cities are dots (one merged mesh) that glow on the night side, six carry labels projected from 3D to the screen, and a drag spins and tilts it.
examples.prompt: Show the Earth as a 3D globe that turns, with the continents, the real day and night for right now, and a few cities as dots; let me drag to spin it.
examples.hand_built: Scene3D has no texture or sun; a textured sphere, a light from the computed sun direction, city dots lit from the night side and labels projected to the screen need the 3D ops by hand.
teaches: Texture a sphere: meshPrimitive3D sphere with "uv": "uv", texture3D on a bitmap resource, white paint, drawMesh3D smooth (the same approach as the textured globes of hoford.github.io/RemoteCompose-Examples, render/textured-sphere and vis-set-10)

Make the texture fit the primitive's UV, not the other way round: the sphere's u is 1 - φ/2π with φ the angle from +X toward +Z, so an equirectangular map whose left edge is Greenwich and which runs east puts longitude λ at (cos λ, ·, -sin λ) with no extra rotation, and world space is Earth-fixed

Place the sun from the clock: declination -23.44° · cos(2π(N + 10)/365), equation of time 9.87 sin 2B - 7.53 cos B - 1.5 sin B, subsolar longitude (720 - UTC minutes - EoT)/4 degrees; the directional light travels along minus that vector

Get a real terminator: with material3D specular above 0 the lighting is one-sided (a face turned away from the light gets ambient only), while specular 0 lights both sides (|N·L|) and the night disappears
Turn the camera, not the globe (lights are in world space): the eye orbits at D·(cos t sin s, sin t, cos t cos s), s from an autorotation, the drag and the sun's longitude

Draw fixed points as one mesh: the 16 city dots are small octahedra merged into a single defineMesh3D (2.3 KB), because each drawMesh3D composites the whole window buffer (a loop of 16 sphere draws cost the TypeScript player about 68 ms a frame at 1080 x 1920, the merged mesh a few); lit from the anti-sun direction, they glow on the night side and are dim by day

Label 3D points in 2D: project each city with the camera basis (right (cos s, 0, -sin s), up (-sin t sin s, cos t, -sin t cos s)) and F = (H/2)/tan(fov/2), and push the label off screen with step() when it is behind the limb
Frame the globe in the free part of the window: the distance D = 1/sin(atan(r/F)) for a target radius r in px, and a 2D translate before the 3D moves the window-sized buffer to the free region

Draw line art on a sphere in mono with a mostly transparent texture (texels with alpha 0 are skipped and write no depth), then the hidden-line wireframe: its own depth prepass hides the back, and objects drawn after it (dots, the terminator ring) stay visible as long as no negative depthBias3D was active during the wireframe
Keep labels readable over a globe and a page of either theme: draw every label first as a 3-px stroke in a dark halo colour (the background in mono), then the fill on top
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players only

The texture is most of the size: 21.7 KB of the document is the 768 x 384 colour map (10-colour palette PNG); a 1024 x 512 map with 1:50m coastlines costs 32 KB. Nearest-texel sampling shows the texels at the coast when the globe is large
Ambient light is a fixed 0.2, so the night side stays dimly visible and cannot be made darker
In the TypeScript web player bitmaps decode asynchronously: the globe can draw untextured for its first frame
The sun uses minute resolution (timeInMin()) and offsetToUtc(); with a wrong device time zone the terminator is wrong by the same amount
The labels are 2D text projected by hand: they are not hidden by the city's own dot or clipped at the limb, only switched off a little before it
The texture is stylised (land, ice, shelf, a 30° graticule from Natural Earth), not a satellite image

A wireframe drawMesh3D fills the z-buffer with its front faces first; with a negative depthBias3D active it writes them biased toward the eye, so later parts close to the surface (city dots, a ring 0.004 above it) disappear. Draw the wireframe without a bias (its prepass already hides the back lines) when anything sits on the surface afterwards

The globe itself is the same in light and dark (the texture is a bitmap and the night side is physical); the page, text and stars follow the theme. The halo is a radial gradient of literal colours (gradients take no themed colours) chosen to read on both
examples.java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players

examples.name: world-clock
examples.title: A world clock with day and night
examples.summary: A world map with the live night side (three soft-edged terminator layers), the sun drawn over the subsolar point, and six cities: on the map each dot glows when the sun is up there, and each city card shows its local time, the day relative to UTC and its own sky (blue by day, dusk colours within 6 degrees of the horizon, stars and a crescent by night) with the sun at its real height. Two columns on a phone or a portrait tablet, one row of six on a landscape tablet.
examples.prompt: Make a world clock: a world map showing where it is day and night right now, with the sun where it is overhead, and a row of cities with their local times that highlights the ones in daylight. It should work on a phone and on a tablet.
teaches: The map is one WorldMap call: fill (takes the column's remaining height and rescales), night + twilight (three shades 5 degrees apart: a soft terminator), sun (the subsolar point) and daylight (the city dots glow where the sun is up), coloured through its params with document colours (sea, land, nightColor, markerColor, dayColor, sunColor)

The sun's position from the clock: declination 23.44 * sin(2 pi (284 + dayOfYear()) / 365), subsolar longitude -15 * (UTC hours - 12). On the equirectangular world box (x = (lon + 180) * 2.778, y = (84 - lat) * 2.778) that is the sun's dot

Is the sun up in a city: sin(elevation) = sin(lat) sin(decl) + cos(lat) cos(decl) cos(lon - sunLon), with sin and cos of the latitude stored once in float arrays. Above sin(6 deg) = 0.105 it is day, within plus or minus 0.105 twilight, below night

Local time per city from one exported float array of UTC offsets (utcOffsets, the app keeps it right through DST): raw = utcMin + off * 60, the time (raw + 1440) % 1440, the day floor(raw / 1440) cut from "YesterdayToday    Tomorrow "

One inline component, CityCard, for the six cards: its sky is a gradient picked by two conditionalOperations, the sun drawn at 0.62 - 0.55 * el of the card's height, so a card's sun rises and sets with the real one

Responsive without branches: cols = 6 on a landscape window from 600 dp, else 2; the card width floor((W - 32) / cols) and its height from what the map leaves (up to 0.8 x its width), in a flow; the map takes the rest (verticalWeight) and keeps its 2.54:1, centred

Four looks: the map's colours are document colours with light, dark, mono-dark and mono-light values (land grey, sea and night shade the background in mono); {"$if": "theme.mono"} forks draw the night edge as a line, the sun as a ring and each card as an outline with a sun or moon glyph instead of a coloured sky, so day and night read by shape
pitfalls: The offsets are standard time in November (New York -5, London 0, Sydney +11): the format has no time-zone database, so the app sets utcOffsets when DST changes
The sun's longitude ignores the equation of time (up to 16 minutes, about 4 degrees), so the subsolar dot and the terminator can be a few degrees off; fine for a clock, not for astronomy
Twilight bands from shifted longitudes are an approximation: the band is wider than civil twilight near the poles
text drawn in a card is white on every sky: keep the day sky saturated enough (#2F78D2) for the white time to read
step(0, 0) is 0: the sign of a zero offset needs step(off, -0.5) to read +0
Medium detail is about 15 KB of the 30 KB: low detail makes the document 21 KB and looks blocky on a tablet-wide map; pick low for a phone-only or widget build

examples.name: living-sky
examples.title: Living sky: a landscape that follows the time of day and the weather
examples.summary: A wallpaper-like landscape whose sky follows the real clock. Night, dawn, day and dusk gradients crossfade with the sun's elevation, and the sun or the moon (in its real phase) travels its arc. Stars twinkle at night, clouds drift, and a cabin's windows light up after sunset. @weather (0 clear, 1 rain, 2 snow) adds overcast, rain streaks or falling snow and snow-covered hills, and @temp is the readout. The same document is a phone screen and a 4x2 widget.
examples.prompt: A living landscape for my phone's home screen or a 4x2 widget. The sky follows the actual time of day: night, dawn, day and dusk colours blending smoothly, with the sun or moon moving across the sky and stars at night. It rains or snows depending on a weather value from the app (0 clear, 1 rain, 2 snow), and it shows the temperature.
examples.hand_built: A whole illustrated scene on one canvas (sky layers, celestial arcs, ridges, pines, a cabin, weather particles). The library's WeatherIcon is a glyph-sized icon, not a scene.
teaches: One elevation drives everything: s = (h − sunrise) / (sunset − sunrise) by day, q = ((h − sunset + 24) % 24) / night length by night, el = ifElse(−sin(πq), sin(πs), isDay − 0.5). This runs from −1 at midnight through 0 at sunrise and sunset to 1 at noon, and it is continuous whatever the day length

A sky interpolated from the clock with no colour expressions: draw the night gradient, then the day gradient at alpha smooth_step(el, 0.32, −0.02), then dawn or dusk at alpha tw = 1 − |el + 0.02| / 0.2, chosen by morning = step(12.5, h). Stars use smooth_step(−el, …), and so do the moon and the cabin lamps

The moon's lit part is a single pathExpression: the limb for a ∈ [0, π], then the terminator back with x scaled by k = −cos(2π·phase). The mirror is ifElse(−1, 1, 0.5 − phase). The phase is the day count since a known new moon (2000-01-06 18:14 UTC), (year() − 2000)·365.25 + dayOfYear() + h/24 − 6.76, modulo the synodic month of 29.5306 days. That is within a day of the true phase. epochSecond() would be exact, but the Java JSON parser does not know it

Clouds are a closed pathExpression each (a flat-bottomed oval with |sin| bumps), so one translucent fill per cloud has no seams. They drift with T = timeInHr()·3600 + continuousSec() and wrap with %. Their count is 3 + 4·min(@weather, 1)

Rain and snow are clock-driven loops, not particle systems: y = (seed·(H + 40) + t·speed) % (H + 40) − 20. Every frame is a pure function of the time, so any clock renders the same in every player and nothing needs warming up. A conditionalOperations on @weather == 1 or 2 runs only the active loop

Ridges are pathCreate plus 49 pathAppendLineTo in a loop, closed along the bottom. Each is painted in its day colour, then a night veil at 1 − dayA, a dusk tint at tw·0.35, and a snow cover when @weather == 2

Sizes come from the box: horizon at 0.7·H, sun and moon radii from min(W, 1.2·H), and text clamp(34, 96, min(H·0.095, W·0.2)). Below 300 dp of height the third line drops its 'Sunrise / Sunset' part (code = isDay + 2·step(H, 300) picks the variant), so the 4x2 widget keeps the temperature, condition and time

Condition text: ci = @weather + 3·step(starA, 0.3)·(1 − wet) picks one of four conditional drawTextAnchored ('Clear', 'Rain', 'Snow', 'Clear night'). addDataList + textLookup would be shorter, but the Java parser drops the list id (U4)

Four looks. The scene is the sky itself, so it stays the same in light and dark. The UI follows the theme: light puts the readout on a white 88% card with dark ink, and dark uses white ink with a soft shadow, a dark scrim and a faint navy card. Mono ({"$if": "theme.mono"}) redraws the scene as a line drawing in onSurface and muted on the background: ridges, pines, cabin and clouds filled with the background and outlined (hidden lines), the sun a disc with a ring by day, the moon its lit part by night, stars as dots, lit windows filled instead of outlined, and static rain dashes or snow dots. It has no time-driven motion, so it repaints once a minute
h = timeInMin() / 60: the sun and moon move per minute, plenty for their arcs, and the mono documents need no faster clock
pitfalls: json2rc writes a `variable` (and a resource variable) where it is first used. If that first use is inside a conditionalOperations whose condition is false, the TypeScript player never computes it, and later uses read 0. Here, S first used in the moon block left the daytime sun at its minimum size and drew no clouds, pines or cabin. The C++ player computes it anyway. Make sure every shared variable is used once outside a conditional before any conditional block (here the sun and moon draw unconditionally, and their alpha hides them). The same goes for a TextFromFloat: a clock text first used inside a skipped conditional showed a stale hour in the TypeScript player. So the three variants of the third line are chosen by paint alpha (step(2, code), …), not by conditionals

Two loops that declare the same variable with the same expression share one FloatExpression: json2rc (like the Java parser, byte-identical) does not write it again in the second loop, so the second loop never recomputes it and reads the first loop's last value. Draw all the passes for a cloud inside one loop body, or use different names
smooth_step is smooth_step(value, upper, lower), and ifElse is ifElse(else, then, condition)
% is a float remainder that keeps the sign: add the span before % ((x + W) % W) when x can be negative
The moon travels the night arc between sunset and sunrise. That is a stylisation: the real moon rises later each day with its phase. The phase itself is real
Every expression stays within Android's 32 entries. The cloud position needed its span (cspan) split out to get there

A paint `alpha` after a `color` replaces that colour's alpha: a transparent themed card followed by alpha 1 drew an opaque black box. Give translucent themed colours their alpha in the colour and add no alpha op after them

drifting clouds, one closed path each, three passes (white, dusk tint, rain grey)

Rain: grey overcast veil, grey clouds, slanted streaks. Snow by night: snow-white ridges, roof and pines, falling flakes, '-3°'.
