examples.name: marble-drop
examples.title: Marble drop: a physics toy with pegs, gravity and tilt
examples.summary: Thirty glowing marbles fall under gravity through a staggered field of pegs, bounce off them and the side walls and drop into bins whose floor flashes in the marble's colour. Tap anywhere to drop a marble right there; tilt the device and gravity follows the accelerometer. The physics is real: velocity, gravity, restitution, peg collisions with push-out, four sub-steps per frame, all integrated by the player in particle equations.
examples.prompt: A physics toy: colourful balls falling under gravity and bouncing off pegs and walls, tap to drop a new ball where I tap, tilt the phone to change gravity. Make it satisfying.
examples.hand_built: A physics simulation is the lesson: the state and the integrator are a particle system written by hand, and nothing in the component library simulates.
teaches: A particle system is a physics engine: each marble's state (x, y, vx, vy and helpers) is a particle variable, and the particlesLoop equations are one explicit-Euler step that the player runs for every marble on every frame
Sub-steps: four particlesLoop ops over the same system, each with dt = min(deltaTime(), 0.04) / 4, integrate four times per frame. Collisions stay tight because a marble moves about 1 px per step

Equations update simultaneously from the previous step's values, so a helper variable lags one step. The peg offsets fu, fw are computed from the position predicted 4 steps ahead (x + y + (vx + vy) * 4 * dt) so they line up with the position the collision impulse acts on

The nearest peg of a staggered lattice in two roundings: pegs sit where u = x + y and w = x − y are multiples of S, so fu = u − round(u / S) * S, fw = w − round(w / S) * S, the offset is ((fu + fw) / 2, (fu − fw) / 2) and the squared distance is (fu² + fw²) / 2

Collision response is an impulse J = (1 + e) / (4R²) * min(v · offset, 0), applied once (J resets on the step after it fires) plus a push-out P that removes the overlap; walls reflect vx with a guarded factor wl

Tap to drop: onTouchDown records @tx, @ty and counts @drops; each marble compares @drops with the count it last saw, and the one whose index equals @slot respawns at the touch. Fifteen marbles auto-rain from the top, fifteen are reserved for taps
Tilt: gravity is (−accelerationX(), accelerationY()) scaled to the screen, falling back to straight down when the sensor reads under 2 m/s² (no sensor, or the device lying flat)

Mono (always-on and e-ink): {"$if": "theme.mono"} forks swap the colour passes for five shape styles (solid, ring, solid with a hole, ring with a dot, ring with a big dot), drop the gradient and halos, and flash a bin by a short line instead of a glow; the physics is the same particle system in every look

Colour per marble without colour expressions: five particlesComparison passes over index ranges [0, 6), [6, 12)… each paint the marbles of one colour; the peg they last hit flashes as a fading ring in that colour
pitfalls: There are no marble-to-marble collisions. The format can express them (ParticlesCompare with two equation sets compares every pair, reading particle1/particle2 values through the CMD1/CMD2 tokens), but json2rc has no infix syntax for those tokens, so pairwise equations cannot be written in JSON today. Marbles pass through each other: visible when a tilt piles them against a wall
Every equation must fit in 32 RPN entries (Android): split long formulas into helper variables, and remember each helper adds a step of lag
createParticles initialValues are evaluated without the document's variables in the C++ player: use literals and the index u only; put spawns in the equations
ifElse is ifElse(else, then, cond): getting it backwards froze the exit timer and no marble ever spawned
rand() in the equations makes runs differ per player and per seed: compare players by behaviour, not pixels (render with seed for a repeatable image)
rc-inspect's audit reports dt as dead_code: it does not count reads from particle equations

check.describe: A dark indigo board titled 'Marble drop' / 'Tap to drop a marble · tilt to tip', a staggered field of pale pegs and seven bins at the bottom. After a few seconds pink, amber, green, blue and violet marbles with soft halos are spread through the pegs, each with a fading ring on the peg it last hit, and a bin floor glows where one has just landed. Taps: five new marbles appear where tapped (120, 200 and 150 px down). Tilted (accelerationX −6, Y 7.5): the marbles slide right and pile along the right wall.

examples.name: energy-flow
examples.title: Home energy flow: a live Sankey diagram with particles and eased transitions
examples.summary: Solar, grid and battery feeding the house, the car, the heat pump and the export, as a Sankey diagram: ribbon widths come from a 12-value host float array, each ribbon is one filled path expression with a source-to-use gradient, white particles flow along it at a speed proportional to its flow, and when the host replaces the array every ribbon, bar and label eases to the new layout in 1.2 s without the stack ever coming apart. Labels with values in kW; the same canvas lays out on a tablet and a phone, light or dark.
examples.prompt: Build a home energy flow diagram: sources (solar, grid, battery) to uses (house, car, heat pump, export) as a Sankey, ribbon widths from host data arrays, animated particles flowing along the ribbons at speeds proportional to the flow, and a smooth transition when the data changes. Labels with values; tablet and phone layouts.

flows.meaning: kW from each source to each use, row-major: solar, grid, battery x house, car, heat pump, export

teaches: The diagram is one Sankey call: {"flows": "@flows", "sources": [["Solar", "@colors.solar"], ...], "uses": [...]}; themed node colours live in resources.colors

Each flow is eased on its own: g_k = arrayGet(@flows, k), then f_k = {value: @g_k, anim: 1.2}. Every offset is a sum of eased flows, so ribbons, bars and labels move together and never overlap mid-transition

A ribbon is ONE closed pathExpression: a in 0..2, x = xs + dx * (1 - abs(1 - a)), y = ya + (yb - ya) * (1 - cos(pi a)) / 2 + w * step(a, 1). The same cosine ease serves the top edge forward and the bottom edge back; flags 4 (linear) keeps the corners square

Particles: phase = fract(T * 0.16 * arrayGet(@flows, i)) and a loop of 7 dots at fract(phase + j / 7), each with a fixed lateral offset sin(j * 2.39 + i) and alpha sin(pi t) so they fade in and out at the bars
pitfalls: C++ player (rc-render): an animated variable whose expression reads the array directly ({value: "arrayGet(@flows, 0)", anim}) never re-animates when the host replaces the array; route it through a plain variable first (g_k = arrayGet(...), then {value: "@g_k", anim})
The particle speed reads the raw host value, so when the data changes the dots jump once to their new phase while the ribbons ease
pathExpression defaults to a spline through the samples: on a closed band that overshoots into a bulge at the corners; pass flags 4
drawTextAnchored panY -1 puts the text above the anchor and 1 below it
rc-render variables accept the float array; rc-inspect interact does not yet (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS I8)

check.describe: 800x500 dark: Energy flow 7.5 kW, 80% of solar used at home; Solar 5.5, Grid 0.9, Battery 1.1 on the left, House 2.4, Car 2.4, Heat pump 1.6, Export 1.1 on the right; amber-to-blue solar-to-car ribbon the widest, white dots along every ribbon. evening (variables, 2.5 s): Solar 0.0, Grid 3.2, Battery 4.2; Car 3.2 fed by the battery; mid (0.5 s): ribbons half-way between the two layouts, still stacked. 360x640 phone, light: same diagram, narrower label columns. Mono: ribbons as thin outlines over a faint fill, bars in the ink colour, no particles (no continuous repaint); the eased transition stays.

examples.name: patient-monitor
examples.title: ICU patient monitor: sweeping ECG, pleth and respiration traces with alarm limits
examples.summary: A bedside monitor drawn in one canvas: ECG lead II, SpO2 pleth and respiration traces sweep left to right with the erase gap of a real monitor, rebuilt every frame from three small float arrays and the clock; heart rate, SpO2, respiration rate and blood pressure come from host variables, and the HR (or SpO2) tile and a top banner flash red when a value leaves its alarm limits. Landscape on a tablet, numerics under the traces on a phone.
examples.prompt: Build an ICU-style patient monitor: a scrolling ECG trace drawn from a waveform array looping with the clock, with the sweep-and-erase gap of a real monitor, an SpO2 pleth wave, heart rate and SpO2 numbers from host variables, and a flashing red alarm when the heart rate is out of range. Dark, crisp, legible, on a tablet and on a phone.
teaches: The three traces are SweepTrace calls in a column laid over the canvas: offset under the top bar, width and height computed from the screen (componentWidth() in a modifier is the parent's), so the same rows serve landscape and portrait

A sweep-and-erase trace without a sample buffer: the head is x_h = fract(T / D) * width, and the sample at x shows the time T - fract((x_h - x) / width + 1) * D, so the new sweep and the previous one both stay put on screen while the head moves

The ECG beat is stored as a fixed 0.62 s window (100 samples) read with min(1, fract(phase) * k): the QRS keeps its real width at any heart rate and the baseline fills the rest of the RR interval, so 148 bpm looks like tachycardia rather than a squashed beat

The alarm is data, not layout: hrA = ifElse(0, 1, max(hr - hrHi, hrLo - hr)) and blink = ifElse(0, 1, 0.5 - fract(T * 2)) drive conditionalOperations that paint the tile red, turn its text white and show the banner
One canvas serves both orientations: land = ifElse(0, 1, W - 1.15 H) and every tile rectangle is lerp(portrait, landscape, @land)
pitfalls: TypeScript player: PathExpression.evalRPN has no case for splineLoop (op 75), so a pathExpression using splineLoop draws vertical spikes there; use spline(@a, fract(t)) with the first value repeated at the end, which both players evaluate
Without flags 2 (monotonic) the default spline path overshoots around the sharp R wave
Changing hr re-times the history already on screen (the trace is recomputed from the clock, not stored), so the old sweep reflows once when the rate changes
continuousSec() wraps at the hour: the traces jump once an hour
Canvas text has no font weight: the big numerics use the default face

check.describe: 800x480 at 14:37:04: three traces (green ECG with narrow R waves, cyan pleth with a dicrotic notch, yellow respiration), each with an 18 px erase gap and a bright head dot; tiles HR 72, SpO2 98 with a perfusion bar, RR 16, NIBP 118/76 MAP 90. At 14:37:06 the heads have moved 200 px (ECG, pleth) and 50 px (resp). hr 148: banner HR HIGH 148, the HR tile red with white text, 148 bpm beats with normal-width QRS. 360x640: traces on top, tiles in a 2x2 grid. alarm-off-phase (0.3 s later in the blink): the red tile and banner dimmed. Light: a light page with white tiles and deeper green, blue and amber traces; the alarm tile red with white text. Mono-dark (hr 148): white on black, no glow, traces and blink step once a second; the alarm tile is filled solid white with black numbers on the blink and outlined 4 px between, the banner a solid pill. Mono-light: the same in black on white.

examples.name: kinetic-type-poster
examples.title: A festival poster where the type moves
examples.summary: A Swiss-style concert poster on one canvas: ECHO in huge letters that drop in one after another with an overshoot and then breathe, five red outline echoes trailing beneath them, a red disc beating inside a ring of text that turns, sound rings spreading past the edges, a sentence flowing along a moving sine wave, and a tilted black band with the dates scrolling. Light (warm paper), a designed dark look (night paper, cream type) and two still mono looks. About 4.2 KB.
examples.prompt: Make a typographic poster that moves, like a concert poster: a big headline whose letters animate in one after another, text running along a curve that flows, a scrolling band with the dates, and a strong graphic design.
examples.hand_built: Kinetic type is per-letter transforms and text on animated paths drawn on a canvas; no library component does this, and the whole poster is under 4 KB.
teaches: Per-letter animation: a loop over the word draws each letter, sliced out with textSubtext("ECHO", i, 1), its own drop (back-out easing 1 + 2.70158 p^3 + 1.70158 p^2 over 0.8 s, 0.14 s apart) and its own breathing scale about the baseline
Echoes: the same letters again in stroke style, five copies from the farthest to the nearest, each offset further down and fainter, the offsets swinging with sin(t)
Text on a circle that turns: a closed pathExpression circle and drawTextOnPath inside save { rotate(t * 14) about the centre }

Text flowing along a moving wave: a pathExpression whose y uses animationTime(), so the path itself moves, and an hOffset of -((t * 38) % width) from textMeasure, so the words slide along it seamlessly

The poster is laid out on a 360 x 640 sheet scaled to fit and centred; the paper, the rings, the wave and the tilted band run past the sheet to the screen edges, so a landscape tablet shows a wide composition, not a letterbox
The band: rotate -5 degrees about its centre, a black bar wider than the screen, and the dates repeated ceil(width / measured) + 1 times, moving by the measured width modulo

Two clocks: animationTime() (from 0 when the poster appears) for the one-off entrance, continuousSec() for everything that loops. A canvas that reads only animationTime() is not repainted by the players (the inspector reports repaint idle); continuousSec() schedules every frame

Four looks from one document: themed colours (paper, ink, red, ringLine, band, bandText) for light and dark, and {"$if": "theme.mono"} forks for the mono looks: the red becomes onSurface or muted, the filled disc an outlined ring, the band two rules, and the clocks are pinned (animationTime 4, continuousSec 0, a still wave) so an always-on screen does not repaint
pitfalls: Canvas text has no font weight in the JSON (paint has textSize and colour only): the headline is made heavy with fillAndStroke and a 3 px stroke
loop with a negative step does not run (from 5 until 0 step -1 drew nothing): count up and compute the reversed index
clamp is clamp(value, max, min) in these players

The TypeScript player draws the wave text off its curve at some frames (from about 4 s into the web render the words run nearly straight while drawPath of the same path still curves); the C++ player follows the wave at every time

A document whose motion reads only animationTime() is not repainted: drive looping motion from continuousSec() (or add wakeIn). It then repaints every frame for as long as it is shown — right for a poster or an idle screen, not for a widget

inputs.clock: animationTime drives the entrance (letters, echoes); continuousSec drives the loops (rings, disc, ring text, wave, band, breathing), which is also what keeps the poster repainting

snippets.note: the sentence flowing along the moving wave
ECHO: each letter drops in 0.14 s after the last, then breathes
the ring of text turning
the five echoes, a loop of loops
the tilted band, repeated at its measured width

check.describe: Light, settled (t = 4 s): warm paper, grey concentric rings centred on a red disc at the top right, the disc inside a ring of small black text SOUND · LIGHT · MOTION · THREE NIGHTS · LISBOA · MMXXVI, N° 07 / LX FACTORY / LISBOA top left, ECHO in huge black letters across the middle with five red outline copies stepping down under it, a sentence (fourteen artists — three nights — one room full of noise) riding a sine wave, a two-line lineup, and a black band tilted up to the right with ECHO FESTIVAL 2026 — LISBON — 14 · 15 · 16 MAY in red. drop (t = 0.62 s): E and C landed or landing, H high up and O not yet in, no echoes yet. ring (t = 7.3 s): the ring text turned and the wave and band moved on. Landscape 1280x800: the sheet centred, rings, wave and band across the full width. Tablet portrait and a 300x300 square: the whole sheet scaled to fit. Dark: the same poster at night: near-black aubergine paper, cream type and ring text, faint lilac rings, the red disc and red echoes, a cream band with red dates. Mono dark and mono light: no red and no motion; the disc is an outlined record with a spindle hole, echoes in grey outline, the band two rules with the dates between, black on white or white on black.

examples.name: split-flap-board
examples.title: A split-flap departure board whose letters flip through the alphabet
examples.summary: A railway departure board drawn on one canvas: rows of flap tiles for time, destination, train and platform, and a whole-word status flap in green, amber, orange or red. Every nine seconds the top train leaves and every tile flips mechanically through the character drum to its new letter, in a wave from top-left; a flap clock flips on the minute and a ticker runs underneath. Dark (classic charcoal), light (white flaps on a warm wall) and two still mono looks where the status is told by a lamp shape. One row of 26 tiles is a loop over a float array of character codes, so twelve trains cost 312 numbers.
examples.prompt: Make an airport or train station split-flap departure board: rows of departures with time, destination, platform and status, where every character flips through the letters with the mechanical flap animation when a row changes. Boarding and Delayed in their own colours. It should look great on a tablet in landscape and still work on a phone.
teaches: Three SplitFlap calls over one canvas: the rows (tiles = the layout's column count, rows = what fits, tileX and tileY read from the layout's cx/cy arrays), the status column (a word drum, glyphWidth 8, align start) and the clock (code from timeInHr/timeInMin, since continuousSec() % 60). The board canvas below draws the header, labels and ticker; one canvas above draws the status colours and lamps once each status has settled

Per tile, as expressions of i (tile) and r (row): code = arrayGet(@chars, ((@k + r) % 12) * 26 + arrayGet(@cols, @cbase + i)), prev the same for the previous cycle, since = the time into the 9 s cycle; SplitFlap steps forward through the drum ((code - prev) mod 40 flaps at 22 a second) and draws the half-flap fold

Text as numbers: each train is 26 character codes into a 40-character drum (space, A-Z, 0-9, ':', '-', '.'), all twelve in one float array; textSubtext(drum, code, 1) turns a code back into its glyph inside the loop, and the status words are 8-letter slices of one string

The board cycle is floor(animationTime() / 9): row r shows train (k + r) % 12 and flips from train (k + r - 1) % 12, so the top train leaves and the list moves up; at load everything flips in from blank
A per-tile delay (row * 0.16 + column * 0.035 + a hashed jitter fract(sin(r * 12.9 + c * 78.2) * 437.5) * 0.25) makes the flurry ripple across the board instead of flipping in lockstep

The status is a whole-word flap (ON TIME, BOARDING, DELAYED, CANCELED) on its own five-entry list; once settled the word is redrawn in its colour through a clip whose width is zero for every other status, with a lamp that blinks for BOARDING
The clock is the same flap fed from timeInHr() and timeInMin(): it flips from the previous minute in the first second of each minute

Three layouts from one document: wide (time, destination, train, platform, status), narrow under 700 dp (train dropped, nine letters of destination), and tall when the height is over 1.2 x the width (two lines per train); the layouts are segments of the same cols/cx/cy arrays, picked by a base offset

Four looks: themed colours (page, tile, flap, ink, split, accent, muted, band, the four status colours) for light and dark; {"$if": "theme.mono"} forks for mono: tiles become outlines with the split cut as a gap, the colour overlay gives way to lamp shapes (ring, disc, half disc, slashed ring) so status never depends on colour, and the board is pinned to its settled state (animationTime 6, the clock's flip second 30), so only the minute changes
pitfalls: Use textSubtext of one string, not addDataList + textLookup, for glyphs chosen at run time: the reference JSON parser cannot name an addDataList (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U4), so a textLookup document does not convert for Android
clamp is clamp(value, max, min) in these players: clamp(x, 1, 12) is always 1
step(a, b) is a > b, strictly: step(@k, 1) is 0 for the first cycle after the intro
ifElse is ifElse(else, then, condition)
The tiles are redrawn every frame (about 270 tiles, roughly 10 000 operations a frame on the wide board): fine on a tablet or a kiosk, heavier than a normal screen
Variables the board canvas declares (@cw, @th, @k, @tc ...) are read by the SplitFlap canvases drawn after it in the same box: keep the board canvas first

inputs.clock: timeInHr and timeInMin drive the flap clock; animationTime drives the board

snippets.note: the rows: one SplitFlap call, codes per tile and row from the float array
twelve trains as character codes, the status codes, and the three layouts' column tables
the board cycle from animationTime()
the rows: one SplitFlap call, codes per tile and row from the float array
the flap clock: a SplitFlap fed from the clock
the ticker, repeated at its measured width

check.describe: Dark, tablet landscape (1280x800): DEPARTURES in amber with ABFAHRT · DÉPARTS · PARTENZE, a five-tile flap clock at the top right reading 08:41, column labels, nine rows of dark flap tiles with warm white letters and a split line: 08:42 MILANO C.LE EC 31 4 BOARDING (amber, blinking lamp), 08:47 ZURICH HB IC 718 7 BOARDING, 08:55 MUNCHEN HBF RJ 64 12 DELAYED (orange), 09:03 STRASBOURG TGV 9 ON TIME (green), ... 09:18 GENEVE IR 15 CANCELED (red); an amber ticker band at the bottom. flip (t = 9.75 s): the board moving up one train, tiles caught mid-flip through other letters (ZURI77, FU-1H2N), some showing half flaps, status flaps white while turning. intro (t = 0.6 s): most tiles still blank or showing early letters A, B, C. Phone landscape 640x360: five rows, no train column. Phone portrait 360x640 and tablet portrait 800x1280: two lines per train, status, train and platform under the destination. Light: white flaps with charcoal letters on a warm grey wall, a darker amber title, deeper status colours (green, amber, orange, red), a black ticker with amber letters. Mono dark and mono light: every tile an outline with the split cut through it, no colour and no motion; the status is the word plus a lamp shape: ring for ON TIME, disc for BOARDING, half disc for DELAYED, slashed ring for CANCELED; the ticker under a single rule.

examples.name: colour-wheel-picker
examples.title: Pro colour picker: hue ring, SV square, hex and WCAG contrast
examples.summary: A precise HSV colour picker in one canvas: a sweep-gradient hue ring around a saturation/value square built from three stacked gradients, two drag handles that grow while held, a live swatch with white and black sample text, the hex code assembled from text lookups, rgb() and H/S/V read-outs, and a WCAG 2.2 contrast check (sRGB linearisation, relative luminance, ratio, AA / AA Large / AAA / Fail badge and a log-scale meter) against white and black text, all computed with expressions. Phone layouts stack wheel and panel; a wide box puts the panel beside the wheel.
examples.prompt: Build an HSV colour picker that looks like a pro design tool: a hue ring and a saturation/value square I can drag, a live preview swatch, the hex code, and a contrast check of white and black text on the colour with the WCAG ratio and pass/fail.
examples.hand_built: No library component draws a hue ring or an SV field, and the touch routing (which control the finger went down on, latched values per control) and the colour maths are specific to this picker.
teaches: Route one canvas's drag to two controls: onTouchDown stores touchX()/touchY() in root variables, and the tree classifies the press (inside the square, or on the ring) from those and the live geometry

Latch a value per control without actions that read tree variables: a touchExpression with expression [0], touchMode 1 and min = max = the live value while its control is held (±100000 otherwise) is a register that keeps its last clamped value
Fill with an exact runtime hue without a computed colour: a linear gradient of the 7-stop hue ramp stretched to 2000 px per degree and offset so the drawn shape sits on @hue
Composite the HSV colour from fixed paints: pure hue, then white at alpha 1 - s, then black at alpha 1 - v (the swatch, both handles and the contrast chips)
Build the SV square from three gradients over the same rounded rect: pure hue, white to transparent left to right, transparent to black top to bottom

Compute WCAG contrast with expressions: sRGB bytes from HSV, linearise each channel (c / 12.92 below 10.31/255, else ((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4), luminance 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B, ratios 1.05 / (L + 0.05) and (L + 0.05) / 0.05
Spell a hex code with textSubtext of "0123456789ABCDEF#" (start floor(R / 16) and R % 16) joined by textMerge, and show a grade by drawing its four labels with alpha 1 - min(1, |grade - j|)

Make a colour tool honest in mono: fork every colour paint with {"$if": "theme.mono"} and draw structure instead (ring edges with the primaries named, an outlined grid for the square, hollow handles), keep every number and grade as text, and show pass versus fail by a filled or outlined pill
pitfalls: A modifier action is parsed before the canvas commands, so onTouchDown/onTouchUp cannot read a tree variable (componentWidth(), a touchExpression): record raw touch positions in root variables and do the geometry in the tree
step(x, edge) is strict (x > edge): step(1, 1) is 0
A computed colour (hsv/argb) cannot read tree values; the gradient trick and alpha compositing avoid it
A gradient paint inherits the paint's alpha: set an opaque colour before a gradient that follows a translucent colour, or the ring draws at 40%
A text starting with '#' is not drawn as text; put the '#' at the end of the lookup string and cut it out with textSubtext
Canvas paints have no font weight: weights need text components
The latch keeps the last drag position, not the up position: an up event far from the last move does not move the value
Java's addDataList drops the list id, so textLookup cannot reach it from JSON (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U4): the grade labels are four texts selected by alpha

snippets.note: the hue register: min = max = @liveH while the ring is held
hue from the finger: atan2 around the ring centre, 0° at the top
the SV square's pure-hue fill: the hue ramp stretched to 2000 px per degree
white to transparent, then transparent to black (next command) over the square
contrast with white text from the relative luminance
hex digits cut from a lookup string with textSubtext
WCAG grade index: step(c, 3) + step(c, 4.5) + step(c, 7); one of four labels is shown by alpha
24 tick marks round the ring
a live description: hex and both contrast grades

check.describe: Default: #3882D6 (H 212, S 74, V 84): white text 3.94:1 AA Large, black text 5.33:1 AA. Dragging the hue handle round to the top right (H 40) and the SV handle up and right gives #F2AA18, rgb(242, 170, 24): white 1.99:1 Fail (red meter), black 10.54:1 AAA; both handles sit where the finger left them and the ring handle keeps its hue while the square is dragged. Dragging the SV handle down darkens the colour and flips the grades. 320x568 shrinks the wheel and compacts the swatch; 820x520 moves the panel beside the wheel. Light: a pale page with dark text and the same colour controls; dark: the dark tool look. Mono (dark and light): no colour can be shown, so the ring is drawn as its two edges with R Y G C B M marked, the square as an outlined grid labelled SATURATION and VALUE, the handles as hollow rings, the swatch says to read the values, and the hex, H/S/V, rgb(), ratios, meters and grades stay readable (passing grades as filled pills).

examples.name: swipe-card-stack
examples.title: Swipe card stack: travel destinations to like or pass
examples.summary: A Tinder-style stack of five drawn travel cards (Lofoten under the northern lights, Kyoto at dusk with a torii, Santorini's caldera, the Wadi Rum desert, Patagonia's towers), each painted from float arrays by one loop: layered sky gradients, stars, aurora ribbons, a glowing sun, three pathExpression ridges, a sea band and landmarks. The top card follows the finger and tilts with it, a LIKE or NOPE stamp fades in, the card behind scales up; a fast flick or a drag past a third of the card flies it off with its release speed, anything else springs back with a damped spring. Buttons fling the card too, and the saved / passed counts update.
examples.prompt: Make a Tinder-style card stack of travel destinations with drawn art: I drag a card sideways and it rotates with my finger, if I fling it past a threshold it flies off left or right with a Like/Nope stamp, the next card scales up from behind, and it counts my likes. It should feel physical: fling and spring back.
teaches: Build a swipe deck from the library SwipeStack: bind liked and passed to resources variables for the header counts, name the card index ("index": "@card") and draw the scene in the card slot from it
Paint five different scenes from one body: per-card float arrays drive layer alphas (night, warm, day skies, aurora, sea, landmarks) and ridge parameters for pathExpression
Close a pathExpression ridge to the bottom by running a[0] slightly past 0..1 with x clamped and y = ifElse(card height, ridge, inside)

Give a picture-led card stack four looks: light and dark keep the painted art and theme only the page, header, counters and buttons; mono redraws each scene as hidden-line art (fill each ridge with the page colour, stroke it in onSurface) with outlined stamps and card edges instead of colour
pitfalls: step(x, edge) is strict: step(1, 1) is 0, so test a direction with step(@dir, 0.5)
A computed colour is evaluated once per frame, not per loop iteration: vary paint alpha and gradients by the loop index instead
Java's addDataList drops the list id, so textLookup cannot reach it from JSON: each card's texts are five drawTextAnchored per field, the right one shown by alpha 1 - min(1, |c - j|)
The card slot is drawn for every visible card each frame (up to four): the scene is one loop-free body driven by float arrays, not five copies

snippets.note: the swipe deck's counts land in the document's own variables
the library SwipeStack: drag, tilt, fling or spring back, stamps, the stack's lift and the Pass / Save buttons
one card's scene drawn from @card: the mono hidden-line drawing and the painted one
the base dusk sky; night, warm and day skies are faded over it by per-card alphas
per-destination sky, sun, ridge and landmark parameters
the header with the saved and passed counts the stack writes

check.describe: Rest: Lofoten on top (night sky, aurora, red cabins), Kyoto and Santorini peeking below, 0 passed / 0 saved. Dragging right by 90 px tilts the card, fades in LIKE and lifts Kyoto. A flick (70 px in 80 ms) flies Lofoten off to the right and SAVED reads 1; a slow 65 px drag springs back with a small overshoot. Dragging Kyoto left shows NOPE over Santorini. The Pass and Save buttons fling the top card the same way. 320x568 and 700x1000 scale the card as one design. Light: a pale page with dark header text and the painted cards; dark: the night page. Mono (dark and light): the scenes become hidden-line drawings in one ink, stamps and card edges outlined, buttons outlined.

examples.name: morphing-weather
examples.title: Morphing weather: one icon path that morphs between sun, cloud, rain, snow and storm
examples.summary: A weather screen whose big icon is a single path morphing pairwise between five outlines (sun disc, cloud, rain cloud, snow cloud, storm anvil) with an eased blend, whether the host changes the condition or a day is tapped in the forecast strip. Spinning sun rays, falling rain, drifting snow and a flickering bolt fade in with their condition, the sky gradient and the icon's colours blend along, and the temperature, high/low, wind, humidity and rain chance count to the new day's values. One canvas lays out a phone screen or, when wide or short, a 4x2 widget.
examples.prompt: A weather screen whose big icon morphs smoothly between sun, cloud, rain, snow and storm when the condition changes or when I tap a day in the forecast strip, with animated details (spinning sun rays, falling drops), the temperature counting to the new value and the background gradient shifting. It should also work as a 4x2 widget.
examples.hand_built: The sky, text and forecast strip are one canvas laid out by expressions (phone or widget arrangement) and blended by the same eased weights as the icon; the icons themselves are WeatherIcon in morph mode
teaches: The big icon is {"WeatherIcon": {"morph": true, "value": "@dc", "look": "rich", "animate": true}}: one outline that morphs pairwise between sun, cloud, rain, snow and storm whenever @dc changes (a host condition or a tapped day), with turning rays, falling rain, drifting snow and a flickering bolt

The strip's mini icons are the same component in the flat look, one per day, value = that day's condition and colours from the document's themed mini0..mini4, drop, flake and bolt: a host update of the forecast arrays morphs them too

Size the icon from an expression: the call sits in a box whose width and height are @isz (a resources variable from windowWidth()/windowHeight()), with a large size; the component scales its drawing to the box it gets. Spacer boxes of @ixl and @iyt place it

The sky blends with the icon: five eased weights w_i = anim(1 - |dc - i|, 0.8 s), the same as WeatherIcon's, turned into chain alphas k_i = w_i / (w_0 + ... + w_i) over five gradient rectangles, so sky and icon change together
The temperature, high/low and stats are anim'd values ({value, anim: 0.9}) printed with textFromFloat: the number counts to the new value

Four looks: the skies are themed colours (light: pale daylight skies under dark ink text; dark: deep dusk skies under white text); text uses the theme tokens onSurface/muted/track, overridden with the art's own light/dark values, so the mono palettes remap them. In mono ({"$if": "theme.mono"} forks) there is no sky and no fill: the same morphing path is stroked in onSurface, rays, drops and flakes are onSurface strokes and dots, the strip and its selection are outlines, and t = 0 holds every ambient motion still (repaint idle); the morph switches

One canvas does both layouts: wide = max(step(W / heroHeight, 1.6), step(400, heroHeight)) picks the widget arrangement (icon left, text right) over the phone one, and the two text blocks are scaled by wide and 1 - wide
The forecast strip is drawn in the canvas; its tap targets are five transparent weighted boxes over it in a column, each with semantics and valueFloatChange sel = i
pitfalls: Six morph calls (the hero and five minis) cost about 1.7 KB each beyond the shared outlines (about 5 KB once): the document grew from 18.8 KB (hand-drawn) to 28.3 KB with the component
Mono has no motion (the expansion removes every anim): the icons and the sky switch instead of morphing
Paint alpha is reset by a following color op in the same paint: set alpha in every paint that sets a colour
Expressions are capped at 32 entries on Android: the chain weights are split into ws, k1..k4
A paint's alpha op overrides the alpha of its colour: a translucent themed colour (#33FFFFFF) drawn with alpha 1 in the same paint comes out opaque. Set the alpha in an earlier paint, then the colour
The clickable boxes get the player's press feedback (a light disc at the tap point for a few frames, in both players), drawn over the canvas
The TS harness in players/typescript/render.mjs pins the clock without advancing it; to see the morph frames in TS use the inspector (interact) or advance the clock per frame

snippets.note: the big icon: WeatherIcon morph mode, rich look, animated details
a mini icon: the flat look in the document's colours
w0: the sky's eased weight, as the icon's
the temperature counts to the selected day's value
the host sets the current condition (0..4); arrays fc/hi/lo/wind/hum/rain carry the forecast

condition.meaning: the current condition: 0 sun, 1 cloud, 2 rain, 3 snow, 4 storm

sel.meaning: the selected day, 0 (now) to 4; taps set it

fc.meaning: condition of the next four days (0..4)

hi.meaning: high temperature, today and the next four days

inputs.clock: the date line and the weekday names of the strip

check.describe: Looks: light = pale skies with dark text (rain shown), dark = deep skies with white text (storm shown), mono-dark = white line drawing of the rain cloud on black with outlined strip, mono-light = black line drawing on white caught mid-morph to the storm after tapping Thu. Clock pinned to Monday 2 November 2026. 360x640: Lyon, Monday · 2 November, a sun with 12 rays on a blue sky, 12°, Sunny, H 14° L 4°, wind/humidity/rain, and a strip Now Tue Wed Thu Fri with mini icons and highs. condition 2/3/4: the same screen with a rain cloud and falling drops on a dark slate sky, a snow cloud with flakes, a dark anvil with a yellow bolt on a near-black sky. morph: 0.3 s after tapping Wed the disc is half-way to the rain cloud, rays shrinking, drops appearing, sky darkening, the number counting down. tapped-storm: Thursday selected, storm icon, 10°. Widgets 360x180 and 400x200: icon left, big temperature and condition, city/day/high-low right, the strip below. 300x300 uses the widget arrangement; 412x915 the phone one.

examples.name: parallax-onboarding
examples.title: Parallax onboarding: a landscape that follows your swipe from day to night
examples.summary: A three-page onboarding whose illustration is a layered landscape drawn from paths: far mountains, hills, a meadow and a foreground ridge tile seamlessly and move at 0.15, 0.4, 1 and 1.35 page widths per page while you drag, so depth comes from the finger. Swiping also moves the sun down and turns the sky from day to dusk to a starry night with a moon; each page has its own scene (pines and a trail sign, a bobbing hot-air balloon, a tent with a flickering campfire and sparks). The pager follows the finger and eases to the nearest page on release, the active dot stretches between dots like a worm, text slides and cross-fades, and the round arrow button grows into a full-width Get started pill on the last page. Light and dark sheets; portrait, tablet and landscape (side panel) layouts.
examples.prompt: A three-page onboarding pager with layered illustrations (hills, clouds, objects drawn with paths) that move at different speeds as you swipe, an animated dot indicator that stretches between pages, and a Get started button that appears on the last page. Make it polished, app-store quality.
examples.hand_built: The Pager component changes page on release and cannot follow the finger, and parallax needs every layer to read the continuous drag position, so the pager, layers and indicator are one hand-built canvas
teaches: A pager that follows the finger without touchExpression: onTouchDown stores start = touchX() and down = 1; while down, live = page + (start - touchX()) / W; onTouchUp sets page = clamp(0, 2, page + clamp(-1, 1, round((start - touchX()) / (0.5 * windowWidth())))) and down = 0

pos = {value: ifElse(@page, @live, @down - 0.5), anim: 0.5}: while dragging the target changes every frame and the anim restarts from the previous target, so it tracks the finger; on release the target becomes the page and pos eases there from where the finger left it

Parallax: every layer translates by -pos * P * speed (P = one page in scene units); objects of page i sit at centre + (i - pos) * P, so speed 1 carries them with the page, the balloon at 0.8 and the far one at 0.4 drift behind
Seamless ridges: each is a periodic function sampled over 1200 units into one cubic path, drawn in a loop of ceil((P + 400) / 1200) + 2 tiles offset by (k - 1) * 1200 - (offset % 1200)

Day to night with chain alphas: the sky, every ridge and the clouds are drawn three times (day colour at alpha 1, dusk at clamp(pos), night at clamp(pos - 1)); the sun's height, the moon, the stars and the firelight read the same pos
Worm indicator: with i = min(1, floor(pos)) and u = pos - i, the pill runs from dot i + max(0, 2u - 1) to dot i + min(1, 2u): its head reaches the next dot half-way, then its tail follows

The arrow button grows into Get started with e = smooth_step(pos - 1, 1, 0): its left edge moves from W - 80 to the panel's left + 24, the arrow fades out and the label in. Tap targets are layout boxes whose visibility is the integer expression min(1, |page - 2|) (Skip, Next) or its complement (Get started, a hostNamedAction)

Four looks: the sheet, text, dots and track are the theme tokens surface/onSurface/muted/track (overridden with the design's light/dark values, remapped by the mono palettes); accents are themed acc0..acc2; in dark a themed 20 % black veil dims the illustration so it sits with the dark sheet. Mono forks ({"$if": "theme.mono"}) turn the illustration into line art: every shape is filled with the background (so nearer layers hide farther ones) and outlined in onSurface, ridge crests are pathExpressions of the same periodic profile (no seams between tiles), sun and moon are circles, the button is an outlined pill; t = 0 stops the ambient motion while the swipe, parallax, worm and button morph still work
Landscape: land = step(W / H, 1.2) turns the bottom sheet into a right-hand panel; the illustration centres on the visible left part and the tap boxes are shifted by a width expression
pitfalls: A paint's alpha op overrides its colour's alpha: the dark-theme veil (#33000000) drawn with alpha 1 in one paint was opaque black. Set alpha in an earlier paint, then the colour
A paint that sets a colour resets the alpha: give every coloured paint its own alpha (the body text was visible on every page until it had one)
Expressions are capped at 32 entries: the cloud wrap-around is split into cw, cv, cx
% of a negative number stays negative: the clouds add 100 page widths before the modulo
Buttons change page on tap, the canvas's onTouchUp also runs: it adds round(0) to the page, so a tap never moves the page by itself
The vocabulary's input.pager evidence is touchExpression only; this pager uses onTouchDown/onTouchUp and touchX(), so it does not claim input.pager
No fling: a fast short flick under a quarter of the width does not turn the page (touchVelX() could be added to the release rule)

snippets.note: live: the page under the finger while dragging
pos: follows the finger, then eases to the page
a tileable mountain ridge: one period of a periodic function as cubics
t = continuousSec(): clouds drift, the balloon bobs, stars twinkle, the fire flickers

page.meaning: the page, 0 to 2; swipes and the buttons set it

check.describe: Looks: light and dark page 1 (dark: dark sheet, light text, the illustration slightly dimmed), mono-dark after a swipe to page 2 (white line art on black: mountain crests, the balloon, page 2 text at full contrast, second dot active), mono-light page 3 (black line art on white: moon, stars, tent and flame outlines, an outlined Get started pill). 360x760 light, page 1: blue sky, sun and clouds, pale mountains, green hills, pines and a TRAIL sign; white sheet with Find your trail, two lines, three dots (first blue), Skip and a round blue arrow. drag: 60, 120, 200 px left the pines slide out faster than the mountains, the sky turns violet, the balloon enters, the dot stretches toward the second. release: eases to page 2 (dusk sky, orange sun low behind the balloon, Go further, safely, orange arrow). page 3: night sky with stars and moon, a lit tent and campfire, Sleep under the stars, a full-width violet Get started pill. Dark: the sheet is near-black with light text. Tablet 800x1280 scales text; landscape 760x360 and 1280x800 put the text in a right-hand panel.

examples.name: kobento-logo
examples.title: Animated Kobento logo for a website header
examples.summary: The Kobento mark and wordmark as a wide header that tells the brand in about three seconds: four rounded tiles pop into a 2x2 grid one after another with an overshoot, turn into small UI parts (an image tile, two text lines, a toggle whose knob slides, a round play button) while the mark slides left, the wordmark rises letter by letter out of a slot on its baseline, and the parts fold back into the clean mark. Then it rests: no repaint until a tap replays it. The wordmark is drawn from strokes and arcs (a heavy geometric sans), so it looks the same in every player. Light (paper), dark (deep ink, paper wordmark) and two still mono looks with outlined tiles. About 6.2 KB.
examples.prompt: Build an animated Kobento logo for the header of the website: the four coloured tiles of the mark pop in, turn into little UI parts for a moment, settle back, and the word Kobento appears beside them; then it rests, and a tap replays it. Wide header, light, dark and mono looks.
examples.hand_built: A logo is drawing, not layout: one canvas scaled to fit, tiles as eased round rects and the wordmark as stroked lines and arcs, so no font is needed
teaches: One clock for the whole story: e = animationTime() - @tapAt; every phase is a clamped ramp min(max((e - start) / duration, 0), 1) shaped by a back-out (1 + 2.70158 p^3 + 1.70158 p^2 with p = ramp - 1) for the pops and smoothstep (x^2 (3 - 2x)) for the morphs and the slide

Rest after the intro: an animated value run = {"value": "@tc", "anim": 3.5}, read by e as 0 * @run, asks for a repaint every frame while it animates: for 3.5 s after the document appears (an animated expression counts from its first evaluation) and for 3.5 s after each tap (tc + 1). Then nothing asks and the header is idle
Replay on tap without a ripple: onTouchDown sets tapAt = animationTime() (restarting every ramp) and tc = tc + 1 (restarting the frames); onClick would ripple over the logo

Shapes that become other shapes by interpolating their numbers: the blue tile is two round rects that start on top of each other and part into two text bars, the green one shrinks to a pill with a sliding knob, the orange corner radius grows to half the side (a circle) under a play triangle

A wordmark without fonts: each letter is butt-capped strokes (lines, a circle, arcs) 15 units wide on a 62-unit x-height; the K's diagonals run past the cap and base lines and a clipRect cuts them flat, as in a type design
The header is a 720 x 220 sheet scaled by min(W / 720, H / 220) and centred, so it reads the same from 360 x 160 to 1600 x 400
Four looks: themed page, ink and tile colours for light and dark; {"$if": "theme.mono"} forks give outlined tiles in onSurface and pin e at 10 (the settled state, no motion)
pitfalls: Canvas text has no font weight and its face differs between players (Skia default vs the browser's sans-serif): a logo wordmark drawn as text would not match the brand, strokes do
An onClick on the canvas paints a ripple in every player (U29); a logo replay uses onTouchDown instead

wakeIn cannot be used to stop: the players keep the smallest wake ever requested (RemoteComposeState.wakeIn only lowers mRepaintSeconds once a repaint was scheduled, as upstream Java does), so "0.016 + 3600 * step(e, 3.4)" keeps repainting at 60 fps forever. A NaN resets it but then no later wakeIn takes. An animated value's own repaint request is what ends

players/typescript/render.mjs cannot pin animationTime: TimeVariables reads performance.now(), so the frames it renders all sit at t = 0 (a blank intro frame). Drive performance.now to render a mid-animation frame in TS
Keep stroke joins overlapping by a unit or two (the n's right stem starts above the end of its arch): butt ends that only touch leave a hairline seam when the header is scaled

inputs.clock: animationTime drives the intro (0 to 3.5 s after load or a tap); nothing runs afterwards

check.describe: Settled (t = 4 s), light: an off-white paper page, the Kobento mark (lavender, blue, green and orange rounded squares in a 2x2 grid) left of a heavy dark-ink geometric wordmark Kobento, the pair centred. pop (0.4 s): lavender tile landed, blue overshooting, orange just appearing, no green, mark centred alone. parts (1.2 s): all four tiles in, a faint image glyph starting on the lavender one. ui (1.8 s): the parts: a white mountains-and-sun image glyph on lavender, blue split into two bars, green a pill with a white knob sliding, orange a circle with a white play triangle, the mark sliding left. word (2.4 s): mark at its place, K-o-b-e up, n rising out of the baseline slot, t and o still hidden below it. Dark: deep ink page, same tiles, paper-coloured wordmark. Mono dark and mono light: outlined tiles and the wordmark in white on black or black on white, settled. narrow 360x160 and wide 1600x400: the same composition scaled.

snippets.note: the mark: four tiles popping in 0.13 s apart with a back-out overshoot, then morphing into UI parts and back
run = {value: @tc, anim: 3.5}: an animated value asks for frames while it runs (3.5 s after load and after each tap), so the header repaints only during the intro
e = animationTime() - tapAt, the one clock of the story (pinned to 10 in the mono looks)
the wordmark: butt-capped strokes, lines and arcs, letter K with its own clipRect, all of them rising out of a clipped slot on the baseline

examples.name: month-grid
examples.title: Month calendar from nested loops
examples.summary: A month calendar drawn by a week loop around a weekday loop: each cell's day number comes from the two indices and the month's first weekday, and step masks hide days outside the month, dim weekends and circle today.
examples.prompt: Draw a month calendar for October 2026 (starts on a Thursday, 31 days) with Monday-first weekday initials, weekends dimmed and today, the 29th, circled.
teaches: Nest two loops (week 0..6, weekday 0..7) and turn the two indices into one value: day = week * 7 + wd + 1 - @firstWeekday
Name a per-iteration value with a variable command inside the loop body and reuse it in later commands of the same iteration
Hide, dim or show an item per iteration without a branch: a 0/1 step mask as paint alpha (inside the month, weekends) or as a radius (today's circle)
Drive a loop's content from exported variables, so the same document renders any month
pitfalls: step(a, b) is 1 only when a > b (strict): test day >= 1 as step(@day, 0.5) and day <= 31 as step(31.5, @day)

Avoid conditionalOperations inside a loop for anything that reads the loop index through an expression: a block updates all its commands' inputs before running them, so an expression computed in the block is one iteration late, and a value computed before the block may not refresh at all (C++). Masks keep it right
There is no break: a loop always runs from..until. Make the bounds cover the worst case (6 weeks) and mask the cells you do not want

Derive the cell pitch from componentWidth()/componentHeight() once (two variable commands before the loops) instead of literal 41 × 38 cells: the loop body reads @cw and @rh every iteration, and the weekday letters step along with translate(@cw), which costs no new expression

This grid is fixed to October 2026 to keep the loop lesson small (rc-inspect flags it: hardcoded_date). For 'this month' or 'today', compute the month, the weekday of the 1st, the day count and today from the clock, as TIM-10 does; never paste them.

snippets.note: outer loop over weeks, inner loop over weekdays
day number from both indices and @firstWeekday
inMonth: 1 for 1 <= day <= monthDays, else 0
paint alpha = inMonth, dimmed on weekdays 5 and 6

today.meaning: day of the month to circle (0 for none)

check.describe: October 2026: 1 under Thursday, 31 under Saturday, Saturday and Sunday columns dimmed, 29 in a blue circle; no numbers before the 1st or after the 31st. Resized (small 200×220, large 450×450) the grid spreads over the canvas: cells are cw = (componentWidth() - 13) / 7 wide and rh = (componentHeight() - 72) / 6 high, and today's circle is 0.42 × the smaller of the two.

examples.name: agenda-pairs
examples.title: Loop over data in pairs
examples.summary: Today's meetings stored as one flat array of start/end hours; a loop with step 2 and until = arrayLength draws one bar per pair, labels its duration and dims the ones already over, over an hour grid drawn by a second stepped loop.
examples.prompt: Show today's meetings (9:00–10:30, 11:00–12:00, 13:30–14:30, 15:00–16:45) as bars on an 8 to 18 h timeline with hour labels, each bar labelled with its length, a red now line at 14:00 and finished meetings dimmed.
examples.hand_built: The bars are drawn in a canvas loop over a float array of start and end pairs, because looping over data in pairs is the lesson; for a real schedule use TimelineTrack, which packs, labels and axes the intervals for you.
teaches: Store records as consecutive values in one floatArrays (start, end, start, end …) and walk them with loop step 2: arrayGet(@meetings, i) and arrayGet(@meetings, i + 1)
Bound a loop by the data, not a constant: until = arrayLength(@meetings), so adding a pair adds a bar
Use a loop's from/until/step for an axis: hours 8..18 every 2 with the index itself as the label
Derive per-item state from the item: alpha 1 - 0.6 * step(@now, end) dims a meeting once it is over
pitfalls: The loop index counts array slots, not records: with step 2 the k-th record is at i = 2k, so a row position written i * 15 moves 30 px per record
until is exclusive and is compared with the index (i < until): until = arrayLength(@meetings) stops at the last pair; until 19 with from 8 step 2 still reaches 18
A loop has no break or filter: hide the items you do not want with a mask (alpha, size), or prepare the array so it only holds what to draw
Put the axis scale in one variable from componentWidth() (px) rather than a literal 31 px per hour in every expression: the timeline then fits any width

snippets.note: loop i from 0 until arrayLength(@meetings) step 2: one bar per (start, end) pair
dim when the end is before @now
hour grid: loop h from 8 until 19 step 2, index printed as the label
the records, flattened

check.describe: Four bars on four rows: 1.5 h and 1.0 h dimmed (before 14:00), 1.0 h (13:30–14:30, crossing the red now line) and 1.75 h bright; hour labels 8 to 18; "4 meetings" top right. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the 8–18 h axis spans the canvas: one hour is px = (componentWidth() - 50) / 10, read by the grid, the now line and every bar, and the count stays at the right edge.

examples.name: loop-bounds
examples.title: Loops with variable bounds
examples.summary: A water-intake tracker whose glasses come from two loops bounded by host variables: filled glasses from 0 to min(drunk, goal), empty outlines from drunk to goal; an empty range simply draws nothing.
examples.prompt: A water tracker widget: a row of glasses for a daily goal of 8, the 5 already drunk filled blue and the rest as outlines, "5 of 8 glasses", a progress bar and "3 to go".
examples.hand_built: The glasses are drawn in a canvas loop because variable loop bounds are the lesson; the progress bar under them is a library ProgressBar.
teaches: Repeat a drawing a variable number of times: loop until "min(@drunk, @goal)" (an expression bound is re-read whenever the variable changes)
Start a second loop where the first stopped (from "@drunk" until "@goal") to draw the remainder in another style
Rely on empty ranges instead of if: when from >= until the loop body never runs (0 drunk: no filled glasses; goal reached: no outlines)
Show the same ratio with a library ProgressBar under the canvas ("progress": "@drunk / @goal"): it clamps a value past the goal to a full bar and eases its fill when the variable changes
pitfalls: Clamp a bound that can exceed the space you drew for: min(@drunk, @goal) keeps a ninth glass off the row
Set the paint before the loop when every iteration shares it; a paint inside the body is re-applied on every iteration
The index is a float: from "@drunk" = 4.5 gives 4.5, 5.5, …; floor the bound if the variable can be fractional

Space loop items by a pitch derived from the width and the item count, g = (componentWidth() - 40) / @goal, rather than a literal 40: a fixed pitch overflows a narrow host and leaves a gap on a wide one

snippets.note: filled glasses: loop i from 0 until min(@drunk, @goal)
outlines: loop i from @drunk until @goal

goal.meaning: daily goal in glasses (8 fit the row)

check.describe: Five filled glasses then three outlines, "5 of 8 glasses", the bar at 62 %, "3 to go". drunk 0 gives eight outlines; drunk 9 gives eight filled glasses and "0 to go". Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the row of glasses spans the canvas: the pitch is g = (componentWidth() - 40) / @goal and each glass is gw = min(28, 0.7 g) wide, so the goal's glasses always fill the row; the bar and the count follow the width.

examples.name: switch-cases
examples.title: Switch on a state code, with a default
examples.summary: A weather card that switches on an integer condition code: one eq block per case, a shared cloud drawn once for the range of cases 1–3, and a default case written as the two complementary blocks lt 0 and gt 3; rem commands label the cases in the document.
examples.prompt: A current-weather card that shows a sun, cloud, rain or snow icon with its name and one line of advice, chosen from a condition code 0–3 (here 2, rain), and a "No data" state for any other code.
examples.hand_built: The icons are drawn in conditionalOperations, which only take canvas commands, because switching on a code with a default is the lesson; to show a weather condition otherwise, call WeatherIcon.
teaches: Write a switch as one conditionalOperations eq block per case value: only the matching block runs
Share drawing between several cases with a range block (ge 1 containing le 3) placed before the per-case blocks, like a fallthrough
Write the default case as the complement of all cases: here lt 0 plus gt 3, two blocks with the same content (there is no else and no or)
Label sections of a long command list with rem: a comment the document carries and players ignore
pitfalls: The Java parser knows only gt, ge, lt, le and eq: any other name, ne included (a json2rc extension), becomes 0, which is EQ, so a ne block silently runs when the values are equal, the opposite of what was meant
eq compares floats exactly: switch on whole-number codes, never on a computed fraction
A gap in the codes needs its own default block: with codes 0, 1 and 3, the default is lt 0, eq 2 and gt 3
Paint state carries across blocks: set colour and size at the top of every case, or a case inherits whatever the previous one set
A canvas laid out at fixed coordinates needs a fit rule: here one variable and a translate + scale at the top keep it centred and on screen at any size, without touching the cases

snippets.note: case 2: eq @condition 2, rain drops and text
range block for cases 1-3: the shared cloud
default, first half: lt 0
default, second half: gt 3
rem: a comment kept in the document

condition.meaning: 0 clear, 1 cloudy, 2 rain, 3 snow; anything else is no data

check.describe: condition 2: a cloud with three blue rain streaks, "Rain", "Take an umbrella.". 0 gives the yellow sun with eight rays, 1 the cloud alone, 3 the cloud with snow dots, -1 or 4 a grey "?" and "No data". Resized, the drawing is centred vertically (translate componentHeight() / 2 - 85) and shrinks below 300 dp wide (scale min(1, componentWidth() / 300)) so the longest line still fits: at 240 it is drawn at 0.8.

examples.name: pattern-list
examples.title: A list from a template and a data list
examples.summary: A favourites list whose five rows are one ContactRow template (definePattern) inflated by patternForEach over a list of names; each row derives its avatar initial from its name with textSubtext, and the name list is hoisted out of the layout with a global section.
examples.prompt: A favourites contact list (Ada Lovelace, Barbara Liskov, Claude Shannon, Edsger Dijkstra, Grace Hopper): each row has a round avatar with the initial, the name and a chevron, built from one row definition repeated over the list of names.
examples.hand_built: The row is a definePattern template inflated from a data list, because the template is the lesson; ListItem with an Avatar draws the same row as a component (expanded in full per call: see STR-07 for the size comparison).
teaches: Define a row once with definePattern (parameter who) and repeat it for every item of a data list with patternForEach {collection, localItem, children}
Pass the current item to the template by name: {"ContactRow": {"who": "@name"}}, where name is the patternForEach localItem
Derive per-row values inside the template from its parameter (textSubtext of @who gives the avatar initial), so the data list stays one string per row
Hoist the data list out of the layout with a global section in a canvas: it is written before the root, like a resource
pitfalls: addDataList cannot be named in the Java parser (U4), so collection is the list's numeric id: 2097194 (0x20002A) for the first array of a document. A floatArrays resource or another list before it moves that id
addDataList is a canvas command, not a component: it needs a canvas around it (here a 0-size one, its command wrapped in global)
A pattern name must not match a built-in component case-insensitively: a template called Row fails with "Cannot override pre-existing component"
patternForEach gives one id per item; a row needing several fields needs them derived from that one string (or one template call per row instead of a data list)

snippets.note: patternForEach over list 2097194, item bound to name, one ContactRow call per item
the ContactRow template: parameter who
textSubtext(@who, 0, 1): the initial
the names list, hoisted before the root

check.describe: Five rows under FAVOURITES, in list order, each with a blue initial avatar (A, B, C, E, G), the full name and a grey chevron. Resized (narrow 220, wide 540) every inflated row fills the width with the chevron at the right edge; a long name ellipsizes on one line.

examples.name: pattern-slot
examples.title: A template with a content slot
examples.summary: One Panel template (rounded surface, muted title) used twice with different content: the template marks where content goes with patternArgument, and each call passes its own components in a patternBlock for that parameter.
examples.prompt: Two dashboard panels in the same style: STORAGE with "41.6 of 64 GB used" and a usage bar, and RECENT DOWNLOADS with two files and their sizes; define the panel frame once and give each its own content.
examples.hand_built: The panel frame is a definePattern with a content slot because that is the lesson; the library Card is the same frame as a component, and the usage bar inside the slot is a library ProgressBar.
teaches: Leave a hole in a template with {"patternArgument": {"parameterIndex": 1}}: parameter 1 (content) is a slot, not a value
Fill the slot at the call: the call's children hold {"patternBlock": {"parameterIndex": 1, "children": [...]}}, any components at all
Mix value parameters and slots: title is passed by name ("title": "STORAGE"), content as a block
Pass a library component in a slot: the ProgressBar call inside the patternBlock is expanded there like any other node, and the template still sees only a block
pitfalls: parameterIndex counts the template's parameters from 0 (title is 0, content 1); the slot parameter still has to be declared in parameters
The block lands where patternArgument sits, inside the template's container: it is laid out by that column, so it is stacked, not overlaid
A slot that is not given renders nothing, with no error

snippets.note: the slot: patternArgument parameterIndex 1
the call's content: patternBlock parameterIndex 1
Panel template, parameters title and content

check.describe: Two identical rounded panels (outlined in mono): STORAGE with 41.6 large, "of 64 GB used" and a 65 % blue bar; RECENT DOWNLOADS with two file names and their muted details. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) both panels fill the width and the storage bar, a ProgressBar drawn from componentWidth(), stays at 65 % of its panel.

examples.name: pattern-vs-component
examples.title: Format template vs library component
examples.summary: The same key/value spec row built twice: four SpecRow calls of a definePattern template that the player inflates, and four calls of the KeyValueRow library component that json2rc expands into plain components before writing. They look the same; the template costs about 48 B per extra row, the expanded component about 200 B (KeyValueRow v3, whose key ellipsizes in a weighted box).
examples.prompt: A phone spec card (Display 6.1 in OLED, Chip A18, Storage 256 GB, Battery 3,561 mAh) built once with a definePattern row template and once with the KeyValueRow library component, to compare them.
teaches: Choose definePattern when the same row repeats: the body is stored once in the .rc and each call is a pattern inflation with its argument ids (measured here: 840 B for 1 row, 1078 B for 6, about 48 B per extra row)

Choose a library component (KeyValueRow) for richer options (slots, $if, theme tokens) resolved at conversion: json2rc expands each call into plain components, so every call costs its full body (788 B for 1 row, 1641 B for 6, about 171 B per row)
Re-theme library components by defining their colours (surface, muted, onSurface) in resources.colors; a template reads the same named colours through @colors
pitfalls: A text inside a template measures as one component for every instance (U7): two intrinsic-width texts in a row collide, clipped to one instance's width. Give template texts a weight or fixed width (here both texts take weight 1, the value right-aligned)
The break-even is about two rows: with one call the template's definition (about 52 B) is pure overhead
The Java parser only sees the expanded document: a library component call is a json2rc feature, and doc.expanded.json is what is byte-checked; definePattern is in the format and every parser reads it

snippets.note: SpecRow template: key and value, both texts weighted
a template call: {"SpecRow": {key, value}}
the library call: {"KeyValueRow": {key, value}}, expanded at conversion

check.describe: Two cards with the same four rows, keys muted on the left and values right-aligned; the top card's label says definePattern, the bottom one KeyValueRow. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) both cards fill the width, keys stay left and values right in both builds, and a caption too long for the card ellipsizes.

examples.name: referenced-include
examples.title: Record once, include anywhere
examples.summary: A verified badge (a small canvas with a circle and a tick) recorded once with referencedOperations and placed after three names with include; the document is 900 B against 1163 B with the badge written out three times.
examples.prompt: A reviewers list (Margaret Hamilton, Ken Thompson, Linus Torvalds, Frances Allen) where every name but Linus's has the same small blue verified tick after it; draw the tick once and reuse it.
examples.hand_built: The tick is recorded once with referencedOperations and included after each name, because recording and including is the lesson; for a ready-made symbol use Icon (verified), whose path is also stored once per document.
teaches: Record a fragment once with {"referencedOperations": {"name": "Verified", "children": [...]}}: it is stored, not shown
Place it wherever it is needed with {"include": {"value": "@Verified"}}: the player splices the recorded components in at that spot
Prefer it over copying for anything drawn more than once without parameters (icons, dividers, logos); use definePattern when the copies differ
pitfalls: Declare referencedOperations at the top level of a root array, next to definePattern: there it is recorded in the first pass. Declared inside a column it is also drawn where it is declared, and in the C++ player its includes then lose components
A recording has no parameters: every include is identical. For a label or colour that changes, use a template (STR-06, RU-05)
The included canvas keeps its own size modifiers; give the canvas a fixed size, since it has no intrinsic size

snippets.note: the recording: one 18 dp canvas with the tick
include @Verified after a name

check.describe: Four names under REVIEWERS; Margaret Hamilton, Ken Thompson and Frances Allen each followed by the same blue circle with a white tick, Linus Torvalds without. Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the list keeps its left edge and each tick follows its name; the rows are as wide as their content, so nothing depends on the header width.

examples.name: modifier-macro
examples.title: Shared styles as modifier macros
examples.summary: Two style macros, a definePattern whose only child is a modifier list: ButtonStyle (height, pill clip, a fill colour parameter, padding) styles three buttons, TagStyle (no parameters) two tags; each box applies one with an includeMacro modifier, then adds its own ripple and semantics.
examples.prompt: A row of three pill buttons (Save in blue, Share in purple, Delete in red) and two small grey tags (draft, 3 attachments) below, with the button and tag styles each defined once and shared.
examples.hand_built: The buttons and tags are styled by shared modifier macros, because the macro is the lesson; a real button is a library Button, and a tag a Badge.
teaches: Define a style as a template holding only a modifier list: {"definePattern": {"name": "ButtonStyle", "parameters": ["fill"], "children": [{"modifier": {"modifiers": [...]}}]}}
Apply it with a modifier, among the component's own: {"includeMacro": {"pattern": "ButtonStyle", "arguments": ["#FF4DA3FF"]}}, then ripple and semantics after it
Parameterise only what varies (the fill colour) and keep the rest of the look in one place
pitfalls: arguments is positional and always required, even for a style with no parameters ("arguments": [])
The macro's modifiers are inserted where includeMacro sits in the list, so order still matters: padding in the macro, after its background, pads the content inside the pill

Small savings: about 73 B here (1113 B against 1186 B with the modifiers written out, measured on the one-row version). A macro is mainly for consistency; byte savings grow with the size of the shared list and the number of uses

A row of intrinsic-width buttons squeezes the last one to a sliver on a narrow host: a flow wraps it to the next line instead (a flow ignores spacedBy, so the gaps are spacer boxes, here 54 dp tall to space the lines too)

snippets.note: ButtonStyle: a template whose body is a modifier list, fill as a parameter
includeMacro ButtonStyle with the blue fill
TagStyle: a style with no parameters

check.describe: Three 44 dp pill buttons (blue Save with dark text, purple Share, red Delete) and below them two small rounded grey tags. Resized: the buttons sit in a flow, so on a narrow host (240×190) Delete wraps to a second line instead of being squeezed; the 10×54 spacers keep a gap between the lines. Below about 300 dp wide the widget needs the extra height.

examples.name: global-section
examples.title: Shared definitions in a global section
examples.summary: A steps widget whose shared numbers (goal, gap) sit in a global section at the top of the root, with a rem comment, and whose ring progress is computed inside the canvas but wrapped in a global command, so the converter moves it before the root where every component can read it.
examples.prompt: A daily steps widget: a green progress ring with the percentage in the middle, and beside it "Steps today", 7,420 and "2,580 to go" against a 10,000 goal; keep the goal and spacing as shared constants.
examples.hand_built: The ring stays a canvas because its global commands section, which hoists @progress before layout, is one of the two global forms taught; to draw a progress ring otherwise, call ProgressRing.
teaches: Group document-wide definitions in {"global": {"children": [...]}} at the top of a root array: variables (and rem comments) defined once, read anywhere as @goal, @gap

Hoist a value computed where it is drawn: {"global": {"commands": [...]}} inside a canvas moves those commands before the root, so @progress is computed before any layout and is visible to every component
Use the same token in a modifier and a drawing: @gap pads the row and sizes the spacer box
pitfalls: A global section's children must be definitions (variable, definePattern, referencedOperations, createFloatFunction, …); anything else in it is silently skipped

Do not use a vtype color variable as a paint colour: Java writes its id as a literal ARGB (transparent) and json2rc writes opaque black. Colours for paints and text belong in resources.colors, used as @colors.accent
global moves bytes, it does not copy them: the hoisted commands leave the canvas, so anything they define is computed once for the document, not per paint of that canvas
A fixed 140 dp ring leaves the numbers no room on a narrow host: give the ring canvas a weight and draw it from componentWidth()/componentHeight(), capped at its design size

snippets.note: global section: rem plus the goal and gap tokens
global command in a canvas: progress hoisted before the root
rem: a comment stored in the document
colours as named colour resources

check.describe: A green ring three quarters full with 74% inside; beside it "Steps today", 7,420 and green "2,580 to go". Resized (narrow 240, wide 540) the ring and the numbers share the row by weight: the ring is centred in its half, its radius min(56, min(componentWidth(), componentHeight()) / 2 - 14) shrinks on a small host, and the percentage's text size follows the radius.

examples.name: float-function
examples.title: A drawing helper as a float function
examples.summary: A heart-rate sparkline whose lowest, highest and latest readings are marked by one helper, pin(i, size, sx, sy), defined once with createFloatFunction: it looks up the reading, draws a ringed dot and the value label, and is called three times with callFloatFunction.
examples.prompt: A heart-rate line chart for today (14 readings) with the lowest (55), highest (95) and latest (64) readings marked with a red dot and their value, the latest one larger; draw the marker with one reusable helper.
examples.hand_built: The chart and its markers are drawn by hand because the float function that draws a marker is the lesson; for a real chart use LineChart (marks) or PriceChart (high and low marks).
teaches: Define a helper once with {"createFloatFunction": {"name": "pin", "params": ["i", "size", "sx", "sy"], "commands": [...]}}: the params are plain names in the body's expressions
Call it with {"callFloatFunction": {"id": "@pin", "args": [6, 3, "@px", "@py"]}}: one call per marker, the latest one bigger (args [13, 5, …])
Read outer data in the body (arrayGet(@bpm, i)) so a call passes only what differs (which point, how big) plus the chart's scale (@px, @py, from componentWidth()/componentHeight())
Let a function return its result by drawing: the body's draw commands run at each call site, in order with the surrounding commands
pitfalls: A variable command inside the body is a new local binding, not an assignment: a function cannot set an outer variable (the Java parser restores the variables after the body), so return values by drawing, or compute them as expressions at the call site
Paint changes made in the body stay in effect after the call: set colours inside the function, and again after it if later commands need another one
Arguments are positional: args must list a value for every param, in the params order
An expression argument ("arrayLength(@bpm) - 1") converts and runs, but rc-inspect's audit then reports it as dead_code: the audit does not yet count function arguments as uses

Pass size-dependent values to the function as arguments (here the scale @px, @py): a body that reads componentWidth(), or a variable computed from it, breaks the C++ player's later drawing in the same canvas (the line and the right-aligned label vanish); TS draws it right

snippets.note: pin(i, size, sx, sy): ring, dot and value label at reading i, placed with the scale passed in
call for the latest reading: args [13, 5, @px, @py]
the line: one segment per pair of readings, px apart

check.describe: A red line over 14 readings; red dots with dark rings and labels at 55 (third point), 95 (seventh) and a larger one at 64 (last). The C++ and TS players render it the same. Resized (narrow 240, large 540×260) the line spans the canvas: px = (componentWidth() - 48) / 13 per reading and py = (componentHeight() - 70) / 60 per bpm, passed to pin as its sx, sy arguments, so the markers stay on the line.

examples.name: digital-clock
examples.title: Digital clock
examples.summary: HH:MM:SS in large digits: hour, minute and second read from the clock and zero-padded to two digits.
examples.prompt: Make a digital clock that shows the current time as HH:MM:SS in large digits.
examples.hand_built: The clock is written out because reading timeInHr(), timeInMin() and timeInSec() and zero-padding them is the lesson; to show the time otherwise, call DigitalClock.
teaches: Read the clock: timeInHr() for the hour, timeInMin() % 60 for the minute, timeInSec() % 60 for the second
Zero-pad each field to two digits with textFromFloat whole 2, decimal 0, flags 12 (PAD_PRE_ZERO)
Lay the fields and colon separators out in a row

snippets.note: hours: textFromFloat(timeInHr(), 2 digits, zero padded)
minutes: timeInMin() % 60 (timeInMin is minutes since midnight)
seconds: timeInSec() % 60 (timeInSec is seconds within the hour)

check.describe: At 10:10:05 it reads 10:10:05; at 09:05:07 it reads 09:05:07 with leading zeros. Resized, the time stays centred in the box (a layout box with centred alignment); it needs about 220 dp of width at fontSize 56.

pitfalls: timeInMin() is minutes since midnight and timeInSec() seconds within the hour, so both need % 60 to give a clock field
Without flags 12 (PAD_PRE_ZERO) textFromFloat pads with spaces, so 9 shows as " 9" rather than 09
timeInHr() is the 24-hour hour (0–23); a 12-hour clock needs (timeInHr() + 11) % 12 + 1
A clock field needs decimal 0: inside a text value object decimal defaults to 3

examples.name: analog-clock
examples.title: Analog clock
examples.summary: Hour, minute and second hands driven by the clock, over twelve ticks drawn with a loop.
examples.prompt: Draw a round analog clock face with twelve ticks and hour, minute and second hands showing the current time.
examples.hand_built: The face and hands are drawn by hand because the rotations from the time functions are the lesson; to show an analog clock otherwise, call AnalogClock.
teaches: Rotate a hand around the centre with save + rotate(angle, pivotX, pivotY)
Drive the angles from the clock: (timeInMin() % 720) * 0.5 for hours, (timeInMin() % 60) * 6 for minutes, (timeInSec() % 60) * 6 for seconds
Draw evenly spaced ticks with a loop and a rotation by index (i * 30)
Set the shared stroke style and round cap once, and only colour and width per hand
