Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre

snippets.note: hour hand: (timeInMin() % 720) * 0.5 degrees
second hand: (timeInSec() % 60) * 6
twelve ticks: loop i, save, rotate i * 30 about the centre

check.describe: At 10:10:30 the hour and minute hands make the classic V and the second hand points to 6. Resized, the face scales to the shorter side and stays centred.

pitfalls: timeInMin() is minutes since midnight: % 720 gives the 12-hour dial position (0.5° a minute), % 60 the minute hand
timeInSec() is the second within the hour (0–3599), so the second hand needs % 60; a smooth sweep would use continuousSec() instead, which repaints every frame
Wrap each rotate in save so it doesn't accumulate onto the next hand

Don't rely on save/restore for the paint: the Java player's save only saves the matrix, while the C++ and TS players also restore the paint. Set every paint field a hand needs (colour and width here) inside its own save
The canvas has no background, so outside the dial it is transparent (white in the screenshot): add a background modifier for a square widget

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: literal coordinates sit in the top-left and get cut off when it is resized, so scale the drawing to fit (or derive positions from componentWidth()/componentHeight())

examples.name: date-card
examples.title: Date card
examples.summary: A tear-off calendar card: the weekday and month names looked up from string lists, and the day of the month as a number.
examples.prompt: Make a calendar-icon style date card showing today's weekday, day number and month, like "Wed 28 Oct".
examples.hand_built: The calendar card is drawn by hand because the date functions and the textLookup of day and month names are the lesson; for today's date as a line of text, call DateLabel.
teaches: Read the date with weekDay() (1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday), calendarMonth() (1–12) and dayOfMonth()
Turn a 1-based date field into a name with textLookup over an addDataList, indexed by field - 1
Print the day number unpadded with textFromFloat whole 2, decimal 0, flags 4 (PAD_PRE_NONE)
Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre

snippets.note: textLookup(@days, weekDay() - 1) -> dayName
textLookup(@months, calendarMonth() - 1) -> monthName
dayOfMonth() as text, no padding
the twelve month abbreviations

check.describe: At 2026-10-28 the card reads Wed / 28 / Oct; at 2026-01-04 it reads Sun / 4 / Jan. Resized, the card scales to the shorter side and stays centred.

pitfalls: weekDay() and calendarMonth() are 1-based: subtract 1 to index a list
addDataList's `id` is a json2rc extension: the Java reference parser discards the list's id, so textLookup cannot name the list there and the document only converts with json2rc
A rounded header band over a rounded card: draw the band as a round rect, then a plain rect over its lower half to square the bottom corners

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: literal coordinates sit in the top-left and get cut off when it is resized, so scale the drawing to fit (or derive positions from componentWidth()/componentHeight())
examples.java_difference: json2rc-only: Java's addDataList drops the list id, so textLookup can't reach it (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U4)

examples.name: pulse
examples.title: Pulsing heart
examples.summary: A heart drawn with pathExpression that pulses once a second: its scale and alpha follow a sine of continuousSec().
examples.prompt: Draw a heart that beats: it grows, shrinks and fades in a loop once a second.
examples.hand_built: The heart is plotted from its curve in the canvas that pulses it, because the time-driven scale and fade are the lesson; for a static heart symbol use Icon (favorite).
teaches: Loop an animation with sin(continuousSec() * 6.2832): one cycle per second, and continuousSec() makes the player repaint every frame
Scale a shape about its centre: draw it around the origin, then save, translate to the centre and scale(sx, sy)
Fade with the same clock through a paint alpha expression
Centre with translate(componentWidth() / 2, componentHeight() / 2) and fold min(componentWidth(), componentHeight()) / 200 into the pulse scale so the heart fits any box

snippets.note: scale 1 ± 0.15 with sin(continuousSec() * 2π)
paint alpha 0.65 ± 0.35 from the same sine
the heart curve: x = 64 sin³t, y from four cosines

check.describe: At a quarter past a whole second (continuousSec() = n + 0.25) the heart is at its largest and brightest; at n + 0 it is mid-size and two-thirds opaque; at n + 0.75 small and dim. Resized, the heart stays centred and scales with the shorter side.

pitfalls: Drive a looping animation with continuousSec(), not animationTime(): an expression that only reads animationTime() never schedules a repaint, so the document is drawn once and stays still (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6)
continuousSec() is the second within the hour with milliseconds (0–3600): it jumps back to 0 on the hour, harmless for a sine with a whole-second period
To pin a frame for a screenshot pin the clock with milliseconds (epoch ms); animation_time does not move continuousSec()
Alpha is 0–1 in a paint alpha expression, not 0–255

examples.name: impulse-bounce
examples.title: Impulse bounce
examples.summary: A ball dropped at start that bounces three times and rests: a 3-second impulse draws the bouncing ball, and a condition draws it at rest afterwards.
examples.prompt: Animate a ball that drops when the widget appears, bounces three times and then rests on the ground.
teaches: Run a one-shot animation window with impulse(duration, start) and draw inside it with impulseProcess
Bounce with |cos(π·t)| scaled by a decay (1 - t/3)² that reaches zero when the impulse ends
Draw the resting state after the window with conditionalOperations gt animationTime() 3
Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre

snippets.note: impulse 3 s from 0, its process draws the ball at the bounce height
after 3 s, the ball at rest on the ground

check.describe: After 1 s of frames the ball is in the air at the top of its first rebound (y ≈ 155); after 5 s it rests on the line (y = 244). Resized, the ball, its drop and the floor scale together to fit and stay centred.

pitfalls: An impulse runs its plain commands on the first frame of its window and its impulseProcess only on later frames, so a single still frame draws nothing from the process: render with `duration` to simulate frames
Nothing is drawn by the impulse outside its window: draw the final state yourself (here a conditionalOperations on animationTime() > 3), or the ball vanishes when the bounce ends
Make the decay reach exactly zero at the end of the window ((1 - t/3)² at t = 3) so the process's last frame and the resting ball line up without a jump

Java's ImpulseOperation asks for no repaint during its window, and animationTime() alone never schedules one (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6): on the Java player the bounce relies on something else repainting; the C++ and TS players animate it

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: literal coordinates sit in the top-left and get cut off when it is resized, so scale the drawing to fit (or derive positions from componentWidth()/componentHeight())

examples.name: countdown
examples.title: Launch countdown
examples.summary: "Launch in HH:MM:SS" counting down to a fixed UTC instant, computed from the day of the year, the local time and offsetToUtc().
examples.prompt: Make a launch countdown timer showing hours, minutes and seconds left until a fixed date and time in UTC.
teaches: Convert local time to UTC with offsetToUtc(): utc = local - offsetToUtc(), so remaining = target - local + offsetToUtc()
Keep float precision by subtracting day and second-of-day parts separately: (targetDay - dayOfYear()) * 86400 + (targetSec - secondOfDay)
Name the remaining seconds once in resources.variables and split it into hours, minutes and seconds with floor and %

snippets.note: seconds to 2026-10-29 12:24:12 UTC (day 302, second 44652), clamped at 0
hours: floor(@remaining / 3600), zero padded
minutes: floor(@remaining / 60) % 60

check.describe: At 2026-10-29 10:10:05 UTC (epoch ms 1793268605000) it reads 02:14:07 in any time zone; at the launch instant and after, 00:00:00. Resized, the column stays centred both ways and keeps its three lines.

pitfalls: Pin the clock as epoch milliseconds: a "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM" clock is local time, so the instant, and a countdown to a UTC moment, shift with the renderer's time zone
epochSecond() converts with json2rc but the Java parser does not know it; build absolute time from dayOfYear(), timeInMin(), timeInSec() and offsetToUtc() instead

A float has 24 bits of mantissa: seconds-since-Jan-1 (~3e7) lose whole seconds, so subtract the target's day and second-of-day separately; the formula counts within one calendar year: for a target in the next year (New Year's Day) add the days left in this year, with the leap rule, to the days into the next
Hours are floor(@remaining / 3600) with no % 24: past 99 hours whole 2 drops the leading digit, so add a days field (or whole 3) for a longer countdown

examples.name: month-calendar
examples.title: Evergreen month calendar
examples.summary: A month calendar computed entirely from the clock: the month name and year, the weekday of the 1st, the number of days (28 to 31, leap years included) and today's circle all come from date expressions, so the same document is right every month without being regenerated.
examples.prompt: Make a month calendar widget for the current month: the month name and year as a title, Monday-first weekday initials, a 6×7 grid of day numbers with weekends dimmed and today circled. It must stay correct next month and next year without regenerating the document.
teaches: Weekday of the 1st from today alone: fw = (weekDay() - dayOfMonth() + 35) % 7 (0 = Monday; the + 35 keeps the left side positive, so % never sees a negative number)

Days in the month without a table: 30 + (m + floor(m / 8)) % 2 for every month but February (31/30 alternate and flip at August), minus (2 - leap) when m = 2, with leap = [y%4=0] - [y%100=0] + [y%400=0] and each [x=0] written 1 - min(1, x)

Month name without a data list: textSubtext of a 12 × 9-character table at (calendarMonth() - 1) * 9, then textTransform operation 3 (trim) to drop the padding; textMerge it with textFromFloat(year())
One cell definition for all 42 cells: a week loop around a weekday loop, day = week * 7 + wd + 1 - @fw; step masks hide the days outside 1..@nd and circle the one equal to dayOfMonth()
Theme colours (@colors.surface, onSurface, muted, primary, onPrimary) with "componentTheme": "auto" at the top give light, dark and (built with componentTheme mono) monochrome from one document

snippets.note: weekday of the 1st: (weekDay() - dayOfMonth() + 35) % 7
days in the month from calendarMonth() and the leap-year flag
Gregorian leap year with % and 1 - min(1, x) as 'is zero'
month name: a 9-character slot of a padded table, picked by calendarMonth()
the 6 × 7 grid: one cell body inside a week loop and a weekday loop
inMonth: 1 for 1 <= day <= @nd, else 0
isToday: 1 when day = dayOfMonth()

check.describe: Canonical 2026-10-30: October 2026, the 1st under Thursday, 31 days, 30 circled. feb-leap (2028-02-14): February 2028, 1st on Tuesday, 29 days, 14 (a Monday) circled. feb-common (2027-02-01): February 2027 fills exactly four rows, 1st on Monday circled, 28 days. jan-sat (2022-01-31): January 2022 starts on Saturday, 31 days spill into a sixth row, 31 (Monday) circled. sep-sun (2024-09-30): September 2024 starts on Sunday, 30 days, 30 alone on the sixth row. Weekend columns are dimmed; no number appears before the 1st or after the last day. light and mono re-colour the same layout. Resized (small 200×210, wide 460×300) the cells are (componentWidth() - 16) / 7 by (componentHeight() - 80) / 6 and the day text scales with them (9 to 20).

pitfalls: Hard-coding the month: a literal "October 2026", a firstWeekday of 3 or a monthDays of 31 makes a document that is wrong in two days. Derive all three from weekDay(), dayOfMonth(), calendarMonth() and year()

weekDay() is 1 = Monday … 7 = Sunday and dayOfMonth() starts at 1: the 1st's offset is (weekDay() - dayOfMonth()) mod 7, and a negative left side must be lifted (+ 35) before %, which keeps the sign of the dividend

Day count: (m + floor(m / 8)) % 2 gives 31 for Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec; forgetting the August flip (m % 2 alone) makes August 30 days and September 31. February is 28 + leap, and leap needs the 100 and 400 rules (2100 is not leap, 2000 was)
Writing 31 (or 42) cell copies by hand: one loop body with a computed day number and step masks is a fraction of the size and covers every month shape (4, 5 or 6 rows)
There is no break: loop over the worst case (6 weeks × 7 days) and hide the extra cells with a 0/1 alpha mask; step(a, b) is strict, so 1 <= day <= nd is step(day, 0.5) * step(nd + 0.5, day)
Don't build the month name with addDataList + textLookup: the Java parser drops the list id (U4). A fixed-width textSubtext table plus a trim converts identically everywhere
Today's text sits on the primary circle: draw the number twice, onSurface with alpha inMonth * (1 - isToday) and onPrimary with alpha isToday, rather than one colour that is unreadable on the circle

Date fields alone never schedule a repaint (only continuousSec, timeInSec, timeInMin and wakeIn do, EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6): this document is idle and turns the page at the host's next redraw. If it must flip at midnight on its own, also read timeInMin() somewhere (a repaint a minute)

examples.name: moon-phase-calendar
examples.title: Moon phase calendar
examples.summary: Tonight's moon drawn large beside its phase name, the percentage lit, its age and the days to the next full and new moon (text components), over the month's title, a weekday row and a calendar grid with each day's moon and the day of each principal phase labelled. Everything comes from the clock through a small lunar ephemeris (mean elongation plus five periodic terms), so the document stays right every month.
examples.prompt: create an app with the phases of the moon for this month
teaches: The moon is the MoonPhase library component, called with a phase computed in the document ({"MoonPhase": {"phase": "@f", "size": 112}}); the 42 day moons are the same geometry drawn once inside the calendar's week x weekday loop, not 42 canvases

Days since 2000-01-01 00:00 UTC at the start of today: 365 * (year() - 2000) + floor((year() - 1997) / 4) + dayOfYear() - 1 - offsetToUtc() / 86400. offsetToUtc() makes the days local, so a phase lands on the user's calendar day

The lunation count L(t) = 0.8104301 + 0.033863192 t (the mean elongation over 2π) plus five sines (equation of centre, evection, variation, the Sun's anomaly, the second centre term): every principal phase from 2015 to 2045 within about 40 minutes of Meeus' full algorithm, on the right day for 99.5% of them

A day holds a principal phase when floor(4 L) changes across it: ev = floor(4 L(k + 1)) - floor(4 L(k)), and floor(4 L(k + 1)) % 4 says which (0 new, 1 first quarter, 2 full, 3 last quarter). The phase name and the grid labels use the same rule, so they never disagree

Days to the next full (or new) moon: the target lunation N = floor(L - 0.5) + 1.5, a first guess at the mean rate, then two Newton steps t -= (L(t) - N) * 29.53; counted from the start of today, so on the day itself it reads "today" until midnight

Words are layout, the drawing is a canvas: the phase name, % illuminated, age and the full / new moon lines are text components in a column beside MoonPhase; the month title is a text and the weekday header a row of seven weight-1 texts, so they measure, wrap (the phase name takes two lines at 300 dp wide) and reach screen readers. Only the day numbers and the small phase labels stay in the grid's loop: they are part of the calendar drawing (42 cells), which uses componentWidth() / 7, the same columns as the weighted header texts

Names from a table for a layout text: a zero-size canvas holds a global block where textSubtext takes a 15-character slot of a padded table (start @ni * 15) and textTransform 3 trims it into phaseName (monthName likewise from calendarMonth()); the layout texts read "@phaseName" and textMerge("@monthName", " ", year). The global section is written before the root and listens to its variables, so the name changes at midnight (checked across Oct 31 / Nov 1). Cleaner than 8 phase texts or 12 month texts switched by visibility

The "Full moon in N days / tomorrow / today" line is a box holding three whole text components, each with visibility bound to a 0/1 variable: fullIn = step(@toFull, 1.5), fullTomorrow = step(@toFull, 0.5) * step(1.5, @toFull), fullToday = step(0.5, @toFull) (same for new). Exactly one is 1; the others are gone, and the box takes the visible one's size

Smaller heights: the hero has a fixed size and the grid canvas takes what is left (verticalWeight 1), so the grid gives way first. Its cells adapt to their shape: the phase labels are dropped when a row is under 44 dp (alpha @ev * step(@rh, 44)), and when a cell is much wider than tall (side = step(@cw, 1.6 * @rh), 360 x 360) the number and the moon sit side by side instead of stacked

snippets.note: days since 2000-01-01 UTC at the start of today, from year() and dayOfYear()
offsetToUtc() turns the local midnight into UTC days
the ephemeris: the lunation count at the start of today, first half (mean elongation and the two largest terms; la adds the other three, since a Java expression holds at most 32 entries)
second Newton step towards the next full moon
phase-name index: a principal phase today, else the in-between name
a 0/1 variable for visibility: 1 only when the full moon is tomorrow
a zero-size canvas whose global block names phaseName and monthName for the layout texts
phase name from a padded table, trimmed by the textTransform after it
tonight's moon: the MoonPhase component at phase @f, 112 dp
the hero's text column: "@phaseName", % illuminated and age as textFromFloat merges, and the full / new moon lines switched by visibility
one line, three wordings: a box holding "Full moon in N days", "tomorrow" and "today", each shown only while its 0/1 variable is 1
the weekday header: seven weight-1 texts, the grid's columns
the 6 x 7 month grid: one cell body in a week loop and a weekday loop
ev: 1 on the day a principal phase happens
the day's moon: lit half, then the terminator ellipses, as MoonPhase draws it

check.describe: Renders pin offsetToUtc() to 0 (system variable 10), so days are UTC days and the result doesn't depend on the build machine's time zone. Canonical 2026-10-30 12:00: a waning gibbous moon lit on the left, "Waning Gibbous", 76% illuminated, age 19.6 days, full moon in 25 days (Nov 24), new moon in 10 days (Nov 9); October 2026 starts on Thursday, Last Q under the 3rd, New under the 10th, 1st Q under the 18th, Full under the 26th, 30 outlined. nov-full (2026-11-24): "Full Moon", full moon today, new moon in 15 days; November starts on Sunday (six rows): Last Q 1, New 9, 1st Q 17, Full 24. nov-new-eve (2026-11-08): "Waning Crescent", new moon tomorrow, full moon in 16 days. pacific (2026-11-08, offset -8 h): the 07:02 UTC new moon is 23:02 on the 8th locally, so "New Moon", new moon today, New under the 8th and Last Q under the 30th (Dec 1 06:09 UTC). light and mono re-colour the same layout (mono: white lit parts, black shade, grey rims). small (300 x 520): the phase name wraps to two lines; small and wide (480 x 640): the cells are componentWidth() / 7 by componentHeight() / 6 under the weekday row and the moons and day numbers scale with the smaller of the two. short (360 x 360): the hero keeps its size, the grid rows are about 25 dp, so the phase labels are off and each day's number sits left of its moon.

pitfalls: Don't draw the moons as text glyphs (🌑 🌓 🌕 ◐): they depend on the device's fonts, can't follow the theme, and show 8 phases at best. Draw them (MoonPhase, or its geometry inside a loop)

Don't paste a canvas per day with the phase typed in: 31 or 42 copies are large, one wrong copy goes unnoticed, and the document is wrong next month. One loop body with the day computed from the loop indices draws every month

Don't hard-code the month, its first weekday, its length or the phase dates ("Full moon Oct 26"): derive the month from calendarMonth(), weekDay(), dayOfMonth() and year() (TIM-10), and the phases from an ephemeris of the clock

Local time vs UTC: the date functions are local, the ephemeris is in UTC days. Subtract offsetToUtc() / 86400, or an evening full moon west of Greenwich (Oct 26 04:11 UTC is Oct 25 in California) lands a day late. For renders, pin system variable 10 (offsetToUtc) so they don't depend on the machine's time zone

The mean lunation alone (t / 29.53 days) puts phases up to 19 hours off. The LLM version's two-term correction (the new/full-moon coefficients) still missed the quarters by up to 6 hours, because evection adds about 0.22 days there: 7.5% of principal phases from 2015 to 2045 landed on the wrong day (Nov 1 2026's last quarter on Nov 2). The five-term series here puts 0.5% of them on the wrong day, each within an hour of midnight

Days to the next full moon from the mean rate alone can be a day off (the true rate varies by about 15%): refine with two Newton steps, and count from the start of today, not from now, so the day of the full moon reads "today" and not "in 29 days" after the moment has passed

A float expression holds at most 32 entries in Java (Limits.MAX_EXPRESSION_SIZE; the parser and the player both throw "to long"), and json2rc, C++ and TS don't check it: the five-term series written as one expression converts and renders, then fails on Android. Split it (la0 = mean + two terms, la = la0 + three terms) and pass each time as a single variable, not "(@d0 + 1)" repeated six times
In a column, the child that takes the remaining height needs verticalWeight; ["fillMaxWidth", {"weight": 1}] there gives a canvas 0 wide and the grid vanishes
Date functions alone never schedule a repaint: the illumination reads timeInMin(), which repaints once a minute and turns the page at midnight

Don't draw the hero's words, the month title or the weekday initials on a canvas next to the drawing (the first version did: 10 texts at fixed offsets): they don't measure or wrap ("Waning Gibbous" ran past a 300 dp screen), don't follow the font scale, and screen readers can't reach them. Keep text components for words and the canvas for shapes; here only the grid's day numbers and phase labels are drawn, because they are cells of the calendar drawing (moving them out would take 42 layout cells)

A layout text can't take textSubtext or textTransform (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U32: Java only allows them among canvas commands). Compute the name in a canvas (here a zero-size one with a global block) and show it as "@name" in the text, or switch whole texts with visibility
visibility reads a variable's integer value: bind it to expressions that are exactly 0 or 1 (step(), 1 - x, products of those); a fractional value truncates to 0 and hides the text

A weighted child of a collapsibleColumn is never dropped (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U36): Java hands out the weights before checking what fits, so the weighted grid always gets the leftover and fits, and heightIn on it only makes the column overflow. A grid that must fill the height is a verticalWeight child of a plain column that adapts its own drawing (labels off under 44 dp rows, number beside the moon in short cells); a collapsibleColumn only drops fixed-height children

examples.name: sunrise-sunset
examples.title: Sunrise, sunset and the sun's path
examples.summary: Today's sunrise, sunset, first and last light, solar noon, the evening golden hour and the day length for a place given as host variables (San Francisco by default), with the sun's path from midnight to midnight and a dot where it is now. Everything is computed from the clock and the latitude and longitude with the Astronomical Almanac's low-precision sun (declination and equation of time) and the sunrise hour angle, in local time through offsetToUtc(). The structure is layout: a column of rows, text components for every word and number, library Icons and two small inline components; the only canvas is the sun-path drawing, sized by the layout and drawn from componentWidth() and componentHeight().
examples.prompt: create a RemoteCompose UI that displays the sunrise/sunset times and sun path for San Francisco
teaches: Layout for structure and text, a canvas only for the drawing: a column of rows holds the place, the date, the altitude line, the axis labels and six time tiles as text components (they measure, wrap, follow the font scale and reach screen readers); the one canvas is the sun path, given the panel's remaining height by verticalWeight and drawn from componentWidth() and componentHeight()

Small inline components (top-level `components`) for what repeats: TimeTile (icon, label, local minutes formatted H:MM) is called six times, Panel is the rounded surface with a mono outline; the icons are the Icon library component (wb_twilight, wb_twilight_2, routine, bedtime, light_mode, photo_camera)

Days since J2000 at local noon: n = 365 * (year() - 2000) + floor((year() - 1997) / 4) + dayOfYear() - 1 - offsetToUtc() / 86400, then the Almanac's sun: L = 280.46 + 0.9856474 n, g = 357.528 + 0.9856003 n, ecliptic longitude λ = L + 1.915 sin g + 0.02 sin 2g, obliquity ε = 23.439 - 0.0000004 n; declination δ = asin(sin ε sin λ), right ascension atan2(cos ε sin λ, cos λ), equation of time 4 (L - RA) wrapped to ±180°

Solar noon in local minutes = 720 - 4 × longitude - EoT + offsetToUtc() / 60; an event at sun altitude h is noon ± 229.18 × acos((sin h - sin φ sin δ) / (cos φ cos δ)) minutes: h = -0.833° for sunrise and sunset (refraction and the sun's radius), -6° for civil twilight (first and last light), +6° for the evening golden hour. clamp the acos argument to [-1, 1] so polar day and night give a full or empty day instead of NaN

The sun now: sin(altitude) = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos((timeInMin() - noon) × 0.0043633); the same expression with a[0] in place of timeInMin() is the pathExpression of the whole day's curve, scaled up above the horizon and down below it with max(0, s) and min(0, s)

Round once (floor(x + 0.5)) into a variable and format from it: hours floor(m / 60) with flags 5, minutes m % 60 zero-padded with flags 13; the day length is setR - riseR so it always agrees with the two times shown
Location as exported host variables (latitude, longitude, the place name as a string variable): the host moves the document anywhere without regenerating it (the sydney render)

exported location, San Francisco by default

the daylight part, a[0] in 0..1 mapped to sunrise..sunset, filled and stroked

longitude.meaning: longitude in degrees, east positive (San Francisco is negative)

place.meaning: the place name shown at the top

check.describe: Renders pin the clock and the UTC offset (system variable 10) so they don't depend on the build machine's zone. Reference: the NOAA solar calculator algorithm (Meeus, iterated on each event), computed offline. Canonical, San Francisco 2026-10-30 15:00 PDT (-7 h): first light 7:06, sunrise 7:33, solar noon 12:53, golden hour 17:36, sunset 18:13, last light 18:40, 10 h 40 min of daylight, 3 h 13 min left, sun altitude 30° (NOAA geometric 30.3°), the dot on the descending side of the curve. june (2026-06-21 10:00 PDT): 5:17, 5:48, 13:12, 19:56, 20:35, 21:06, 14 h 47 min, 10 h 34 min left, altitude 47°, the tallest curve. december (2026-12-21 20:00 PST, -8 h): 6:52, 7:22 (NOAA 7:21.5), 12:08, 16:13, 16:54, 17:24, 9 h 32 min, 0 h 0 min left, altitude -36°, the dim dot below the horizon on the night curve. sydney (host variables -33.8688, 151.2093, "Sydney", 2026-10-30 15:00 at +11 h): 5:31, 5:57, 12:39, 18:47, 19:21, 19:47, 13 h 24 min, altitude 52°. Every time within a minute of NOAA. light and mono re-colour the same layout (mono: the panel and tiles outlined in grey). narrow (300 x 600) and wide (640 x 520): the canvas takes the panel's remaining height and the curve, horizon (64% down) and dot scale with it; the tiles split the width in two.

pitfalls: offsetToUtc() is the DEVICE's zone: a widget for a place elsewhere (Lisbon from a phone in California) must compute that place's offset itself (its standard offset plus its daylight-saving rule, e.g. the EU rule: last Sunday of March to last Sunday of October), or its times shift with the viewer's zone

Don't draw the whole UI on one full-screen canvas with every text placed at fixed coordinates: it doesn't relayout on another screen, ignores the font scale, and screen readers get nothing. Text and structure are layout components (column, row, text, Icon, small inline components); the canvas is only the drawing, sized by the layout

Don't type the date or the times in ("Thursday, Oct 30", "Sunrise 7:33 AM"): the document is wrong tomorrow. Read the date from the clock (DateLabel, dayOfYear(), year()) and compute the times from the location

Local time vs UTC: the solar formulas give UTC; offsetToUtc() (seconds, local minus UTC: -25200 in PDT) converts to local minutes (+ offsetToUtc() / 60) and shifts the day count (- offsetToUtc() / 86400). For renders, pin system variable 10, or the result depends on the build machine's zone
Longitude sign: east is positive, so San Francisco is -122.42 and solar noon there is 720 + 4 × 122.42 minutes UTC; a positive west longitude puts noon around 04:00

A float expression holds at most 32 entries on Android (rc-inspect expression_too_long): the solar position is ten named variables (n, L, g, lam, eps, dec, ra, E, eot, noon), not one formula; the curve's pathExpression is 31 entries because it reuses A and B

The mean-sun shortcut (noon = 12:00 + longitude offset, a fixed 12 h day) is off by up to 16 minutes (equation of time) and hours (season). The NOAA 'fractional year' Fourier series is within about 2.5 minutes for San Francisco; the Almanac formula used here is within a minute

Weights ignore spacedBy (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U3): a column with a verticalWeight child and spacedBy overflows by the gaps. Use fixed spacer boxes between the children of such a column, and between weighted tiles in a row

textSubtext and textTransform are canvas commands in the JSON: a text component can't pick a word from a table, and a choice of whole text (above/below, until sunrise/left) needs a visibility state. Keep the dynamic texts to numbers ("Sun altitude -36°", "0 h 0 min left"), and use DateLabel for the day and month names

If drawTextAnchored is used for a label on the drawing, panX 0 centres the text on x (-1 puts it right of x, 1 left of x): centred text at an edge is cut in half. Here the axis labels are text components in a spaceBetween row under the canvas instead
Date functions alone never schedule a repaint: the altitude and the dot read timeInMin(), which repaints once a minute and rolls the day over at midnight

examples.name: tide-today
examples.title: Today's tides: a forecast curve with live status
examples.summary: Today's tides for a harbour (Brest by default): the host pushes the day's forecast as exported data (a water-level array sampled every 30 minutes, the turning points' times, heights and kinds, and the place name), and everything that depends on now is computed from the clock: the current level interpolated on the curve at timeInMin(), rising or falling, the next high or low tide and the time left until it, which of the day's tides are past, and the chart's now line. The structure is layout: a header with Icon and DateLabel, a panel with the status texts switched by visibility and a LineChart that takes the remaining height, and a row of four tiles for the turning points; the only canvas is inside LineChart.
examples.prompt: Make a remotecompose widget that shows the tides for today in Brest: a curve of the water level over the day, the times of the high and low tides, and whether it's rising or falling right now
teaches: Split the data from the clock: the host pushes what it knows about the day (the forecast) and the document computes what depends on now. The forecast is exported resources: floatArrays waterLevel (49 half-hourly levels, 00:00 to 24:00), tideTime (turning points in local minutes since midnight, ascending), tideHeight and tideKind (1 high, 0 low), and the place as an exported string variable. Now is timeInMin() (local minutes, repainted once a minute), never a host variable set to a time: a status or a countdown stored as data is right for one minute

The current level is the curve read at now: arraySpline(@waterLevel, clamp(0, 1, @now / 1440)), the same mapping LineChart uses for its line, so the number and the chart's now dot agree. LineChart draws the forecast (values "@waterLevel", x_min 0, x_max 1440, now "timeInMin()", marks at the event times, xLabels and yLabels as texts) and takes the panel's remaining height with fill

The next turning point without a loop: each event time ti is arrayGet(@tideTime, min(i, @nEv - 1)) + 9999 * (1 - step(@nEv, i + 0.5)) (a missing 4th event moves past the end of the day), k = step(@now, @t0) + ... + step(@now, @t3) counts the events already passed, and the next one is index min(@k, @nEv - 1): nextT = arrayGet(@tideTime, @ki). after = step(@k, @nEv - 0.5) is 1 once the day's last tide has passed

Rising or falling is the kind of the next turning point (rising when it is a high), and after the last one the opposite of the last kind: rising = abs(arrayGet(@tideKind, @ki) - @after). Deriving it from the next event, not from the curve's slope, keeps the status and the "High tide at ..." line consistent at the turning point itself

Whole texts switch with visibility bound to float variables that are exactly 0 or 1 (step, 1 - x, products): visibility reads the variable's integer value, and a float variable's integer is its truncation, so "Rising"/"Falling", the north/south Icon, "High tide"/"Low tide", the "at 9:52, in 1 h 22 min" part (before), the hours part (hidden under an hour) and " tomorrow" (after) are separate text components and each shows only when it applies. Only the numbers are formatted (textFromFloat, H:MM with flags 5 and 13)

Per-event tiles from one small inline component (TideTile): visibility gone for a missing event, "High"/"Low" by kind, and the passed ones dimmed with graphicsLayer alpha 1 - 0.5 * step(@now, @ti); the spacing is padding inside each weighted box, so it disappears with the tile and a three-event day gives three wider tiles
The date comes from the clock (DateLabel), never typed in

snippets.note: the day's forecast curve as an exported float array the host replaces
turning points in local minutes since midnight; tideHeight and tideKind run parallel
now from the clock, in local minutes
the current level: the forecast curve read at now with arraySpline
an event time guarded by the array's length: a missing event moves to 9999
how many turning points have passed: a sum of steps, no loop
rising when the next turning point is a high, or after the last one when it was a low
"Rising" and "Falling" as two texts, each with a visibility bound to a 0/1 float variable
the next-event line: kind word, "at H:MM, in", hours (hidden under an hour), minutes, or "tomorrow"
LineChart in array mode: now = timeInMin(), marks at the event times, fill
a tile in a weighted box whose padding is the gap, gone when the event is missing
header: Icon, the exported place name and DateLabel

waterLevel.meaning: today's predicted water level in metres, sampled every 30 minutes from 00:00 to 24:00 (49 values; any count spread evenly over the day works)
waterLevel.default: a Brest spring-tide day: 4.7 m at midnight, low 2.0 m at 03:40, high 6.4 m at 09:52, low 1.9 m at 16:04, high 6.0 m at 22:16

tideTime.meaning: today's high and low tides in local minutes since midnight, ascending (3 or 4 of them; up to 4 are shown)

tideKind.meaning: 1 for a high tide, 0 for a low tide

check.describe: Renders pin the clock (local). Data: the default Brest day, low 2.0 m at 3:40, high 6.4 m at 9:52, low 1.9 m at 16:04, high 6.0 m at 22:16 (a cosine between turning points, sampled every 30 min). Canonical (2026-10-30 18:45): 3.5 m now, north arrow, "Rising", "High tide at 22:16, in 3 h 31 min", the now line at 18:45 with its dot on the rising flank, the first three tiles dimmed (passed) and 22:16 bright. night (02:00, before the first low): 2.7 m, south arrow, "Falling", "Low tide at 3:40, in 1 h 40 min", no tile dimmed, the now line left of the first mark. morning (09:20, rising mid-morning): 6.3 m, "Rising", "High tide at 9:52, in 32 min" (the hours part gone), only 3:40 dimmed. late (23:00, after the evening high): 5.9 m, "Falling", "Low tide tomorrow" (no countdown), all four tiles dimmed, the now dot past the last mark on the falling curve. three (host data for a neap day, 2026-11-05 20:00, "Le Conquet", three turning points: low 2.4 m 5:50, high 5.8 m 12:02, low 2.5 m 18:14): 3.1 m, "Rising", "High tide tomorrow", three wider tiles, all dimmed, the date from the clock (Thursday, 5 November 2026). light and mono re-colour the same layout (mono: the panel and tiles outlined, no area wash, passed tiles grey). narrow (300 x 600) and wide (640 x 520): the chart takes the panel's remaining height and width, the tiles split the width in four.

pitfalls: Don't freeze now: a host variable "nowMinutes" or a status string "Rising" stored in the data is right when it is sent and wrong a minute later (and a widget is refreshed rarely). Read timeInMin() and compute the current level, the status, the next event and the countdown from it
Don't type in the status, the next event or the date ("Rising · High tide at 9:52 in 1 h 22 min", "Friday 30 October"): each is a value of the clock and the forecast. Only the forecast itself is data
A float expression holds at most 32 entries (json2rc refuses longer ones, Android throws): name the pieces (nEv, t0..t3, k, ki, after, um) instead of one formula for "the next event"

arrayGet with an index past the end throws in the Java player and the document stops (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U34; the C++ player clamps, so only a device shows it), and expressions evaluate every branch (ifElse included): clamp the index with min(i, arrayLength(@a) - 1) and mask the result with step(arrayLength(@a), i + 0.5) to support days with three turning points

visibility takes a variable that is exactly 0, 1 or 2: it reads the variable's integer value, so a float variable works only when its value is a whole number (step(), 1 - x, products of those); 0.999 truncates to 0 and hides the text
A layout text can't pick a word with textSubtext (canvas only, EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U32): switch whole text components with visibility instead, one per wording

Weights ignore spacedBy (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U3): the status row and the tile row use fixed spacer boxes or padding inside the weighted box, not spacedBy, or the last child is pushed out (the current level was cut off before this fix)

After the day's last turning point there is no next event in today's data: say so ("Low tide tomorrow") and let the host push tomorrow's forecast, instead of showing a negative countdown or the last event again
Event times are local minutes since midnight, like timeInMin(): a server sending UTC times must convert them (or the document adds offsetToUtc() / 60, as TIM-12 does)

examples.name: stopwatch
examples.title: Stopwatch with a work-period ring
examples.summary: A stopwatch the user controls with buttons, entirely inside the document: one Button toggles Start / Pause / Resume and an outlined Reset clears it. The state is three host-settable variables (running, startAt, accumulated) changed by click actions; the elapsed time MM:SS.t is computed from them and the clock (timeInMin() * 60 + continuousSec() % 60), and a ProgressRing empties over a target duration (1500 s, a 25-minute Pomodoro work period, by default). The button's label follows the state through a text variable cut from one padded string in a global textSubtext, and a fitBox swaps the layout for smaller hosts: ring with the time inside, time and buttons, one row, the time alone.
examples.prompt: Make a stopwatch with start, pause and reset buttons, showing minutes, seconds and tenths, and a ring that empties over a 25-minute work period
teaches: Keep a timer's state in three host-settable variables instead of a clock reset: running (0 or 1), startAt (the clock value when the current run started) and accumulated (seconds of the runs before it). elapsed = accumulated + running * (now - startAt): paused it is accumulated, running it grows with the clock, and the host can read or set all three (a server-side session, a restore after a restart)

Read the clock as seconds of the day with fractions: now = timeInMin() * 60 + continuousSec() % 60. continuousSec() alone is seconds within the hour (minute * 60 + second + millis) and wraps at 3600; (now - startAt + 86400) % 86400 survives midnight for runs under a day

Toggle with one Button and three valueFloatExpressionChange actions, in this order: accumulated = @elapsed (folds the run in; paused, elapsed is already accumulated), startAt = now (a fresh start; harmless when pausing), running = 1 - @running. Reset is three valueFloatChange to 0: a literal belongs in valueFloatChange, valueFloatExpressionChange refuses one

Give the toggle a live label without three buttons: state = running * 2 + (1 - running) * step(accumulated, 0) picks 0 Start, 1 Resume, 2 Pause; a zero-size canvas's global block cuts a 6-character slot from "Start Resume Pause " with textSubtext (start @state * 6) and trims it with textTransform 3 into @stateLabel, which the Button takes as its label (and so as its accessibility label). One button in a fixed-width box keeps Reset still while the label changes

Format MM:SS.t from seconds: textMerge of textFromFloat(floor(@elapsed / 60), whole 2, flags 13) + ":" + textFromFloat(@elapsed % 60, whole 2, flags 13), and the tenths as (@elapsed * 10) % 10 with whole 1 and flags 5, in a smaller muted text aligned to the bottom of the row

Empty a ProgressRing over a target: progress = max(0, 1 - @elapsed / @target), with the time text overlaid in the ring's box (showLabel false). target is exported (1500 s), so the host makes the same document a 5-minute break or a 50-minute block, and the header shows it as @target / 60 min

Survive smaller hosts with a fitBox of fixed-height, fillMaxWidth alternatives, largest first: the ring layout (268 dp), the time over the buttons (132 dp), one row of time and buttons (40 dp), the time alone. Header, TimeText and Controls are inline components, so each alternative is a short composition, not a copy

snippets.note: elapsed = accumulated + running * (now - startAt), wrapped at midnight
seconds of the day with fractions; continuousSec() alone wraps every hour
the state the buttons change and the host may set: running, startAt, accumulated, target
one tap: fold the run into accumulated, capture startAt, flip running
Reset: literals go in valueFloatChange
the button's label: a 6-character slot of "Start Resume Pause " cut by @state, trimmed into @stateLabel
MM:SS with zero padding (flags 13), the tenths smaller and muted
ProgressRing emptying from 1 to 0 as elapsed approaches target, the time text inside
four layouts of the same content, fixed heights, the first that fits wins

running.meaning: 1 while the stopwatch runs, 0 when paused or reset

startAt.meaning: the clock (seconds of the day, timeInMin() * 60 + continuousSec() % 60) when the current run started; only read while running

accumulated.meaning: seconds elapsed in the runs before the current one; the whole elapsed time while paused

target.meaning: the work period in seconds the ring empties over (1500 = 25 minutes); the header shows it in minutes

check.describe: Canonical (fresh): 00:00.0 inside a full ring, the filled button says Start, an outlined Reset next to it, "25 min" top right. interact: tap Start (154,264) then wait 1.5 s: running 1, startAt = the pinned clock in seconds of the day (37200), elapsed about 2.0 and the ring 0.9987; the label reads Pause. Tapping again pauses: running back to 0, accumulated keeps the run (Start, 1.5 s, Pause, 1 s, Resume, 1 s, Pause ends at accumulated 2.57), the label reads Resume and the time stops. Reset (243,265) returns every variable to 0 and the ring to full. running render: the Start tap at 0.2 s then 65 s simulated: 01:04.8, Pause, the ring open by 4%. paused render: 00:02.7 with Resume. over (accumulated 1234.5, paused): 20:34.5 with the ring at 18%. light and mono recolour it (mono: thin grey track, white arc, outlined buttons). narrow (240 x 180) drops the ring: header, 12:34.3 at 40 sp, the two buttons. short (360 x 140) is one row: the time left, the buttons right. Repaint: 3 expressions listen to continuousSec() (now and the two startAt captures), so a player repaints every frame paused or running; the inspector's runtime says settled while paused because nothing changes on screen.

pitfalls: continuousSec() is seconds WITHIN THE HOUR (minute * 60 + second + millis), not since boot or since the epoch: elapsed = continuousSec() - startAt goes negative at the next full hour. Build seconds of the day, timeInMin() * 60 + continuousSec() % 60, and wrap with (+ 86400) % 86400; a single run longer than a day needs a day count too

Any expression that reads continuousSec() registers a listener, and the player's repaint schedule (getOpsToUpdate) repaints every frame while one exists, whether the value matters or not: this document repaints every frame while PAUSED too (the inspector's runtime says settled, because nothing on screen changes). The format has no way to drop the listener when running is 0; a pure clock display with timeInSec() would be idle but cannot show tenths. Accept it for a stopwatch the user is looking at; don't leave one in a widget that is meant to idle

Order the toggle's actions: accumulated = @elapsed must run before startAt and running change, because elapsed reads both; and write it as "@elapsed + 0" or the full formula. A literal (1, 0) is refused by valueFloatExpressionChange: use valueFloatChange, as Reset does

Don't make Start / Resume / Pause three buttons stacked in a box and switched by visibility: the TypeScript player gives a tap to the last child whose (stale) bounds contain it, GONE or not, and a row's intrinsic width still counts the hidden ones, so a fitBox rejects the layout (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U45). One Button with a text-variable label avoids both; a layout text cannot take textSubtext itself (U32), so the slot is cut in a zero-size canvas's global block

ProgressRing's progress is animated (0.3 s): a single-frame render at a host-set accumulated still shows the ring full; check.renders that set variables pass duration 0.5 so the arc settles. Mono has no animation and shows the value at once
step(x, edge) is x > edge: step(@accumulated, 0) is 1 after any pause, so the label says Resume; a run paused within the first frame (accumulated 0) still says Start, which is right
Pinned clocks: interact and render take clock "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS" (local); startAt then equals that time in seconds of the day (10:20:00 = 37200), which is what check.describe quotes
Weights ignore spacedBy (U3): the header row puts its gap as padding on the weighted title, not spacedBy, or the "25 min" text is pushed past the edge

teaches: Set a text's weight with fontWeight, a number from 100 (thin) to 900 (black); 400 is regular (the default) and 700 bold
Slant a text with fontStyle "italic", alone or with a bold fontWeight
Spread letters apart with letterSpacing, in em (0.25 is a quarter of the font size)

snippets.note: fontWeight 700 (bold)
fontStyle italic with fontWeight 700
letterSpacing 0.25 (em)

check.describe: Five lines grow from thin to black weight; two italic lines lean; the second TRACKING line is wider than the first and the second paragraph's lines sit further apart than the first's (the C++ screenshot does not show these two yet: EXAMPLES_FINDINGS C13). pitfalls: fontStyle takes "italic" (or 1); bold is not a style, it is fontWeight 700
letterSpacing is in em, not dp: 0.25 at fontSize 18 adds 4.5 dp per letter, and 2 would be enormous
lineHeightMultiplier only shows on text that wraps onto several lines: give the text a bounded width (fillMaxWidth) so it wraps
A font renders only the weights it has: on a system font with few weights neighbouring values (500 and 600, say) can look the same
A specimen or settings page is taller than a short or narrow screen: give the root column a verticalScroll so the rest can be reached

examples.name: text-overflow
examples.title: Text overflow and ellipsis
examples.summary: The same long sentence in 120 dp boxes, cut after 1, 2 and 3 lines with an end ellipsis, on one line with start and middle ellipses, and clipped with no mark.
examples.prompt: Show how a long sentence is truncated in a narrow box: maxLines 1, 2 and 3 with an ellipsis, plus start and middle ellipsis and plain clipping.
teaches: Clamp a text to N lines with maxLines and mark the cut with overflow "ellipsis"
Keep the end of a string visible with overflow "start_ellipsis", or both ends with "middle_ellipsis"
Give the text a fixed width (a width modifier on the text itself) so it has something to overflow

snippets.note: maxLines 2, overflow ellipsis, in a 120 dp width
maxLines 1, overflow start_ellipsis
maxLines 1, overflow middle_ellipsis

check.describe: Rows 1–3 show 1, 2 and 3 lines ending in …; the start_ellipsis row begins with … and shows the sentence's end; the middle_ellipsis row has … in the middle; the clip row is cut without a mark. Resized: the caption column takes the remaining width (weight 1), so at 240 the captions crowd the 120 dp sample boxes without overlapping, and at 540 the boxes sit at the right edge. (C++ player: at other widths the maxLines 2/3 boxes show fewer lines — it counts lines against the row width, not the 120 dp box.)

pitfalls: overflow defaults to clip, which cuts mid-letter with no mark: ask for "ellipsis" explicitly
An ellipsis needs a bound: without maxLines the text just wraps onto more lines, and without a bounded width (width, fillMaxWidth or a weight) it grows to fit and never overflows
start_ellipsis and middle_ellipsis are meant for a single line (as on Android, where multi-line start/middle truncation is not supported): use them with maxLines 1
The width modifier includes the text's own padding: width 120 with padding 4 leaves 112 dp for the letters

teaches: Let a text choose its own size with autoSize true, bounded by minFontSize and maxFontSize
Give an auto-sized text a width to fit (fillMaxWidth) and keep it on one line with maxLines 1
Check a responsive text by rendering the same document at several widths
pitfalls: minFontSize and maxFontSize alone change nothing: autoSize must be true for the player to search between them
An auto-sized text needs a bounded width; in a box that wraps its content there is nothing to fit to, so give the text fillMaxWidth (or a fixed width)
Without maxLines 1 the player may prefer wrapping onto two lines at a larger size over shrinking a single line

snippets.note: autoSize true, minFontSize 12, maxFontSize 48, maxLines 1, fillMaxWidth, in a Card's content

check.describe: At 400×120 the title fills the Card's width in large letters; rendered at 150×120 (render_rc with width/height) it should be much smaller and still whole on one line (the TS player does this; the C++ player still clips it: EXAMPLES_FINDINGS C14). The narrow render is the resize check (C++ still clips it, C14); at 600 wide the title stops growing at maxFontSize 48.
