Rows and markers share one selected variable (from 0): a row tap selects, a marker tap (within hit dp of it) selects its row, highlighted with a tint and a bar. The list does not scroll to a marker's row; with more rows than fit, the selected row can be off screen on a phone

Each marker is its place's number (from 1), the same number leading its row. Rows are 64 dp with a subtitle, 52 without; title and subtitle are one line each (ellipsized), meta (a distance, a rating, a time) is not cut: keep it short

Bytes: the map geometry dominates (a world of land at low detail ~6 KB, Europe with borders ~10 KB, a world with borders at medium ~40 KB), then about 1.4 KB per place (its row, its marker in both panes, its tap test). The map is written twice (stacked and side panes, one shown); its path is one shared resource

Marker taps run on the map canvas's touch down (touchX/touchY against each marker), so they work where the marker is drawn in all players; rows are ordinary clicks with a spoken label (title, subtitle, meta)

A worldwide set of places frames the whole world, which cannot fill a square or tall box: the stacked map's height is capped at the frame's own aspect, but a side pane on a squarish window shows empty sea above and below. Places within a continent or a country fill every size; use detail medium when the frame is one region (a few states), where low detail shows crude coasts
width and height default to the window: pass them when it is not the whole window. The list sits on surface (background), the map on mapBackground; land is track

components.name: math-plot
components.title: MathPlot
components.prompt: Plot y = x³ − 3x with its roots and turning points marked and let me drag along the curve to read values; then plot ln x against 1/x and mark where they cross.
teaches: Give the formula, not data: {"MathPlot": {"fn": "x^3 - 3x", "x": [-2.5, 2.5], "mark": ["roots", "extrema"]}}; the server finds the points (to 1e-9) and prints them
The curve is a pathExpression of the formula, evaluated by the player at the plot's real size: about 100 B, exact at any width or aspect
scrub: true adds a drag across the plot (touchExpression) with a dot riding the curve and x, y printed from whole numbers
Several functions get colours (dashed in mono) and a legend; mark: ["intersections"] finds where the first meets the second

snippets.note: the call: formula, domain, marks, scrub
the curve is a pathExpression of the formula
scrub: true, a touchExpression over the plot
the plot's description lists every marked point
two formulas and their intersection

check.describe: Two plots. Top: an S-shaped cubic from −2.5 to 2.5, dots at (−1.73, 0), (0, 0), (1.73, 0), (−1, 2) and (1, −2) with their coordinates, a guide line at x = −1 and a readout 'x = −1.00  y = 2.00' above. Bottom: ln x rising through (1, 0) and 1/x falling, a dot where they cross near (1.76, 0.57), and a legend.

components.summary: A function graph from formulas in x ("x^2 - 2x - 3", "exp(-x/4)*cos(x)"): the server finds the roots, maxima, minima and intersections you ask to mark and picks the axes and ticks (multiples of π when the domain is written with π); the curve is a runtime expression, exact at every size; optional legend and a draggable x that reads the value off the curve.
pitfalls: Write the formula, not numbers: never sample a curve yourself or type in where its roots or peaks are; mark: ["roots", "max"] makes the server find them (to 1e-9), and the labels print what it found

x is the variable (2x, x^2, sin x all work); ^ is a power and e^(...) is exp(...); log is base 10, ln is natural. A formula that leaves the format's limits (over about 28 operations, Android's 32-entry path expression) is sampled into a 161-point float array instead, which costs about 650 B
Write a domain with π ([0, "4pi"]) to get π ticks (0, π, 2π, ...) and marks printed as π/2 when they are; ticks: "decimal" turns that off
Poles (tan x, 1/x) are split out: the curve stops short of each and no line joins the two sides; give y to choose how much of the spike shows
Marks label the first function; {"at": "max", "of": 1} marks another. intersections are where the first meets the second
scrub is a drag on the whole plot: inside a scrolling column the scroll may take vertical drags first
Mono draws every curve in one colour, the second and later ones dashed (the legend shows which is which), and no grid

components.name: meter-breakdown
components.title: MeterBreakdown
components.prompt: Show calories eaten against a target as a ring, with macros as labelled bars.
teaches: One call adapts by itself: ring over parts when tall, beside when wide, parts dropping when short, ring alone on a watch
Past target: a second lap on the ring, a marked excess and +N on a bar

snippets.note: the whole component
one spoken summary with every part
every length and sweep is an expression of the value and the box
numbers are rounded, formatted and fitted

check.describe: A blue ring with 1,640 of 2,000 kcal, 360 left, then Carbs, Protein with +25 and Fat bars. Wide: ring left. 160: ring alone. eaten 2600: a red second lap and 600 over.

components.summary: A meter and its parts, arranged by the space it gets: a big ring of value against target with the number and what is left in the centre, and one labelled bar per part (macros, categories). Ring over parts when tall, ring beside parts when wide, parts dropping one by one when short, ring alone on a watch. Past the target the ring runs a second lap and a bar marks its limit, also in mono. Read as one sentence by a screen reader.
pitfalls: It fills the box it is given and arranges itself from that box, not the window: put it in a sized or weighted parent with the padding on the parent. In a scrolling column give the parent a height

Regimes: width >= 1.2 x height puts the ring on the left and the parts on the right (the pair stays centred, parts at most 380 wide); otherwise ring over parts. A part row needs 32 dp: parts that do not fit are dropped from the end, so list the most important first. A near-square box of 240 or less (watch, 2x2 widget) shows the ring alone. The summary still speaks every part

The ring is drawn, not ProgressRing: pass value and target unclamped. Past the target the first lap dims and a second lap in overColor runs over it (mono: the white ring carries a cut line). Very large overshoots wrap: the lap shows the remainder and the text says the amount

All text is on one canvas, as in BigNumber: an empty box after it carries the spoken summary, which needs the canvas's text variables, so it reads one sentence per part. Drawn text does not follow the system font scale
List items: value and target may each be a number, "@variable" or an expression string, and are bound to canvas variables first because a list field that is a string is otherwise treated as text

components.name: moon-phase
components.title: Moon phase
components.prompt: Draw the moon at any phase of its cycle, from new through full and back, without glyphs or images; show the eight principal phases captioned, and one bound to a variable.
teaches: {"MoonPhase": {"phase": 0.3}} draws a 48 dp moon; phase is the fraction of the lunation (0 new, 0.25 first quarter, 0.5 full, 0.75 last quarter) and may be a variable or an expression from the clock

One definition draws every phase: a disc in the shade colour, the lit half (right while waxing, step(phase, 0.5) flips it), and a terminator ellipse of half-width r·|cos 2π·phase|, shaded for a crescent and lit for a gibbous moon
Draw in a 100-unit box and scale it to size once; with a literal phase every expression folds to a number, so a static moon costs no expressions

snippets.note: 0, a new moon: the 100-unit drawing scaled to 48 dp, a rim and an unlit disc
0.125, a waxing crescent: the right half lit, then a shaded ellipse over it
0.375, a waxing gibbous moon: the right half and a lit ellipse
bound to the exported variable phase: the terminator follows cos(2π·@phase)

phase.meaning: lunation fraction 0..1 of the large moon

check.describe: Two rows of four 48 dp moons, captioned with the phase and its name: 0 new (an empty disc inside its rim), 0.125 a thin crescent lit on the right, 0.25 the right half lit, 0.375 gibbous lit on the right, 0.5 full, 0.625 gibbous lit on the left, 0.75 the left half lit, 0.875 a crescent on the left. Below, a 72 dp moon bound to phase 0.3 (a waxing gibbous moon, 65% lit). Dark: amber on slate; light: the theme's darker amber on pale grey; mono and mono light: the lit part in onSurface, the rest background inside a grey ring. At 260 dp the columns close up and at 480 dp they spread; the moons keep their size.

components.summary: The moon at a phase of its cycle (0 new, 0.25 first quarter, 0.5 full, 0.75 last quarter), drawn from circles, a half-disc and an elliptical terminator in a square canvas.
pitfalls: Don't draw a moon as a text glyph (🌒 ◐ ☾): it depends on the device's fonts, can't take theme colours or a size, and shows eight phases at best. Call MoonPhase with the phase computed in the document
Waxing is lit on the right (phase < 0.5) and waning on the left, as seen from the northern hemisphere; for the southern hemisphere mirror it (a scale of -1 around the centre) or pass 1 - phase
phase is the fraction of the lunation, not the fraction lit: the lit fraction is (1 - cos(2π · phase)) / 2, so a quarter moon (0.25) is half lit, and 0.125 is about 15% lit

The terminator is an ellipse of half-width r · |cos(2π · phase)|, in the shade colour for a crescent (cos > 0) and in the lit colour for a gibbous moon (cos < 0). Each is drawn with a width of max(0, ±cos), so the other one has zero width: no paint alpha to switch and reset
At exactly new moon the lit half isn't drawn (its sweep is 180 · step(0.9999, cos)): the shaded ellipse covers it, but the half-disc's antialiased edge would still leave a lit hairline on the limb
The edge ring is a disc 1 dp larger drawn first, not a stroke drawn last: a stroke over the disc dulls the lit limb

Mono ignores lit, shade and rim: the lit part is onSurface and the rest background inside a 1.5 dp outline ring, so the phase reads as shape. On black (mono) that is a white full moon; in mono light (e-ink) the lit part is the ink, so a full moon is a black disc, the reverse of a printed almanac's ● new / ○ full: label the phases there

The drawing is scaled to the box the layout actually gives the canvas (min of its width and height, centred), so a call clamped by a smaller parent shrinks instead of being cut off; the 1 dp rim is computed from `size`, so it is thinner in proportion there

components.name: NavShell
components.title: NavShell: an app shell with adaptive navigation in one call
components.prompt: An app with three to five top-level destinations, each with its own page: a bottom navigation bar on a phone, a navigation rail on a landscape phone or small tablet, a drawer with full rows on a wide window.
teaches: Call {"NavShell": {"selected": "@tab", "destinations": [{"icon": "home", "label": "Home", "page": PAGE}, ...]}}: only the pages are yours; the bar, rail, drawer, highlight, heading and switching come with it
The form follows the width: bottom bar under 600 dp, rail from 600, drawer with the title from 840; the same call in light, dark and mono
Bind selected to a document variable to preset the destination or to read it elsewhere; onClick tells the host which one was tapped

snippets.note: three navigation forms and three pages by visibility
each destination sets tab
each destination is a labelled click with its state
bottom-bar items share the width by weight
each destination's Material Symbols icon, drawn in bar, rail and drawer
each destination announces Selected or Not selected

check.describe: Phone (360x640): heading Home, Recently played with three albums and playlists, a bottom bar with Home (blue icon on a pale pill), Search and Library. 640x360 and 800x1280: the same destinations in an 80 dp rail on the left. 1280x800: a drawer titled Tune with full rows, Home in a pale pill. The tap renders select Library on the phone, Search in the rail and Library in the drawer: the heading and page follow. Mono: the selected destination is a filled white (black on mono-light) pill.

components.summary: A whole app shell with 3 to 5 top-level destinations: you give each one an icon, a label and its page; it brings the adaptive navigation (a bottom bar with icons and labels on a phone, a navigation rail from 600 dp wide, a drawer with full rows and the app title from 840 dp), the selected destination's highlight in every form, its title over the page, and switches the page on a tap.
pitfalls: The form is chosen by the shell's width, never by content: under railAt (600) a bottom bar, from railAt a rail 80 dp wide on the left, from drawerAt (840) a drawer 240 dp wide with the title. A tablet held upright (800 wide) gets the rail

A page cannot read the shell's values. Its width is width - 2 * pagePadding on a phone, width - 81 - 2 * pagePadding with the rail and width - 241 - 2 * pagePadding with the drawer: compute the same in your document (for example ifElse(windowWidth() - 273, ifElse(windowWidth() - 113, windowWidth() - 32, step(windowWidth(), 599.5)), step(windowWidth(), 839.5))) when a page must change its own layout, such as cards in two columns when wide

Its height is the window minus the 56 dp header, minus the 80 dp bottom bar on a phone. With scroll (the default) a taller page scrolls; inside a scrolling page, weights and fillMaxHeight do nothing: give heights
Every page is in the document at once, each with a visibility on the selection, so the document is the sum of its pages; each page has its own scroll position
Labels are written three times (bar, rail, drawer) and drawn twice in each (a plain and a highlighted copy), so they must be static strings; icons are one path per name however often drawn

The selection animates: the indicator pill and the highlighted copy fade with an animated local over 0.25 s, while the page switches at once on the new value. Mono: no motion, the selected item is a filled pill with a black icon
Accessibility: each destination is one labelled click (its label) with Selected or Not selected as its state, cut from "Not selectedSelected    " as in Tabs; the header is the selected label as text
Keep to 5 destinations: the bottom bar gives each 1/n of the width, 72 dp at 360 for 5, and a longer label is cut

components.name: numberedlist
components.title: NumberedList
components.prompt: Show instructions in order: a number beside each step's text, which wraps, and a plain bulleted list of things with the same call.
teaches: items are strings, or [text, note] for a muted line under a step
marker bullet gives a plain list with no numbers

snippets.note: three numbered items, one with a note
the text wraps in the weighted column
a bullet list
see the call

check.describe: Numbers 1, 2, 3 in discs beside wrapped text, a muted note under item 2; then two bulleted lines.

components.summary: A list of instructions in order, a method: each item a number and text that wraps, spoken as one item ("3. Cut in the edges"). marker bullet makes it a plain list of things. For progress through stages (Ordered, Shipped, Delivered) use Steps.
pitfalls: Not Steps: Steps shows where a process has got to (done, current, to do). This shows what to do, in order, with text that wraps
The items are static text, chosen when the document is built. Nothing can be ticked off: for that, a Checkbox per row
The number is drawn, not a text, so a numbered item is one spoken item: "3. Tape the edges". A note under it is a second item
Give it the width of a Card or a column. In a row, weight its parent or the text has no width to wrap in

components.name: pager
components.title: Pager
components.prompt: Make a three-page onboarding carousel: swipe left or right to change page, tap a dot to jump, the new page fades in, and a screen reader hears "Onboarding, Page 2 of 3".
teaches: Call {"Pager": {"page": "@page", "pages": [PAGE1, PAGE2, PAGE3]}}: each page is any JSON node, shown alone; the dots, the swipe and "Page N of M" come with it
A swipe is onTouchDown storing touchX() into the call's own `start`, and onTouchUp setting page = clamp(0, n − 1, page + clamp(−1, 1, round((start − touchX()) / (0.5 × windowWidth()))))
Pages switch by visibility (only the current one is laid out and read) and fade in with graphicsLayer alpha over an animated copy of the page
Each dot sits in a 24 × 40 dp tap target that sets the page and is announced "Go to page N"

snippets.note: a dot tap sets page; the swipe is onTouchDown / onTouchUp on the pager
only the current page is visible
the new page fades in and the accent dot slides
Onboarding, Page N of 3; Go to page N on each dot
the dots

check.describe: Page 1, "Welcome" over "Plan your week in a minute", centred, with three dots at the bottom, the first blue. A swipe to the left shows "Track your runs" (fading in) and moves the blue dot to the second; a swipe to the right goes back; a swipe at the last page stays there; a tap on the third dot jumps to "Share with friends"; a tap on the page changes nothing. page 2 shows the third page. Mono: white (black) filled current dot, grey rings, no fade. A screen reader hears "Onboarding, Page 1 of 3", the page's two texts and the three dots "Go to page 1" to "Go to page 3".

components.summary: Swipeable pages with dots: a horizontal swipe on the pager moves one page (onTouchDown keeps where the finger went down, onTouchUp steps the page by the clamped, rounded distance), the new page fades in, the dots under it follow and a tap on a dot jumps to its page. A screen reader hears "Page N of M" and can tap each dot.
pitfalls: The swipe is two touch modifiers on the pager's column: onTouchDown stores touchX() into the call's own `start`, onTouchUp sets page = clamp(0, n − 1, page + clamp(−1, 1, round((start − touchX()) / (0.5 × windowWidth())))): a swipe of more than a quarter of the window moves exactly one page, a tap (no distance) moves none. No drag tracking: the page does not follow the finger, it changes on release

Each page is a box with visibility 1 − min(1, |k − i|) (k = clamp(0, n − 1, round(page))) and graphicsLayer alpha 1 − min(1, |f − i|) over the animated local f = {value: page, anim: 0.3}: the new page fades in, and the old one disappears when the layout next reads its visibility (in the TS player it fades out alongside; a visibility is an integer expression and cannot read the eased value itself, U57). Mono has no motion: pages switch

The pager fills its parent (the pages box has verticalWeight 1, the dots row is 40 dp): give it a parent with a height (a box with a height, or a weighted child of a screen column). Pages are stacked in one box, each fillMaxSize: centre their content yourself

pages is a static list of JSON nodes: one page box each, written out when the document is built (a page can call components). With `count` and the `content` slot, the pager only owns the swipe, the dots and the description: your content reads the page variable

The dots are 8 dp at a 24 dp pitch so each one sits in a 24 × 40 dp tap target (onClick sets page to its index, announced "Go to page N"); the accent dot slides with f. The pages box carries "Page N of M" (textFromFloat(k + 1)), prefixed by `label`
windowWidth() is the document's width: in a pager narrower than the window, a swipe must still cross a quarter of the window, not of the pager

components.name: pager-dots
components.title: PagerDots
components.prompt: Add page indicator dots under an onboarding carousel that show which of the five pages is current.
teaches: Call {"PagerDots": {"count": 5, "current": "@page"}}: count is a literal (the dots are generated at build time), current a 0-based number or variable
Drive current with the same variable as the pager or Tabs; an animated variable makes the accent dot slide
Centre it with the parent's horizontalAlignment: it is only count × 16 − 8 dp wide

snippets.note: three dots, the first one current (a literal)
five dots bound to page: the accent dot is at x = 4 + 16 × @page

check.describe: Two centred rows of dots: three with the first blue, five with the third violet; page 4 moves the violet dot to the last. The dot rows stay centred at 234 and 540 dp wide.

components.summary: A page indicator: `count` 8 dp dots 8 dp apart, and an accent dot that sits on (or, with an animated variable, slides to) the one at `current`.
pitfalls: One canvas, not a row of boxes: the plain dots are generated with $each, and a single accent dot is drawn at x = 4 + 16 × current, so it costs one expression however many pages there are
The canvas is count × 16 − 8 dp wide: centre it with the parent's horizontalAlignment
The current dot eases to a new index: an animated local c = {"value": "@current", "anim": 0.25} (paint time) is what the canvas reads; mono themes jump

components.name: piano-keys
components.title: PianoKeys
components.prompt: Show a B♭maj7 chord on a piano with the note names on the keys and the intervals under them, then an E7♯9 voicing I give as notes, labelled by interval.
teaches: {"PianoKeys": {"chord": "Bbmaj7"}}: the server spells (B♭ D F A, not A♯) and voices the chord, and fits the range
notes: "E3 G#3 D4 G4" with chord "E7#9" respells G as F𝄪 and labels it ♯9
Keys are literal rectangles in a box one unit per white key, scaled per axis to the canvas; labels fade when keys get too narrow for them

snippets.note: a chord name, with intervals below
one scale for every key
a note list; the description names the chord and keys

check.describe: Two keyboards. B♭maj7: C4..B5, B♭4 (black, label under it), D5, F5, A5 highlighted with names, R 3 5 7 under. E7♯9: C3..B4, E3 G♯3 D4 G4 highlighted, labelled R 3 ♭7 ♯9.

components.summary: A piano keyboard with notes highlighted and labelled, from a chord name ("Dm", "Cmaj7", "Bb/D": the server spells and voices it) or a note list ("D4 F4 A4"); the range fits the notes unless given, and it fills its width.
pitfalls: Write the chord or the notes; never colour keys yourself. The server spells the chord from its intervals, so Bbmaj7 reads B♭ D F A, F#7 reads F♯ A♯ C♯ E and E7#9 has an F𝄪
notes with octaves are taken as written (a voicing you choose); without octaves they rise from octave 4

White and black keys are ivory and ebony in every colour theme (they are a piano, not surfaces); the highlight follows the theme. Mono draws white keys as outlines, black keys grey, and highlighted keys solid
Labels need about 7 dp a character per key: on a narrow keyboard they fade out rather than overflow; give fewer keys (range) or a wider box
One canvas, every key a literal rectangle in a box one key wide per white key, scaled to the canvas: about 30 B a key

components.name: pricechart
components.title: PriceChart
components.prompt: A stock's price today: a line and area coloured against previous close, a price axis with round ticks, the latest price in a tag, high and low marks, time labels.
teaches: Call {"PriceChart": {"values": "@prices", "baseline": "@prev", "fill": true}}: the axis ticks, tag and marks all come from the array, and move when the host replaces it
baseline splits the colour above and below, without it the colour is last against first; color fixes one colour for things without good and bad
points leaves room for the rest of the day, with a marker at now
It drops the axis and marks when small, so a 2x2 widget gets the line, baseline and dot

snippets.note: the whole chart from one exported array
line and area are path expressions, clipped at the baseline
see the call
see the call
see the call
see the call

check.describe: A line, green above the dashed previous close and red below, with a fading wash, round ticks on the right, the latest in a coloured tag with a guide to it, high and low values with dots, time labels and a marker where the day has got to.

components.summary: A line chart of one series with a computed y axis, for any measurement that moves over time and may have a reference value: a price, a balance, heart rate, temperature. Line with a fading area, axis labels on round ticks, an optional baseline with one colour above and another below, high and low marks, x labels, the latest value in a tag. Use it rather than LineChart when the axis must follow data the host replaces; LineChart when you write the labels yourself or plot several series. Fills its box and drops axes and marks when small.
pitfalls: Use this rather than LineChart for a single series judged against a reference or read off an axis (a price, a balance, heart rate): LineChart's axis labels are fixed text you write, these are computed from the data, on round steps (1, 2, 5 × 10ⁿ), and move when the host replaces the array. Finance is only its default: without color, green means up and red down, so pass color for anything else

Which chart: PriceChart for a hero chart of one series with an axis; TrendSparkline for a word-sized trend in a row; LineChart for time-of-day curves with function mode or labels you choose; BarChart for separate quantities
The line is straight segments through the samples, not a spline: a spline invents highs and lows between prices. High and low are the samples' own; pass the session's real high and low in your stats

Set a height through fill and a sized parent: with fill in a column, give the parent a verticalWeight or an exact height. Under 200 dp wide the y axis and marks go, under 110 dp tall the x labels go, so a 2x2 widget keeps line, area, baseline and dot

Every number on the axis is a text built at run time (printed with six decimals and cut), about 6.5 KB a chart, 7.5 KB with a baseline. It is meant for the one hero chart of a screen; rows take TrendSparkline
Mono: no area and no direction colours. With a baseline the line is white above and grey below; the tag is a filled face
A float holds about 7 digits: prices above 99,999.99 lose cents on the axis
The area fades to `surface` under an alpha, not to transparent, so it looks the same in every player: on another background, pass that colour as surface or the bottom edge of the wash shows faintly

components.name: progress-bar
components.title: ProgressBar
components.prompt: Show a horizontal progress bar for a download that fills as the host updates its progress.
teaches: Call {"ProgressBar": {"progress": 0.3}} with progress 0..1: a literal, or a "@variable" the host updates (download, exported here)
It fills its parent's width: in a column it spans the row; in a row wrap it in a weighted box
`height` sets the thickness (the ends stay fully round) and `color` the fill; the track is @colors.track

snippets.note: a literal 30% bar: two round rects, track and fill
bound to the exported variable download, 12 dp thick and green
the fill is componentWidth() × progress, so the bar follows its parent's width

check.describe: A blue bar 30% full, and below it a thicker green bar 72% full; setting download to 0.25 shrinks the green fill to a quarter. Both bars draw from componentWidth(): at 234 and 540 dp they span the width and keep 30% and 72% fills.

components.summary: A horizontal progress bar filling its width: a rounded track with a fill of progress × width (progress 0..1, a number or a variable). With overshoot, a value past 1 rescales the bar: the fill stops at a limit tick and the excess is its own segment.
pitfalls: clamp takes (min, max, value): clamp(0, 1, @pa). clamp(@progress, 0, 1) is always 0 (the RPN is min max value CLAMP)
It fills its parent's width (componentWidth()): in a row put it in a weighted box, or it has no width
The fill is at least a round dot (max(height, width × progress)), so 0 % is not empty

A progress change animates: the drawing reads an animated local pa = {"value": "@progress", "anim": 0.3} (paint time). A literal progress folds to a number, so a static bar costs nothing extra; a value driven every frame just follows 0.3 s behind. Mono themes jump

overshoot: a value past the limit is drawn, not clamped: the bar's full width is max(value, limit), the fill ends at the limit tick and the excess is an overColor segment (hatched with oblique lines in mono). Pass progress unclamped (@spent / @limit); a 0 limit gives an infinite ratio, guard it (@spent / max(@limit, 0.01)). Pair it with a text that says the amount over, for screen readers and mono.

components.name: progress-ring
components.title: ProgressRing
components.prompt: Draw a circular progress ring showing how much of today's step goal is done, with the percentage in the middle.
teaches: Call {"ProgressRing": {"progress": 0.66}}: progress 0..1 sweeps from 12 o'clock, and the percentage is drawn in the centre
Bind progress to a "@variable" for a live ring (goal, exported here); keep it in 0..1: past 1 the ring is just full, with no second lap (ActivityRings and MeterBreakdown have one)
`size` and `thickness` scale the ring (the label follows the size); showLabel false leaves just the arc, for small rings

snippets.note: the default 64 dp ring at a literal 66%
bound to the variable goal: sweep = @goal × 360
the centre label is textFromFloat(@goal × 100)
40 dp, no label, amber

check.describe: Three rings in a row: blue 66 with its label, a larger green ring reading 40, and a small amber quarter ring with no label; goal 0.9 makes the green ring read 90. The row spreads the rings with spaceEvenly instead of a fixed gap: at 220 dp they close up and still fit, at 540 dp the extra space is shared out evenly.

components.summary: A circular progress ring: a track circle and an arc of progress × 360° starting at 12 o'clock, with an optional percentage in the centre.
pitfalls: Not a meter for overshoot: a progress of 1.34 draws the same full ring as 1, with 134 as its label. Use ActivityRings or MeterBreakdown when passing a target must show
A literal progress costs nothing at run time: "@progress * 360" folds to a number when the component expands. Wrapping it in clamp() would turn it back into an expression
If you do clamp a live value, clamp takes (min, max, value): clamp(0, 1, @p). clamp(@p, 0, 1) is always 0
The label is textFromFloat with flags 5 (no padding): the default flags pad the number with spaces, which pushes it off centre

`size` is the box the call asks for: in a row whose width varies, spread the rings with horizontalAlignment spaceEvenly (or weighted boxes) rather than a spacedBy gap, and pick sizes that fit the narrowest host. The drawing is scaled to the box the layout actually gives the canvas (min of its width and height, centred), so a call clamped by a smaller parent shrinks instead of being cut off, with the stroke scaled in proportion

A progress change animates: the drawing reads an animated local pa = {"value": "@progress", "anim": 0.3} (paint time). A literal progress folds to a number, so a static bar costs nothing extra; a value driven every frame just follows 0.3 s behind. Mono themes jump (the percentage label shows the true value at once)

components.name: qr-placeholder
components.title: QrPlaceholder
components.prompt: Put a QR code on a boarding pass, and a small pairing code next to an instruction in a row; the codes stay black on white in dark mode and on e-ink.
teaches: Call {"QrPlaceholder": {"seed": 7, "contentDescription": "Boarding pass QR code"}}: three finder patterns, timing lanes and a 21 × 21 pseudo-random grid, black on white in every look
441 modules cost two nested canvas loops: each module's paint alpha is an integer hash of its column, row and the seed, so the pattern is exact and identical in every player
The drawing is a 29-module unit square scaled by min(width, height) / 29 and centred: an 88 dp code in a 56 dp row draws at 56 dp instead of being cut

snippets.note: the module grid: two nested loops over r and c
finder patterns as three nested squares
asked for 88 dp in a 56 dp row: scaled to 56 dp, centred
says what the code is for

check.describe: A 168 dp QR-like code centred at the top: a white rounded square with a thin outline, three black 7 × 7 finder rings at the top-left, top-right and bottom-left corners, alternating timing modules between them and a random-looking module grid; under it a 56 dp row with a small code (asked 88 dp, drawn 56 dp) and "Scan with the app to pair the speaker". The codes are black on white in light, dark, mono-dark and mono-light. A screen reader hears "Boarding pass QR code, flight AF 1234" and "Pairing code for the living room speaker", then the text.

components.summary: A believable QR code picture for a ticket, a boarding pass or a pairing screen: a 21 × 21 module grid with the three 7 × 7 finder patterns and the timing lanes, data modules from a deterministic pseudo-random seed, black on white in every look inside a 4-module quiet zone, scaled to the square its box allows. It is a placeholder, not a scannable code.
pitfalls: Black on white in every look, on purpose: ink and paper default to literal #FF000000 and #FFFFFFFF, not theme colours, because a code inverted for dark or mono-dark would not scan (and would not look like one). In mono-dark that is a lit white square: keep it the size the task needs. Only the 1 dp frame round the quiet zone is a theme colour (outline), so the white square still has an edge on a white page

Not a real QR code: there is no encoder in the format. The 441 modules come from two nested canvas loops (r, c), each module's paint alpha step((7c² + 13r² + 5cr + 3c + 11r + 17 seed) mod 23, 11), an integer hash every player computes exactly, so the pattern is the same in Java, C++ and TypeScript. For a scannable code, render it on the server and send a bitmap
The finder corners and the row and column 6 timing lanes are cleared with paper and redrawn over the data, so they are always clean: 7 × 7 rings at three corners, alternating modules between them

Drawn in a 29-module unit square (21 + 2 × 4 quiet zone) under one scale of min(width, height) / 29, centred: an 88 dp code in a 56 dp row is a 56 dp code, never cut. Modules overlap by 0.02 so no hairline shows between them at fractional scales, and the clearing rectangles reach 0.02 further so no sliver of a neighbour shows along them
One accessibility node, the canvas, with contentDescription: say what the code is for

components.name: quoterow
components.title: QuoteRow
components.prompt: A watchlist of stocks, each row with symbol, name, a small trend, price and change.
teaches: Call {"QuoteRow": {"symbol": "AAPL", "price": "@p", "change": "@c", "values": "@week"}}
The trend goes under 300 dp of window

snippets.note: price and change from host values
see the call
see the call
see the call

check.describe: Three 53 dp rows: names on the left, a green and a red trend, prices and pills aligned on the right; BTC with no trend and a flat pill. Under them two compact 32 dp rows on one line, their trends lined up. The trends go at 200 wide.

components.summary: One row of a watchlist or holdings list: symbol and name, a trend coloured by direction, the price or value, and its change in a pill. A row is 53 dp, or 32 dp on one line with compact, and folds by itself in a narrow window. Numbers are rounded and signed for you, and it keeps its right edge aligned down a list.
pitfalls: Height: a normal row is 53 dp with or without a name, so 3 rows clip at the 4x2 widget's 320x160. For a widget use compact: true, rather than writing your own row: 32 dp a row from 240 dp of window (4 fit 320x160), 38 dp folded under that (3 fit 160x160 and 200x150, and 4 do not). Under about 150 dp price and change wrap too, about 55 dp a row: 2 fit 130x130
Rows are expanded, not patterns (they hold text), and one with a trend is about 2.8 KB: keep to the 5 to 10 a screen shows. For more, RowList on host strings is smaller

The trend goes under 300 dp of window. A normal row keeps symbol, name, price and change on two lines down to 150 dp, but only 2 rows fit 160x160. Under 150 dp it folds to about 68 dp, symbol above price above change, without the name: 1 full row at 130x130. In a wide layout, put these rows in one column of a split, don't stretch them: the far right is a long way from the name
A row does not draw its own divider or padding: put them in a column with spacedBy, or a Divider between
A price above 7 digits loses its cents: a float holds no more
The trend is spoken as the symbol and "trend": "AAPL trend". The direction comes from the change beside it
The fold reads the window, not the row's own width: in a narrow pane of a wide window it does not fold, so give that pane enough room or a smaller symbolWidth

components.name: ranked-list
components.title: RankedList
components.prompt: Show a café's five best sellers this week as a leaderboard, with rank badges, unit counts and share bars, and the top three baristas by orders under it; one item per row for a screen reader.
teaches: Call {"RankedList": {"names": ["Espresso beans", "@special", ...], "values": "@sales", "unit": " units"}}: names is a static JSON list (an entry may be a host string variable), values a float array read with arrayGet(values, i)
Each row is one canvas with its own semantics, so a screen reader hears "Number 1, Espresso beans, 412 units" once per row, not the rank, name and value as three items
The bars are value / max(arrayMax(values)), so the leader's bar is full; showBars false gives a compact list
Rank 1 is a filled disc, the others rings: the leader stands out without colour, in mono too

snippets.note: five rows over an exported float array; the second name is a string variable
one description per row: Number N, name, value unit
rank discs and share bars
a long name is clipped before the value
no bars, grouped numbers with a unit, secondary colour

check.describe: Five rows: a filled blue 1 and Espresso beans 412 units with a full bar, then rings 2 to 5 for Pumpkin spice latte 288, Oat milk flat white 231, Butter croissant 154 and Cinnamon bun 97, bars shrinking with the value; then a compact list, a violet 1 Ana 1,284 orders, 2 Bilal 1,102 orders, 3 Chloé 876 orders. A screen reader hears eight items, "Number 1, Espresso beans, 412 units" … "Number 3, Chloé, 876 orders". Mono: white (black) filled first disc, rings, white bars over 1 dp outlined tracks. At 240 dp the long names shrink and are clipped before the value; at 480 dp the rows widen.

components.summary: A leaderboard of a few rows (top products, longest runs, busiest stations): each row a rank badge, a name, its value with a unit at the end and a share bar of value / the largest value, read by a screen reader as one item per row: "Number 1, Espresso beans, 412 units".
pitfalls: One canvas per row, with its own semantics ("Number N, name, value unit" from textMerge): the rank, the name and the value are drawn, not layout texts, so a screen reader stops once per row instead of three times. The JSON semantics has no merge mode

names is a JSON list written into the document ($each); values is the name of a float array ("@sales" in resources.floatArrays), read with arrayGet(values, i): a host can change the numbers (and the names, through string variables) but not the number of rows. Give one value per name, sorted, highest first: the list does not sort
The bar is (width − 36) × value / max(arrayMax(values), 0.0001), at least 6 dp so a tiny share still shows; the track is the full width (mono: a 1 dp outline instead of a track fill)
A long name shrinks to 80 % to fit before the value and is then clipped (drawn text has no ellipsis); the value never shrinks. Numbers are grouped by thousands (textFromFloat flags 23)
The rank is textFromFloat(i + 1), a constant per row; rank 1 is a filled disc in `color`, the others a ring, so the leader stands out in mono too
It fills its parent's width, 48 dp per row (32 without bars): in a row, give it a weighted box
Each row measures its own name and value (per-row names nw_@i, vw_@i...): a long name shrinks only its own row

components.name: rating
components.title: Rating
components.prompt: A five-star "Your rating" row that starts at three stars and changes when a star is tapped, a small read-only 4.5-star average next to its review count, and a three-star difficulty in the primary colour.
teaches: {"Rating": {"value": "@rating"}} draws five stars out of the variable and tapping the i-th star sets it to i; the host reads the new value back from the variable
A number value (4.5) with interactive false is a read-only score: .25 to .75 over a star's index draws star_half, .75 and above a full star
max (a literal) sets the number of stars, size the star size, color and emptyColor the lit and empty colours; mono always draws onSurface on outline

Accessibility follows the value: each tappable star is announced 'N stars' and the row '<label>, N of max stars' ('Not rated' at 0); tappable stars under 48 dp get a 48 dp touch target. A host hears the new rating with {"onRate": "rate"} or one onClick hostNamedAction carrying "@rating" (json2rc extensions, not used here so the gallery stays identical with the reference parser)

snippets.note: bound to @rating (3): tapping a star writes it
a read-only 4.5 at 16 dp: four stars and a half
three stars in primary, labelled Difficulty
each star is three icon paths (star, star_half, star filled) switched by paint alpha

check.describe: Under the title, 'Your rating' over five 32 dp stars, three amber and two outlined, each in a 48 dp touch target (16 dp gaps); tapping the fourth lights four. Below, a 16 dp row of four and a half amber stars before '4.5 · 1,284 reviews', then 'Difficulty' beside three 24 dp stars (24 dp gaps) of which two are blue. A screen reader reads 'Your rating, 3 of 5 stars', each star '1 star' ... '5 stars', 'Average rating, 4.5 of 5 stars' and 'Difficulty, 2 of 3 stars'. Light and dark follow the theme; mono draws lit stars white (black in mono light) and empty ones grey. At 280 dp nothing wraps, at 480 the rows keep their left edge.

components.summary: A row of stars showing a rating out of max (5 by default): lit stars in the accent colour, a half star for a .5, the rest outlined; tapping the i-th star sets the value to i (then sends `onRate` and runs any `onClick` actions). Each star is announced "N stars" and the row its label and current rating
pitfalls: Each star is one canvas holding three Material Symbols paths (star outlined, star_half, star filled) in the empty colour and the accent, switched with paint alpha step(value - i, 0.25) and step(value - i, 0.75): below .25 over the star's index it is empty, from .25 a half, from .75 full. The three paths are stored once per document however many ratings it holds
The stars are generated when the document is built ($each over max), so max must be a literal; the value is a variable and may change at run time

A tap sets whole stars only (the i-th star sets i); a half star comes from the value a host writes (3.5). Tapping the lit count again does not clear it: give a reset of your own when 0 must be reachable by touch

The tap writes a literal with valueFloatChange, not valueFloatExpressionChange: both the Java parser and json2rc read a literal number in the latter's value as a float id (Java writes id 0, json2rc the float's low bits), so a literal there sets nothing
Mono draws lit stars in onSurface and empty ones in the outline grey whatever colours the call passes, so the state stays readable on a 1-bit display

Accessibility: each tappable star is labelled "1 star", "2 stars"... (a textMerge of a literal textFromFloat and " stars"; the first a plain text); the row carries the label (contentDescription) and the rating as its state (stateDescription): "3 of 5 stars", "4.5 of 5 stars", "Not rated" at 0. The state is cut by textSubtext from "Not rated" + whole part + ".5" (when fract(value) > .25) + " of max stars", in the global section of a 0-size canvas in a box before the row (the parsers bind the name in document order), so it follows a bound variable at run time. About 300 B for a first call (later calls share the texts) plus about 45 B per tappable star; the named text ops keep it from compiling to a pattern
The spoken half follows fract(value) > .25 while the drawn star rounds at .25/.75 too, but a 4.8 is spoken "4.5" while five stars are lit: hosts should write whole or half values

Tappable stars under 48 dp sit in a 48 dp touch target each (padding (48 - size) / 2 inside the clickable canvas) with no gap between targets, so a 24 dp row is 240 dp wide; read-only stars keep size and the size / 12 gap

onRate and onClick actions run after the star's valueFloatChange: a hostNamedAction carrying "@rating" (valueType float) sends the star just tapped. Write ONE action name for all stars (onRate, or one onClick hostNamedAction): json2rc declares the shared name once; the reference JSON parser does not support value-carrying actions

components.name: row-list
components.title: RowList
components.prompt: Make a titled list of rows from data that adapts to any window, with rows that can show a value, a switch or a slider.
teaches: Give rows as named objects: {"title": "London", "subtitle": "+7 h", "value": "10:30"}. A few hundred bytes replace a hand-written adaptive list

It decides by itself: rows at 48 dp that scroll, or with readOnly rows down to 18 dp that say "+N more" if some still do not fit; columns when wide; under 180 dp a cell keeps its title and one other thing
A trailing control sits in trail; trailWidth gives a Slider its share of the row

snippets.note: a three-row list: the whole call
control rows, card surface, inside a screen
a control's value is a document variable

check.describe: Cities: three divided rows, each a name, an offset and a time. Settings: a card row with a slider and one with a switch. No text touches other text at any size. Cities is readOnly, so its rows shrink at 160x160 and 320x160 and all stay; Settings rows keep 48 dp and scroll when cut.

components.summary: A titled list of uniform rows from data, each a title with an optional subtitle, value, leading mark, trailing control, bar under it and details to tap open; or a check list. It adapts to any window: tappable rows keep 48 dp and the list scrolls; read-only rows shrink to 18 dp and say "+N more" if some still do not fit. Columns when wide, an empty state when the app sends no rows.
pitfalls: Status or data list: add readOnly: true, always, or every row keeps 48 dp and a 160 dp window scrolls through 2 or 3 of 6. With it rows go down to 18 dp, too small a target, so no onClick, details or Switch in those rows. The expander cannot read the rows' fields into a global height, so this one is yours to say

Without readOnly the list scrolls under its header when rows do not fit, and the header says "8 items". There is no scroll bar. With readOnly it cannot scroll: it says "+5 more", in the header or, when short, under the rows. That does not say which: put what matters first, or a down service in last place can be the one left out

Narrow, by the cell's width and never by content: under 180 dp (a window under about 190) a row keeps its title and one other thing: the trail if it has one, else the value, else the lead. The chevron goes too. If the lead is a status, say it in the trail, value or label as well

A trail or a value takes its own width, up to half the row, and pushes the title, which ellipsizes. A text longer than that is cut, not hidden, and the check reports it: shorten it or move it to the subtitle

Rows from the app: put "@name1" in the fields, declare the strings as exported root variables (with distinct initial values, or they share one text id) and give count: "@n". rows is the capacity: the app can show fewer, never more than were written, and each written row costs 300 B to 1 KB

A row with details, detailsNode or onClick is one tappable item. Its label is built live from title, subtitle and value; the label field replaces it, and says a status only an icon shows. Other rows are read text by text; a trailing Switch or Slider is its own target: give it a label. To flip a switch from the whole row, give the row onClick and draw the state without a tap of its own
below goes while the row is under 24 dp plus belowHeight, so it must not be the only place that says something. Details are detailsHeight tall (two lines of text): raise it for a taller detailsNode
embedded: pass the width and height of the box it gets, because a visibility cannot read its parent's size. A surface or padding of your own around the list needs width passed too
A Slider in a trail is safe without onRelease. With onRelease it misbehaves in a scrolling list, and tappable rows scroll: use readOnly rows or leave onRelease out

components.name: sankey
components.title: Sankey
components.prompt: Show where this week's visitors came from (search, social, direct) and what they did (browsed, signed up, left) as a flow diagram whose ribbons follow the numbers the app sends, with something moving along them.
teaches: {"Sankey": {"flows": "@visits", "sources": [...], "uses": [...]}}: one exported row-major float array, sources x uses
The host replaces the array and every ribbon, bar and total eases to the new layout in 1.2 s, still stacked
Particles run at a speed proportional to their ribbon's flow; particles: false makes the diagram idle
It fills the box it is given: label columns, gaps and text scale with it

snippets.note: the call
the flows, row-major
exported: the host sets new flows
eased on every data change
each ribbon is one closed pathExpression
source-to-use gradient per ribbon

visits.meaning: thousands of visits, channel x outcome

check.describe: Title 'Where visitors went'; Search 7.9k, Social 4.6k, Direct 2.8k on the left, Browsed 7.4k, Signed up 4.1k, Left 3.8k on the right; gradient ribbons from each channel's colour to each outcome's, dots along them. New data (0.5 s): half-way to the new layout; settled (2.5 s): Social the largest source. Mono: outlined ribbons, ink bars, no dots.

components.summary: A two-column Sankey diagram, sources on the left flowing into uses on the right: ribbon widths from a row-major float array the host can replace, every ribbon, bar and label easing to new data together, optional particles flowing along each ribbon at a speed proportional to its flow, and each node labelled with its total.
pitfalls: flows is the NAME of a float array with sources x uses values, row-major; a wrong length draws missing ribbons as zero rather than failing
Totals are the sums of the ribbons: a node that both receives and sends (a battery charging and discharging) needs to be split into a source and a use
The particle speed reads the raw host value while the ribbons ease, so on a data change the dots jump once to their new phase
Each ribbon costs about 400 B and each particle loop about 300 B: 3 x 4 nodes is about 9 KB with particles, 6 KB without; keep the node count small
Particles use continuousSec(): the diagram repaints every frame while shown; particles: false makes it idle once the data settles
Mono: ribbons become outlines over a faint fill and the bars ink; node colours carry no meaning there, the labels do

components.name: scaledamount
components.title: ScaledAmount
components.prompt: Show an amount scaled by a factor as one readable value with its unit: fractions like 1½ cups, decimals like 2.5 L, rounded to 5 g, or rounded up to whole rolls; spoken as one item.
teaches: Give amount and factor; format fraction or number; unit and unitOne for singular and plural
With name the call is a whole row: the amount is one spoken item, after the name

snippets.note: a fraction row with singular and plural
amount times factor
spoken unit differs from the shown one

scale.meaning: what the amounts are multiplied by

check.describe: At scale 1: 1½ cups, ½ cup, ⅓ cup, 2.5 L, 0.25 kg, 245 g, 3 rolls, 1¾ tsp. At scale 2: 3 cups, 1 cup, ⅔ cup, 5 L, 0.5 kg, 495 g, 5 rolls, 3½ tsp.

components.summary: A base amount times a factor, shown as one readable value with its unit and spoken as one item: 1½ cups, ¾ L, 2.5 kg, 250 g, 3 rolls. Fractions snap to eighths and thirds; numbers round to a step or up to what you can buy. With `name` it is a whole row: the name on the left, the amount on the right.
pitfalls: The amount is one spoken item. A row with name is two, the name then the amount: the format has no way to merge a row that cannot be tapped (only a click merges, and semantics here adds a node, it does not replace the texts inside)

One text node, so nothing is measured apart: the value, its fraction and its unit move together when the value changes. In a row, neighbours move as it widens; give it the end of the row (name does this)
amount and factor are live, unit and name are literal text: a unit the host sends as a text variable is not supported

Fractions never snap to nothing: any value above 0 shows at least the smallest fraction. A value of exactly 0 reads 0. The same in number format: 0.04 at 1 decimal reads 0.1, so nothing needed ever reads as none
⅓ and ⅔ win only when closer than the nearest eighth: 0.3 reads ⅓, 0.28 reads ¼
Fraction glyphs come from the device's font. ⅛ ⅜ ⅝ ⅞ ⅓ ⅔ are outside Latin-1, so a device font without them shows a fallback. Use format number with decimals where that matters
Fixed amounts that never scale (a pinch) are not this: use a plain text or KeyValueRow
Do not use for currency or large figures: see CompactNumber. Whole part up to 999,999
Each call is always expanded, never a template. A number call costs about 500 B, a fraction call 1 to 1.5 KB. In a long list use number, or fractions quarters

A factor bound to a Slider's variable does not follow the drag, only the release: the live value is a touch value read after the Slider in the tree. For a live result use a Stepper, or read the Slider's value in a text placed after it

components.name: scene-3d
components.title: Scene3D: a 3D scene from named primitives
components.prompt: Show a ring-stacking toy in 3D that I can drag to turn, without working out a camera or any matrices.
teaches: Name the parts, not the maths: {"Scene3D": {"objects": [{"shape": "box", "size": [w, h, d], "at": [x, y, z], "color": "@colors.primary"}]}}; units are yours, Y up, Z toward the viewer
The server frames the scene: one camera distance expression of the window's aspect keeps every part in view at every angle the drag can reach, phone to landscape to a 2x2 widget
orbit (default on) is two touchExpressions on touchX() / touchY(); autorotate adds the clock; assemble flies the parts in by step and back out, eased with smooth_step
Mono: every part is a background-filled mesh with its quad edges drawn in onSurface (hidden lines removed), and nothing moves unless dragged
3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): this plays in the C++ and TypeScript players
pitfalls: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the scene plays in the C++ and TypeScript players (rc2image, the web player, the MCP renders) and the Java JSON parser drops its 3D operations. Don't use it for a screen that must play on Android today

Scene3D fills the window: the players draw 3D into a window-sized buffer placed at the canvas's top left, so a 3D canvas in a column or beside other content is drawn off-centre and spills out of its box. Put titles and captions in the overlay slot and reserve their height with insetTop / insetBottom (dp), so the scene is framed below them
Name parts, don't compute views: give sizes and centres in the object's own units; the camera, the tilt and spin and the framing are the server's. Don't add your own camera3D or matrix3D around it

Each part is drawn in software every frame: keep to about 30 parts (each costs about 60 to 90 B and a few ms per frame on a phone-sized window); spheres, cylinders and tori are 100 to 600 triangles each, boxes 12

Colours are theme colours lit by the preset: a light part on the light background (surface on background) loses its edges; use outline, surfaceHigh, muted, primary and secondary for bodies, or style outlined
autorotate and assemble repaint every frame for as long as the scene is shown (continuousSec); leave both off for a still product shot that only moves when dragged
A plane is single-sided (seen from above); for a panel seen from both sides use a thin box
The overlay slot is the place for a title: the scene itself always fills the window

snippets.note: the whole call: parts with shape, size, position and theme colour; camera, lights and framing are the server's
cylinders, tori and a sphere: each a meshPrimitive3D, shared by parts of the same shape and size
orbit is on by default: drag left-right to spin, up-down to tilt

check.describe: A ring-stacking toy seen from slightly above and to the right: a grey base disc, a dark rod, four rings (red, orange, green, blue) getting smaller upward and a purple ball on top, title 'Ring stacker' at the top left. Mono: white hidden-line wireframes on black. Turned: seen from higher, from the other side.

components.java_difference: 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming): the Java JSON parser does not know camera3D, lights3D, matrix3D, meshPrimitive3D or drawMesh3D; plays in the C++ and TypeScript players
components.summary: A 3D scene from named primitives (box, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, plane), each with a size, a position, a rotation and a theme colour: the server frames them with a camera that fits every angle at any window shape, lights them, and adds drag to orbit, autorotate and an assembly animation. No 3D maths for the caller. Plays in the C++ and TypeScript players; 3D support has not landed in androidx yet (coming).

components.name: seekbar
components.title: Seek bar
components.prompt: A seek bar for a player: position and duration from the app, elapsed and remaining times, drag to seek, then it follows the app again.
teaches: position and duration are host variables; the bar shows the position until a finger is down, and after
onSeek runs on release with the position already written, so the action carries the value

snippets.note: the call
the call
the call
the call
the call
the call
the call

check.describe: Two bars. First at 37% with 1:23 at the left and -2:22 at the right. Second purple at 11% with 1:02:03 and -8:27:57 and a muted buffered part. A drag moves the thumb and the times; after the release the bar follows pos again.

components.summary: A media seek bar the app drives: it follows the host's position, a drag takes over while the finger is down (the thumb grows, the times follow the finger), the release sends a host action and writes the position, and it follows the host again. Elapsed and remaining times below, m:ss or h:mm:ss by the duration, --:-- with no thumb and no touch when the duration is 0.
pitfalls: Write the position as seconds, about once a second: the bar shows what the app last sent and does not advance by itself, so a document with no host stands still

How following works: a drag state (onTouchDown 1, onTouchUp and onTouchCancel 0) chooses what the thumb shows, the host position or the touch value. A plain Slider has no such state: its touch value wins from the first drag on
Keep the position variable exported and do not compute it: the release writes it. For an expression, keep a variable and give the expression to the app
The track is inset 8 dp from the box on both sides so the thumb fits, and the times are inset to match: to line it up with something at margin m, give the bar m - 8
Do not put it in a scrolling container: touch-up actions fire for the wrong child inside a scroll (U80). A player screen does not scroll; shrink the cover instead

The elapsed and remaining texts are computed inside the canvas (after the touch expression, the only place the live touch value exists), so the times stay with the finger. They are in the tree after the track: nothing placed BEFORE this call can read them

components.name: skeleton
components.title: Skeleton
components.prompt: A loading placeholder for a list row (an avatar circle and two text lines) above an image block, with a shimmer sweeping across.
teaches: shape picks a line (text), a circle (an avatar, `height` wide) or a block (an image); width omitted fills the space
The shimmer is a linear gradient whose ends move with continuousSec(), so every skeleton sweeps on the same clock
Mono draws a static grey outline: no gradient and no motion

snippets.note: circle, 40 dp: an avatar placeholder
a 150 dp text line
a block filling the width; the band crosses it every 1.5 s

check.describe: A grey avatar circle and two grey text lines, and a wide grey block below, each with a lighter band (darker in dark) crossing it; render-later, 0.5 s on, has every band further right. Resized, the block and the lines' column keep their sizes but the block fills the width: 200 dp narrow, 450 dp wide.

components.summary: A loading placeholder: a grey line, circle or block with a light band sweeping across it every 1.5 s, standing in for text, an avatar or an image until the content arrives.
pitfalls: The sweep is a linear gradient (colour, highlight, colour) whose ends move with continuousSec(): the document repaints every frame while a skeleton is on screen, so replace it with the content as soon as it arrives
Its colours are theme colours inside the gradient (the parsers mark them as colour ids), so light and dark both work: surfaceHigh with a surface band (lighter in light, darker in dark)
Each skeleton sweeps on its own width but on the same clock, so a column of them shimmers together; the band is 240 dp wide whatever the shape
Mono has no motion and no gradient: a 1.5 dp grey outline of the shape

components.name: sleep-stages
components.title: SleepStages
components.prompt: Show last night's sleep as stages over time from an array the app sends.
teaches: One exported float array of stage indexes draws the night; runs join into rounded bars by themselves
minutes per lane come from the host, shown as 1h 12m and spoken

snippets.note: bound to the exported array
one loop per stage over the array
rounded bars on one canvas
one spoken summary

night.meaning: one value per equal slice: 0 awake, 1 REM, 2 light, 3 deep

check.describe: Four lanes labelled with minutes, coloured bars joined by thin steps, 23:10 and 06:50 below. 160: no labels, no gutter.

components.summary: A hypnogram: sleep stages over the night from one host array, one lane per stage, runs as rounded bars joined by thin steps, with stage names and times at the left and the start and end times under it. The lanes read in mono; labels drop in small boxes.
pitfalls: stages is the name of a float array, not a JSON list. A value outside the lanes draws nothing in that slice

An expression cannot total an array by stage, so minutes per lane comes from the host: pass them in lanes, or leave them out and the left column has names only. If the host sends both, they cannot disagree only if it derives them from the same data
It fills the box it is given: use a sized or weighted parent. Under 200 wide the left column drops; under 96 tall the times drop
Each stage has its own loop over the array, so cost at run time grows with slices x stages: 30-minute or 5-minute slices are fine, one per minute is not
Stage colours are theme colours; in mono the lane alone says the stage, which is what a hypnogram is

components.name: slider
components.title: Slider
components.prompt: A volume slider from 0 to 100 that shows its value, and a brightness slider with its own state.
teaches: Bind value to a document variable ({"value": "@volume", "max": 100}) to preset it and read it below the slider; omitted (or a number), the slider keeps its own state, starting there
showValue prints the live value at the end of the track (decimals sets the digits after the point)
Dragging is a touchExpression in absolute mode: the thumb jumps under the finger and the value stays clamped to min..max

snippets.note: bound to @volume (40), 0 to 100, value shown
showValue: textFromFloat of the live value
unbound: its own state, starting at 0.7; label is the accessibility label

check.describe: Volume shows a blue track 40% full with 40 at its end; Brightness is an amber track 70% full. A tap on a track jumps the thumb under the finger and a drag follows it, clamped at the ends (checked in the Java reference: a tap at x=150 on Volume gives 50). Resized, the tracks fill the width: at 200 dp they are shorter with the thumbs at the same fractions, at 450 dp longer.

components.summary: A horizontal slider: dragging or tapping the track sets its variable between min and max (the thumb jumps under the finger and follows it); it can show the value at its end, and onRelease runs actions with the released level (a host action sends it to the app). A screen reader hears the label and the current value.
pitfalls: The drag is a touchExpression in absolute mode (touchMode 6) named after the bound variable: from the slider on, "@volume" is the touch value (it starts at the variable's own value and keeps where the finger left it). LIVE values derived from it (a preview, a time, a status) must be computed AFTER the slider in the tree: a text or canvas expression placed after it, or a tree `variable` command after it. The document's own resources.variables and computed resources.colors that read the bound name are moved there automatically by the expander (right after the slider), unless something reads them before the slider: then they update only on release (with onRelease), and expand_components warns

onRelease: the canvas carries an empty onTouchDown (without it Java never registers the canvas, so a drag runs no onTouchUp at all) and one onTouchUp list, in order (Java runs separate onTouchUp modifiers last first). The list recomputes the level from where the finger lifted into the bound variable, because modifiers come BEFORE the touchExpression and "@volume" there still names the bound (resources) variable; then it runs the caller's actions, which read it. A plain tap ends the same way. About 120 B per call with one host action
touchX() is in document coordinates, so the slider measures where it sits (componentValue POS_ROOT_X into a local) and subtracts it: it works anywhere in the layout, scrolled or padded

Inside a scrolling container, onRelease also fires for the last child wherever the finger lifts, and the dragged slider's own may not fire: the reference player does this, so a device does too. There, tell the app from the exported value instead of onRelease, or keep the slider outside the scroll. A plain Slider without onRelease is safe in a scroll
step snaps the value (round to multiples of step from min) in the drag and on release; without it the value is continuous (the notch stop modes need touchSpec, which the Java parser ignores, U8)
It fills the width it is given (fillMaxWidth) and is 40 dp tall: in a row, give it a weight or a box with a width
No easing on the value: the thumb follows the finger frame for frame (an animated value would trail it). In mono it looks the same, a thin grey track, a thicker white active part and a smaller thumb

Accessibility: a transparent box over the track carries the label and the value as its state (textFromFloat of the live value: `decimals` digits, at least 2 when max - min is under 1.5, so 0..1 reads 0.7, not 0; stateText replaces it, e.g. a time "16:30"). It comes after the canvas because only from the touchExpression on does the name read the dragged value; it takes no touch, so the drag still works. No role (the JSON semantics has no role key), and no adjust actions: a screen reader announces the value but cannot step it. About 85 B per call
A slider does not follow the app after a drag: the touch value wins from the first drag on. For a position the app keeps writing (a seek bar) use SeekBar

components.name: sparkline
components.title: Sparkline
components.prompt: Show weekly visits as a small trend line next to its label, and a temperature series as a sparkline across the card.
teaches: Call {"Sparkline": {"values": "@visits"}} with the name of a float array in resources.floatArrays; export it and the host can replace the series
A fixed width × height (120 × 32 by default) sits beside a label; fill: true takes the space of a sized or weighted parent
The line spans the data's min..max and ends on a dot at the latest value

snippets.note: bound to the exported float array visits
one drawLine per pair of values, in a loop over the array
fill: true, scaled with componentWidth()/componentHeight()

check.describe: A blue rising line 120 × 32 beside 'Visits, 8 weeks', ending on a dot at 84; under it a violet line across the full width, peaking at the ninth value. With variables {visits: [84, 69, 73, 58, 61, 48, 55, 42]} the small line falls instead. At 234 and 540 dp wide the lower line stretches to the width; the small one stays 120 dp.

components.summary: A word-sized trend line: one stroke through every value of a float array, scaled from its min to its max to fill the canvas, with a dot on the latest value.
pitfalls: values is the name of a float array ("@visits" declared in resources.floatArrays), not a JSON list: the chart reads it with arrayGet in a loop, so a host that sets the exported array redraws it with no new document, and any length works
The line is a loop of drawLine segments (round caps hide the joins), not an SVG path: a path string costs about 4 KB in Java

The y range is the data's own min..max, so a flat series sits on the bottom edge and small changes look large; that is what a sparkline is for, but don't put one next to a bar chart and expect the same scale
Everything scales with componentWidth() and componentHeight(), read inline in each coordinate; it keeps the call out of pattern mode, which is fine for a chart drawn once or twice

components.name: split-flap
components.title: SplitFlap
components.prompt: Show text on split-flap tiles, like an old station departure board, that flip through the letters to the new text when it changes.
teaches: Smallest call {"SplitFlap": {"text": "DEPARTURES"}}: one tile per letter, flipping in from blank when the document appears

Changing text: code is the drum index per tile, an expression of i (tile) and r (row); prev is the index before; since restarts at the change. The tiles step forward through the drum like a real flap unit
A clock: code and prev from timeInHr()/timeInMin() of now and the previous minute, since continuousSec() % 60, so it flips in the first second of each minute
Word flaps: a drum of equal-width words (glyphWidth 8) and align start; rows: a float array of codes read as arrayGet(@cities, row * 8 + i), cycling every 6 s
Mono: outlined tiles showing the final glyph, the split cut as a gap, no flipping

snippets.note: the smallest call: a fixed word
a clock that flips on the minute
a word flap cycling every 4 s
three rows from a float array
each tile's halves are clipped to either side of the split
the flap is a half tile scaled toward the split

inputs.clock: the clock row reads timeInHr/timeInMin; everything else animationTime

check.describe: Light and dark: DEPARTURES on ten tiles; a five-tile clock still reading 08:41 at 0.3 s into 08:42 (its tiles flip from 0.34 s on; mono shows 08:42 at once); a DELAYED word flap (ON TIME at the intro); three rows of destinations (PORTO, MADRID, SEVILLA after the first move, some tiles still flipping). Mono dark and light: the same tiles as outlines with the final glyphs. intro (0.35 s): most tiles blank or on early letters. flip (6.5 s): the rows caught mid-flip. Landscape 640x400: the same column, scrolled to the top (the rows below the fold).

components.summary: Split-flap tiles (a Solari board): a fixed number of tiles that, when the text they show changes, flip forward through a drum of characters (or whole words) to the new ones, with the mechanical half-flap fold, rippling across the tiles and down the rows.
pitfalls: A real flap only moves forward: from prev to code it shows every glyph in between, (code - prev) mod the drum size steps at speed flaps a second, so a long jump takes longer. Order the drum so frequent changes are short
SplitFlap does not remember what it showed: when code changes, pass the old index as prev and restart since (a board cycling through an array passes the previous entry and animationTime() % period)
Inside code, prev and tileX, i is the tile and r the row (the component's loop indices); don't name document variables i or r
The tiles redraw every frame while since moves (about 25 draw operations a tile): a 26 x 9 board is around 6 000 operations a frame. Fine for a board or a kiosk, heavy for a small widget
Mono shows code as it is, with no flip and no shading: outlined tiles and a split cut through them

components.name: stat-tile
components.title: StatTile
components.prompt: Show two KPI tiles side by side, revenue and latency, each with its value, unit and change since last week.
teaches: Call {"StatTile": {"label": "Revenue", "value": "@revenue", "unit": "k€", "delta": "@revenueDelta"}}: the delta's sign picks the chevron and the colour
Set invert true for metrics where lower is better (latency, churn, cost): a rise turns red
The tile fills its width: two side by side are weighted boxes with a fixed 12 dp spacer box between them

snippets.note: value and delta bound to exported variables
a rounded surface tile
invert: a positive delta is drawn red

check.describe: Two tiles: Revenue 128 k€ with a green up chevron and 4.2, Latency 182 ms with a red up chevron and 12.0; revenueDelta -3 turns the first one red with a down chevron. The tiles are weighted halves: at 234 dp they narrow and the numbers and units still fit, at 540 dp each tile widens.

components.summary: A KPI tile filling its width: a label, a live value with its unit, and an optional delta with an up chevron when positive, a down chevron otherwise, green when the change is good and red when it is bad (invert for metrics where lower is better).
pitfalls: Colour by sign without colour expressions: the delta is drawn twice, green with paint alpha @up and red with 1 - @up, where the local up is step(@delta, 0); step(x, edge) is x > edge, so 0 counts as a fall
Numbers use textFromFloat flags 5: the default flags pad the integer part with spaces (whole 6 puts four spaces before 42), which shifts the value right
The tile fills its width: put two side by side as weighted boxes with a fixed spacer box between them (weights ignore spacedBy)
abs(@delta) and step(@delta, 0) are locals, each computed once for the call (a literal delta folds both to numbers)

The label is one line with an ellipsis, so a narrow tile shortens it with … instead of wrapping it into the value. The value and unit do not shrink: a 128 k€ tile needs about 100 dp, so below that use one tile per row

components.name: StepExplainer
components.title: StepExplainer: a whole step-by-step explanation in one call
components.prompt: Explain how something works, step by step, with a drawing, a caption and Back and Next.
teaches: Call {"StepExplainer": {"step": "@at", "eased": "@e", "steps": [{"title", "text", "short"}...], "slots": {"visual": [DRAWING]}}}: only the subject is yours. Vary it with progress (dots, bar, numbers, timeline, scrub), controls (buttons, play, none), buttons (icons, labels), layout, frame, tappable, loop; compute it with count and captionIndex; ask first with the input slot
Light, dark and mono come from the same call; the demo's check.renders sweep the sizes

snippets.note: the call and its slots
the call and its slots
the call and its slots

check.describe: A ring a third full in the visual area, Step 1 of 3 and dots, Boil and its text, a dim Back and Next.

components.summary: A complete step-by-step explainer screen: you give the steps' captions and a drawing, it brings the background, the visual above or beside the caption, the progress (dots, segmented bar, numbers, vertical timeline or a scrubbed track), Back / Next / play, and shortens itself to fit any size. The step count and captions may be computed at run time, so it can end early.
pitfalls: Do not name your variable step: a document variable called step hides the step() function in every expression, and this component uses it. Bind "@at" or "@stage"

Three ways to read the current step. Non-autoplay: bind a resources variable to `step` and read it anywhere, in resources.variables too; that is what computed explainers need. Autoplay: `step` stays where play started, so read `shown` / `eased`, tree variables, inside the visual slot only

A tree variable (`shown`, `eased`) must not go through a param that a component turns into a local: TextChoice's index reads item 0 silently and a resources expression does not convert. Read it directly in canvas or modifier expressions, or as an arg of CellRow

Computed steps: `count` is a runtime expression ("@total + 2") and `captionIndex` picks an entry of `steps`, so `steps` lists caption STATES, each of whose title and text may be a textMerge over live values. Back, Next and the progress follow the count; it needs bar or dots (not tappable, timeline or scrub, which are one node per listed step)

loop: `eased` runs back through the middle steps when the cycle wraps. A drawing for a cycle should read `shown` and fade each stage with its own {"value": "1 - min(1, abs(@now - k))", "anim": 0.5} (CMP-28)

scrub: a touch variable cannot switch layout, so while the finger is down the title and thumb follow it (drawn on the canvas) and the wrapped caption is hidden; on release the step snaps to the nearest stop and the caption returns. `eased` follows the finger with 0.2 s of lag

controls none with scrub leaves a screen reader unable to change the step: the format has no adjust action. Keep the buttons unless the host offers another way. timeline rows and tappable stops are labelled clicks and are fine

Sizes: usable from about 160 x 120 dp (icons) and 200 wide with labels. Stacked, the caption's full text needs captionLines lines plus 90 dp left for the visual, else the short form, else the title only; the visual takes what remains and can be about 40 dp at 160 x 160, so a visual must scale itself from componentWidth() / componentHeight(). Set captionLines to the longest text's line count at the narrowest width: a longer text is cut
width and height default to the window. Inside your own padding or beside other content, pass them, or the sizes come out too large

input with inputWhen start shows on the first step only and replaces the short text when room is short; with no room it hides and the current value is used. Put anything that changes the computation there: nothing can then change under a running explanation
Mono: no play button, no motion; the drawing snaps, and the visual is the caller's: use theme colours and $if theme.mono in an inline component

The whole frame is expanded, never a pattern (texts, U7). About 6.9 KB for dots and icon buttons with four steps, plus about 90 B per text. Against that: play +830 B, numbers +310, bar +60, tappable +230, panel +210, title +180, scrub +360, input +310, timeline +1800, controls none -850; mono is about 700 B less

components.name: stepper
components.title: Stepper
components.prompt: Add a plus / minus control to pick the number of guests, from 1 to 8.
teaches: Call {"Stepper": {"value": "@guests", "min": 1, "max": 8, "label": "guests"}}: − and + change the bound variable by `step`, clamped to [min, max]
For fractional steps give step and decimals together (step 0.5, decimals 1), and bind a variable that starts at the value you want
`label` names the quantity for accessibility ("Decrease guests"); show the same words as text beside the stepper
